name: Peter Thiel
domain: startups and monopoly, competition, secrets and contrarian thinking, definite optimism, technology stagnation, founders and power laws in venture, and the future
sourcesLabel: lectures, interviews, essays and class notes

sources.title: Competition is for Losers: why startups should aim for monopoly and avoid competition
sources.originalTitle: Competition is for Losers with Peter Thiel (How to Start a Startup 2014: 5)
sources.summary: Thiel argues value creation (X) and value capture (Y%) are independent, so industries like airlines create huge value but capture almost none. There are only two kinds of businesses, perfectly competitive ones and monopolies, and people lie about which they are. Start in a small market, build durable monopoly traits, and aim to be the last mover.

principles.text: A valuable company both creates value and captures a share of it; the two variables are independent.
principles.quote: X and Y are completely independent variables and so um X can be very Big Y can be very small

principles.text: There are really just two kinds of businesses, perfect competition and monopoly, with almost nothing in between.
principles.quote: there are exactly two kinds of businesses in this world there are businesses that are perfectly competitive and there are businesses that are monopolies

principles.text: Monopolists and competitors both lie about their markets: monopolists claim a huge market, competitors claim a tiny unique one.
principles.quote: the basic lie you tell as a non-m monopoly is that we're in a very small Market the basic lie you tell as a monopoly is that the market you're in is much bigger than it looks

principles.text: Start with a very small market, dominate it, then expand in concentric circles; going after a giant market on day one is a mistake.
principles.quote: you start with a really small market and you take over that whole market and then uh and then over time you find ways to expand that market in in concentric circles

principles.text: Monopolies come from proprietary tech roughly 10x better, network effects, economies of scale and branding.
principles.quote: you want to have a technology that's an order of magnitude better than the next best thing

principles.text: Aim to be the last mover, since most of a company's value lies far in the future; durability matters more than growth rate.
principles.quote: we always overvalue in Silicon Valley is growth rates and we undervalue durability

sources.title: Peter Thiel on stagnation, institutional failure, growth and violence (The Portal #001)
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel on "The Portal", Episode #001: "An Era of Stagnation & Universal Institutional Failure."
sources.summary: Thiel argues that science and technology have stagnated in the world of atoms since about 1970, with computers as the narrow exception, and that institutions built on expected growth have turned pathological. He ties growth to political stability, and discusses preference falsification, political correctness, Girardian mimesis and violence.

principles.text: Real progress has been confined to bits; the world of atoms has stagnated for about 50 years.
principles.quote: I sort date the this era of stagnate relative stagnation and slowed progress all the way back to the 1970 so I think it's been close to half a century

principles.text: Tech progress has been a narrow cone around computers: a Star Trek computer but no warp drive or transporter.
principles.quote: we've been working on the Star Trek computer in Silicon Valley but we don't have anything else from Star Trek

principles.text: Extreme specialization makes progress hard to verify, so people should be suspicious of experts policing themselves.
principles.quote: the specialization should make you suspicious it should because it's gotten harder to evaluate what's going on then it's presumably gotten easier for people to lie and to exaggerate

principles.text: Institutions built on expected growth go pathological when growth stops; honest resets would have been healthier but incentives prevented them.
principles.quote: there's probably a way the universities could function if they did not grow you know you'd be honest most people in PhD programs don't become professors

principles.text: Stable parliamentary democracy depends on growth; without it, expect more violence or a deformed, pacified society.
principles.quote: I think a world without growth is either going to be a much more violent or a much more deformed world

principles.text: Automation is oversold; productivity data say it isn't happening, so get growth before redistribution or UBI.
principles.quote: if automation is not happening and you do ubi then you just you know blow up the economy

sources.title: Peter Thiel on stagnation, AI, Mars and the Antichrist: Interesting Times with Ross Douthat
sources.originalTitle: A.I., Mars and Immortality: Are We Dreaming Big Enough? | Interesting Times with Ross Douthat
sources.summary: Thiel reaffirms the stagnation thesis, calls AI the only broad progress left and roughly internet-scale, and argues we need far more risk-taking. He frames existential-risk talk as the route to a one-world "peace and safety" Antichrist, and explains why Mars stopped being enough for Musk.

principles.text: Stagnation is real but not absolute: the velocity of progress slowed after 1970, outside the world of bits.
principles.quote: I still broadly believe in the stagnation thesis. Uh it it was it was never an absolute thesis.

principles.text: Without a path back to growth, a middle class society unravels, since the middle class is defined by expecting kids to do better.
principles.quote: I would define the middle class as the people who expect their kids to do better than themselves. And when that expectation collapses we no longer have a middle class society.

principles.text: AI is roughly internet-scale: more than a nothing burger, less than total transformation, and an unhealthily unbalanced sole bright spot.
principles.quote: it's more than a nothing burger and it's less than the total transformation of our society. So my my placeholder is that it's roughly on the scale of the internet in the late '9s

principles.text: Raw intelligence may not be the gating factor; society's tolerance for heterodox smart people may be.
principles.quote: it's not the individually smart person, but it's how this fits into our society. Do we tolerate heterodox smart people?

principles.text: The default political answer to existential risk is one-world governance, which may be the worse singularity; the Antichrist rises by preaching Armageddon.
principles.quote: The way the antichrist would take over the world is you talk about Armageddon non-stop. You talk about existential risk non-stop.

principles.text: We should take far more risk in science and medicine; Alzheimer's has made no progress in decades.
principles.quote: We should take a lot more risk. We should be doing a lot more.

sources.title: Thiel on Zero to One: monopoly, tech stagnation, the education bubble, and agency
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel on markets, technology, and education
sources.summary: In this 2014 Hoover interview on Zero to One, Thiel argues that all happy companies are unique monopolies while unhappy ones are alike in competition. He says the developed world has stagnated outside of information technology, blames regulation and an overpriced education bubble, and urges planning and agency over fatalistic optimism or pessimism.

principles.text: Happy companies are each unique monopolies; unhappy ones are alike because they never escape competition.
principles.quote: all happy companies are different because they found something unique that gives them a mission and that also gives them a monopoly of sorts

principles.text: Competition destroys profits; aim for a monopoly rather than being the fourth or tenth player in a crowded market.
principles.quote: you don't want to be the fourth online pet food company you don't want to be the 10th thinf film solar panel company

principles.text: Brand is the weakest form of monopoly; prefer technological advantage or vertical integration, which are more robust.
principles.quote: brand is a is a is a very is is the weakest form of Monopoly

principles.text: Sales and distribution matter as much as product, and engineers systematically underestimate them.
principles.quote: it's typically the component that people under the mo underestimate the most especially if they're coming from an engineering background

principles.text: The developed world is in stagnation outside computers; technology has been redefined narrowly as IT, with atoms held back by regulation.
principles.quote: we have this uh we have this very powerful but very narrow cone of progress around the world of bits not so much in the world of atoms

principles.text: Extreme optimism and extreme pessimism both breed inertia; treat the future as open-ended and up to human agency.
principles.quote: extreme optimism and extreme pessimism both lead to uh sort of this inertia and so I think uh I think it's always a healthier attitude to think of it as somewhat open-ended

sources.title: Peter Thiel on Rogan: AI passes the Turing test, tech stagnation, and why nuclear stalled
sources.originalTitle: Joe Rogan Experience #2190 - Peter Thiel
sources.summary: Thiel argues progress for 50 years has been confined to computers while the physical world of energy, transport and medicine stagnated. He frames passing the Turing test as an internet-scale event, compares AI today to 1999, and offers a contrarian reading of nuclear and science stagnation as a response to dystopian, dual-use technology.

principles.text: Progress since the 1970s has been narrow: big in bits and computers, relatively stagnant in the physical world of atoms.
principles.quote: we've been not absolute stagnation we in an era of relative stagnation where there has been um very limited progress in the world of atoms the world of physical things

principles.text: When technology came to mean only computers, that shows how lopsided progress has become.
principles.quote: when you talk about technology you're normally just talking about information technology technology has been reduced to meaning computers and that tells you that the structure of progress has been weird

principles.text: Passing the Turing test is the real AI milestone, more important than the AGI debate.
principles.quote: maybe the AGI question is less important than passing the touring test

principles.text: AI today looks like the internet in 1999: clearly huge, but a long path to apply it.
principles.quote: maybe Ai and 2023 24 is like it's like the internet in 1999 where on one level it's clear the internet's going to be big and get very a lot bigger

principles.text: A key cause of stagnation is that much science and tech carried a dystopian, apocalyptic dimension, as with dual-use nuclear.
principles.quote: an awful lot of Science and Technology had this dystopian or apocalyptic uh Dimension

principles.text: Talking about problems can substitute for acting on them, so ask whether talk leads to action.
principles.quote: talk is often a substitute for action

sources.title: Thiel at Stanford 2014: competition is for losers, secrets, and developing the developed world
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel Returns to Stanford to Share Business Tips from "Zero to One"
sources.summary: Thiel presents three contrarian answers from Zero to One: all happy companies are different, secrets still exist outside closed fields like geography, and the 21st century needs vertical technology progress rather than copying (globalization). The Q&A covers monopoly policy, themes, the Thiel Fellowship, education, and libertarianism.

principles.text: Capitalism and competition are opposites; the goal is to build a monopoly, since perfect competition competes away all profits.
principles.quote: most people believe that capitalism and competition are synonyms um and I believe capitalism and competition are antonyms

principles.text: All happy companies are different; unhappy ones are alike because they fail to escape the sameness of competition.
principles.quote: all happy companies are different they're doing something unique all unhappy companies are alike because they fail to escape the essential sameness of competition

principles.text: Monopolists downplay their monopoly by claiming a huge market; competitors claim a tiny fictional niche to look unique.
principles.quote: the people who don't have monopolies pretend to have them the people who have monopolies pretend not to have them

principles.text: Great businesses rest on secrets: things hard but possible to learn that others don't yet know. Fields like geography are closed, but many others are not.
principles.quote: a secret or um sort of some idiosyncratic body of knowledge is often at the core of all these great businesses

principles.text: Progress is either globalization (1 to n, copying) or technology (0 to 1). The 'developed' label implicitly accepts stagnation, which we should reject.
principles.quote: how do we go about uh developing the so-called developed world

principles.text: Monopolies are bad when static rent collectors, but good when they invent something new like the iPhone.
principles.quote: a good Monopoly is one that actually has invented something new

sources.title: Thiel vs Schmidt (2012): Technology Stagnation, Outlawed Atoms, and Why Big Tech Hoards Cash
sources.originalTitle: Eric Schmidt and Peter Thiel - Fortune Debate, 2012
sources.summary: In a 2012 Fortune debate, Thiel argues that the developed world has had 40 years of stagnation: flat median wages, no energy progress, and innovation confined to bits because regulation outlawed the world of atoms. He pushes back on Schmidt's techno-optimism, and says cash-hoarding tech giants show they have run out of ideas.

principles.text: Technological progress has stalled in the developed world; flat median wages since 1973 are the key data point.
principles.quote: if you look at the US say in the last 40 years 1973 to today um median wages have been stagnant

principles.text: Progress has been narrow: relentless in computers, near zero in energy, with computers only offsetting the energy failure.
principles.quote: we've had incremental but Relentless progress on the computer side and on the other hand uh we've had basically no progress on energy

principles.text: Regulation has outlawed innovation in atoms, leaving only bits (and finance) free to advance.
principles.quote: We've basically outlawed everything having to do with the world of stuff and the only thing you're allowed to do is in the world of bits

principles.text: Emerging markets only need to copy what works; real innovation is only needed in the developed world.
principles.quote: in places like China India Africa Latin America there's zero need for Innovation all they need to do is copy things that work

principles.text: Big tech sitting on huge cash piles signals a lack of ideas; a true tech company would reinvest in the future.
principles.quote: if we're living in an accelerating technological world and you have 0% interest rates in the background you should be able to invest all of your money in um in uh in things that will return it many times over

principles.text: Thiel cares about vertical, intensive growth (doing fundamentally new things), not just globalization.
principles.quote: what I'm interested in is vertical growth intensive growth doing fundamentally new things

sources.title: Peter Thiel on tech stagnation, the AI wave, small markets and why courage is scarce
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel: The Stagnation of Science and the AI Revolution
sources.summary: Thiel argues science and atoms-based technology have been stagnant for about 50 years, with only computers progressing, and that LLMs are a breakthrough on par with the internet. He explains why a narrow initial market beats a huge one, why wokeness distracts from stagnation, and why existential risks deserve attention without shutting everything down.

principles.text: Start with a small, tight market you can dominate, then expand; a huge TAM usually means heavy competition.
principles.quote: I always think the uh you know the best uh Tam narratives are ones where you have a you know have some sort of tight fairly narrow Tam for the initial market and then there's some kind of expansion capability

principles.text: In investing, you must know what others don't understand about a company, or you are the sucker at the table.
principles.quote: when you're investing in a company it's always what do we understand about this that other investors do not understand and um if you don't know the answer to the question then you're the sucker

principles.text: Technology and science outside the world of bits have been stagnant for about 50 years.
principles.quote: we've had this uh broad uh stagnation in technology and science for for something on the order of 50 years

principles.text: LLMs and ChatGPT are a real AI breakthrough, comparable to the internet itself.
principles.quote: it's probably a breakthrough that's you know I would I would rank as on par with the internet itself

principles.text: Stagnation is mainly cultural: we became too risk averse and bureaucratized, living in a soft lockdown for decades.
principles.quote: it's not that nature um has run out of things for us but that there's something that's changed in our culture we've become too risk averse

principles.text: Society fears what could go wrong from acting but not enough what goes wrong if we do nothing.
principles.quote: we're scared of the things that can go wrong but we're not scared enough of the things that will go wrong if we do nothing

sources.title: Peter Thiel on the Triumph of the Counter-Elites: liberalism's collapse, stagnation, and a WWI-style future war
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel on the Triumph of the Counter-Elites
sources.summary: Post-election 2024 conversation with Barry Weiss. Thiel argues the Democratic "machine" and identity politics collapsed, that stagnation made "Make America Great Again" a powerful pessimistic frame, and that science and institutions have grown dogmatic. He also covers trade, nuclear proliferation, and why a future world war would look more like WWI.

principles.text: Naming stagnation openly is the first step to progress; MAGA worked because it admitted the country is no longer great.
principles.quote: make America great again was the most pessimistic slogan that any any presidential candidate certainly any Republican candidate had had in a 100 years

principles.text: The internet's social impact outran its economic impact; a world of bits is no substitute for progress in atoms.
principles.quote: this world of bits you know is not really a substitute for the world of atams

principles.text: Science began as a two-front fight against both dogmatism and skepticism; today's establishment has lost that balance toward dogmatism.
principles.quote: it started as a two-front war against both excessive dogmatism and excessive skepticism

principles.text: Contrarian view on war: we always fight the last war, so a future world war would more likely resemble WWI than WWII.
principles.quote: my you know contrarian intuition where I'd be maybe 60 70% focused on World War I and 30 or 40% on World War II is I think we always have a recency bias we're always fighting the last war

principles.text: Ideological free traders make bad negotiators because they assume nothing needs to be negotiated; tariffs are a game-theory lever.
principles.quote: I never want free trade treaties negotiated by people who are ideological free Traders because they will always think they don't need to negotiate anything

principles.text: Nuclear proliferation is destabilizing because a nuclear shield lets a power back proxies with impunity, igniting regional wars.
principles.quote: every time a country got a nuclear weapon we got a regional War

sources.title: Peter Thiel: AI as the end of stagnation, Europe's decline, and thinking for yourself
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel: The AI Crisis, Europe’s Decline & the Battle for America
sources.outlet: MDMEETS - Essential Talks with Mathias Döpfner and 2 more
sources.summary: Thiel restates the stagnation thesis (progress in bits, not atoms since the 1970s) and argues AI may be bigger than the internet and could reaccelerate growth. He warns that a zero-growth "safe" world is not peaceful, that societies fray when progress stops, and that Europe is far behind in AI and in building new scalable companies. He also covers contrarianism as independent thinking, generalism, and longevity.

principles.text: Since the 1970s progress came in bits (software, internet) but not in atoms; this broad slowdown is the stagnation thesis.
principles.quote: there had been progress in the world of bits, you know, computers, internet, mobile internet, software, but not so much in the world of atoms.

principles.text: AI may be bigger than the internet and could reaccelerate growth, which retroactively proves the stagnation thesis.
principles.quote: perhaps um AI um is bigger than the internet and is at least has the potential to to reacelerate growth with all the good and bad things that that that come with that.

principles.text: Stagnation makes politics zero-sum and polarized, since every winner needs a loser.
principles.quote: when there's a loser for every winner it becomes this very zero- sum game and uh you you sort of get a a much you know much worse society

principles.text: The alternative to AI is not a peaceful zero-growth society; when intergenerational progress breaks, society deranges.
principles.quote: there's a picture that people implicitly have that the alternative to um AI let's say a zero growth world where there's no progress at all will somehow be this you know peaceful social democratic society. And I don't I don't think that's true.

principles.text: Moralizing is overdone; the real problem is badness (incompetence), not evil. Evil at least gets things done.
principles.quote: 99% of the businesses, companies, people, political leaders, business leaders are totally incompetent. Uh that's that's the problem we should actually be talking about.

principles.text: Contrarianism is not reflexively negating consensus; the real goal is thinking for yourself, which generalists are suited for.
principles.quote: I think the real goal is always to try to think for oneself.

sources.title: Scale and its limits: Thiel's 2019 Wriston Lecture on AI, China, and quality over quantity
sources.originalTitle: 2019 Wriston Lecture: Peter Thiel
sources.summary: Thiel argues the central question for institutions and nations is what scales well. Ideas, innovation, science and elite universities scale badly, while finance and the internet scale easily. He frames AI as centralizing and communist versus crypto as libertarian, says Silicon Valley's real failing is insufficient innovation, and urges the US to shift from quantity to quality in its rivalry with China.

principles.text: Scale can bring qualitative change, but not always a good one; each technology's scaling effects must be examined.
principles.quote: there are things where you scale things up and you get a qualitative difference but the quality difference isn't always a good one and we need to think very hard about which ones play out in in which ways

principles.text: Ideas and innovation do not scale well; as tech grows bigger, innovation slows.
principles.quote: one of the things that does not scale terribly well at all are ideas and innovation

principles.text: Technologies carry ideological valence: crypto is libertarian, while AI centralizes and is communist.
principles.quote: if we say that crypto is libertarian why can't we say that AI is communist and and at least have the sort of alternate account of scale

principles.text: Silicon Valley's real failing is not innovating enough, which explains the political pushback against it.
principles.quote: what we should be paying attention to is that people in Silicon Valley have not been doing enough

principles.text: Growth is slow because sectors immune to automation became a bigger share of the economy, not because automation is running away; the ubiquitous job-loss story is a distraction.
principles.quote: the simple reason it slowed is because the sectors that were immune to automation have just become bigger and bigger parts of parts of this economy

principles.text: Against China, the US should shift from quantity to quality: intensive growth, IP protection, fewer but real scientists.
principles.quote: perhaps we have to shift a little bit from quantity from simply scaling in size to to quality

sources.title: Thiel on PayPal's survival, Elon Musk, bubbles, and why monopoly beats commodity
sources.originalTitle: a16z Podcast | The (Definite) Optimism of Peter Thiel
sources.summary: Thiel recounts PayPal's chaotic 2000-2002 survival, explains why Tesla and SpaceX worked (weak competition plus vertical coordination), and argues the real bubble sits in government bonds, not venture-backed tech. He also says startups should seek monopoly, that many incumbents are bets against technology, and that founders keep monopolies innovating.

principles.text: Avoid intensely competitive businesses; pick industries where incumbents are weak or something is off.
principles.quote: opening a restaurant is my sort of the Paradigm example of an intensely competitive and really bad business idea

principles.text: Aim for monopoly through real differentiation, then keep innovating on top of it.
principles.quote: the goal should be to do something super Innovative where you're so differentiated that you get a monopoly

principles.text: Monopolies decay by default; founders running the company keep the pressure to innovate.
principles.quote: as long as the founders run the companies um there's normally enough pressure to keep doing things

principles.text: Many large incumbents are bets against technological innovation, not technology companies.
principles.quote: there's a whole set of companies in the NASDAQ 100 that are actually bets against technological innovation

principles.text: Tesla and SpaceX won through complex coordination of many pieces, not a single breakthrough.
principles.quote: I think both Tesla and SpaceX were stories that involved complex coordination where you needed to get a lot of different pieces uh to fit together in just the right way

principles.text: Believing building a great company is easy or impossible are both wrong and both kill effort.
principles.quote: both the lesson that it's easy and the lesson that it's impossible are sort of equally wrong

sources.title: The Education of a Libertarian: why Thiel left politics for technology as the escape from it
sources.originalTitle: The Education of a Libertarian
sources.summary: Thiel explains how two decades of political activism led him to conclude that democratic politics cannot deliver freedom. He argues libertarians should instead build new spaces for freedom through technology (cyberspace, outer space, seasteading), framing the future as a deadly race between politics and technology.

principles.text: Freedom is the goal; politics is a poor means of reaching it, so escape politics rather than win it.
principles.quote: In our time, the great task for libertarians is to find an escape from politics in all its forms

principles.text: The future is a deadly race between politics and technology, and the outcome is open.
principles.quote: A better metaphor is that we are in a deadly race between politics and technology.

principles.text: Reject technological determinism: technology has no will of its own and does not automatically bring freedom.
principles.quote: we must resist the temptation of technological utopianism — the notion that technology has a momentum or will of its own

principles.text: In technology, unlike politics, individuals can still be decisive, so a single builder can change the world.
principles.quote: The fate of our world may depend on the effort of a single person who builds or propagates the machinery of freedom

principles.text: Escaping requires a new, untried process that opens a new frontier, so focus on technologies that create new space for freedom.
principles.quote: I suspect that the mode for escape must involve some sort of new and hitherto untried process that leads us to some undiscovered country

principles.text: Be realistic about timelines: rocket technology has barely advanced since the 1960s, so space frontiers are far off.
principles.quote: Rocket technologies have seen only modest advances since the 1960s, so that outer space still remains almost impossibly far away.

sources.title: The End of the Future: Why technological progress stalled outside computers, and what it means
sources.originalTitle: The End of the Future
sources.summary: Thiel argues that progress outside information technology has stalled since roughly 1970. The evidence he cites is slower travel, energy failure, stagnant real wages and weak biotech. He says finance, politics and culture all assumed easy progress, and that a real future needs concrete ideas and serious engineering again.

principles.text: Progress is not automatic; it is rare, and the West's rise need not continue.
principles.quote: Progress is neither automatic nor mechanistic; it is rare.

principles.text: Computers boomed while energy, travel and medicine slowed; the two roughly canceled out, leaving wages flat.
principles.quote: To a first approximation, the progress in computers and the failure in energy appear to have roughly canceled each other out.

principles.text: Stagnant real wages since 1973 are the key economic evidence that tech progress has been narrow, not broad.
principles.quote: The single most important economic development in recent times has been the broad stagnation of real wages and incomes since 1973

principles.text: Leverage cannot substitute for real technological progress; bubbles came from assuming easy growth.
principles.quote: Leverage is not a substitute for scientific progress.

principles.text: Modern democratic politics assumes growth; without it, politics turns zero-sum and nasty.
principles.quote: in a world without growth, we can expect a loser for every winner.

principles.text: The honest first step is to admit we are in a desert, not an enchanted forest.
principles.quote: The first and the hardest step is to see that we now find ourselves in a desert, and not in an enchanted forest.

sources.title: The Optimistic Thought Experiment: why there are no good bets against globalization
sources.originalTitle: The Optimistic Thought Experiment
sources.summary: Thiel's 2008 essay argues that apocalyptic risk is real, so investors should ask what must happen for the world not to end. His answer: the only workable path is good globalization. Every major bubble has been a miscalculation about globalization's pace. He separates real bets (China, technology, hedge funds) from their financial lookalikes in quotation marks.

principles.text: Anti-globalization is incoherent; the real alternative to good globalization is world war, so investors must bet on globalization.
principles.quote: Because there would be no winners in a new world war, every path away from globalization will end in catastrophe. Thus, in spite of the many uncertainties surrounding the costs and benefits of a more globally integrated world, investors have no choice but to bet on globalization.

principles.text: Since the world is far from equilibrium, the future will be much more or much less globalist than the present.
principles.quote: Since we are very far from any stable equilibrium, the future is likely to be much more or much less globalist than the present.

principles.text: Almost every financial bubble has been a miscalculation about the probability and pace of successful globalization.
principles.quote: Almost every financial bubble has involved nothing more nor less than a serious miscalculation about the true probability of successful globalization.

principles.text: The Great Boom is either not a bubble at all or the final and greatest bubble in history; the outcome is binary.
principles.quote: Because there is not much time left, the Great Boom, taken as a whole, either is not a bubble at all, or it is the final and greatest bubble in history.

principles.text: Technology entrepreneurs should return to hard, important problems like security against destructive technologies; easy engineering problems rarely hold long-term value.
principles.quote: The solutions to hard engineering problems are not necessarily valuable, but it is unusual for the solutions to easy engineering problems to have much value in the long term.

principles.text: Internet businesses are global and winner-take-all, making venture returns an extreme distribution.
principles.quote: Internet businesses are essentially global, and for this reason successful internet businesses involve a winner-take-all dynamic that is extreme even by the standards of the technology industry.

sources.title: Against Edenism: Why technological progress is a moral necessity, not a Faustian trap
sources.originalTitle: Against Edenism
sources.summary: Thiel argues that returning to an Edenic, pastoral existence is impossible for a planet of 10 billion, and that technological acceleration is the only alternative to a zero-sum, Malthusian world. He traces postmodern distrust of technology to the 1970s collapse of post-Manhattan Project optimism, and frames Judeo-Western optimism as the belief that chaos and chance can be mastered.

principles.text: A planet of 10 billion people cannot return to Eden; it requires highly advanced science and technology.
principles.quote: the necessary precondition for the planetary civilization of 10 billion people that will be Earth in the twenty-second century is a highly advanced level of science and technology.

principles.text: Without technological progress the world turns zero-sum, threatening capitalism and democracy.
principles.quote: Technology means doing more with less. In the absence of technological progress, we end up with a zero-sum world, in which there must be a loser for every winner.

principles.text: Opposing technological acceleration is not ethically or politically neutral; the alternatives have real costs.
principles.quote: we should never forget that the alternatives to technological acceleration are far from ethically or politically neutral.

principles.text: We are far from a technological cornucopia; stalled progress shows up as scarcity and stagnant living standards.
principles.quote: We are much further from this technological cornucopia than we would like to believe.

principles.text: Culture broadly distrusts technology, and Hollywood both reflects and creates that consensus.
principles.quote: Just about every science-fiction movie of the past quarter century portrays science and technology as a trap that humanity is building for itself.

principles.text: The loss of hope in the future dates to the 1970s, when science was put on a short leash of incremental grant-writing.
principles.quote: Whether by chance or design, scientists were placed on a short leash and made to spend their time writing grant applications for modest extensions of existing paradigms.

sources.title: Back to the Future: Why decadence is stagnation and how to escape it
sources.originalTitle: Back to the Future
sources.summary: Thiel reviews Ross Douthat's The Decadent Society and argues technological stagnation is the central problem of the 2020s, with a science enterprise nobody can honestly measure. A renaissance needs goals that are both ambitious and achievable within our solar system, and the path to radical progress begins with moderation, not extreme optimism or pessimism.

principles.text: Stagnation is real: outside faster computers, the physical world looks much like 1969.
principles.quote: As for the world outside of MIT’s PR materials, it appears much the same as it was in 1969—just with faster computers and uglier cars.

principles.text: No one can credibly measure the health of science, so claims of rapid progress deserve suspicion.
principles.quote: We are forced to wonder whether things are as rosy as the grant writers insist.

principles.text: Stagnation is not a law of nature; reject 'spend more' and 'low-hanging fruit is gone' excuses.
principles.quote: He maintains that more of the same is not enough, and stagnation is not a fate imposed by the universe.

principles.text: A renaissance needs goals that are both ambitious and achievable, so aim within the solar system, not at distant stars.
principles.quote: To be motivational, a goal must be both ambitious and achievable.

principles.text: Technologists should chase hard-but-possible goals; statesmen should dismantle institutions that falsely claim to pursue them.
principles.quote: For technologists, that means pursuing goals that are difficult but possible: cures for cancer and Alzheimer’s; compact nuclear reactors and fusion power.

principles.text: Extreme optimism and fatalistic pessimism both lead to apathy; agency requires a moderate, definite view.
principles.quote: Extreme optimism and fatalistic pessimism may seem to be stark opposites, but they both end in apathy.

sources.title: Developing the Developed World: Monopoly, contrarian questions, and technology vs globalization
sources.originalTitle: Developing the Developed World
sources.summary: Thiel's 2015 Independent Institute talk argues capitalism and competition are opposites, that startups should aim for monopoly by starting in a small market, and that courage is scarcer than genius. He separates globalization (1 to n) from technology (0 to 1) and says "developed world" implies nothing new will happen.

principles.text: Every moment in business happens once, so copying past founders teaches little; ask contrarian questions instead.
principles.quote: The next Mark Zuckerberg will not be starting a social networking company, the next Larry Page will not start a search engine, the next Bill Gates will not be starting an operating system.

principles.text: Good contrarian answers are uncomfortable truths; courage is scarcer than genius.
principles.quote: I think we live in this world where courage is in far shorter supply than genius

principles.text: Capitalism and competition are opposites: perfect competition competes away all profit, so aim for monopoly.
principles.quote: I believe capitalism and competition are antonyms. I believe the capitalist is someone who’s in the business of accumulating capital. A world of perfect competition is a world where all the profits are competed away.

principles.text: Monopolists understate their monopoly and competitors understate their competition, hiding the real difference.
principles.quote: So the apparent difference, I think, is always much smaller than the real difference.

principles.text: Start in a very small market and dominate it, then expand; in a giant market you are a minnow in a vast ocean.
principles.quote: you always want to start with very small markets. You don’t want to start with incredibly big markets.

principles.text: Globalization copies what works (1 to n); technology does new things (0 to 1). The two are not synonyms.
principles.quote: I describe it as copying things that work, going from one to ten, horizontal, extensive growth. I describe technology as vertical, intensive growth, doing new things, going from zero to one.

sources.title: The Straussian Moment: Thiel on 9/11, Schmitt, Strauss and Girard
sources.originalTitle: The Straussian Moment
sources.summary: Thiel's 2007 essay argues 9/11 exposed the Enlightenment's blind spot: it abandoned the question of human nature and treats people as rational economic actors. He works through Locke, Schmitt, Strauss and Girard to ask how the West can survive without destroying itself, and ends with a Christian call to favor peace in close cases.

principles.text: Economic models of human nature fail to explain people who seek glory for God or country.
principles.quote: If humans can be approximated as rational economic actors (and, ultimately, even Adam Smith and Karl Marx agree on this point), then those who seek glory in the name of God or country appear odd

principles.text: Wealth transfers did not contain violence; the 9/11 attackers were wealthy and educated, not the global poor.
principles.quote: the perpetrators were upper-middle-class Saudi Arabians, often with college degrees and with great expectations.

principles.text: The Enlightenment avoided questions about human nature because they were too dangerous to debate.
principles.quote: The question of human nature was abandoned because it is too perilous a question to debate.

principles.text: Understanding a system requires asking how it was founded and where it could be threatened, not just how it runs.
principles.quote: An account of politics that speaks only of the smooth functioning of the machinery of government is incomplete

principles.text: There is more room for action than formal institutions suggest, because power operates outside the legal system's domains.
principles.quote: there are more possibilities for action than first appear, precisely because there are more domains than those enumerated by the conventional legal or juridical system.

principles.text: Choose your enemies carefully, because conflict makes you resemble them.
principles.quote: one must choose one’s enemies well, for one will soon be just like them.

sources.title: Thiel on Stagnation: Atoms vs. Bits, Human Agency, Conformity, and Contrarian Questions
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel on Stagnation, Innovation, and What Not To Name Your Company
sources.summary: In a 2015 conversation with Tyler Cowen, Thiel argues stagnation is concentrated in the regulated world of atoms rather than bits, and that the future depends on human agency, not automatic progress. He also covers conformity, the contrarian interview question, why to start good businesses rather than more of them, and why extreme optimism and extreme pessimism both lead to doing nothing.

principles.text: Stagnation is a story of atoms, not bits: software was unregulated while physical-world innovation was regulated.
principles.quote: we lived in a world in which bits were unregulated and atoms were regulated.

principles.text: The future is not automatic; progress requires human agency, and sitting back to watch it unfold guarantees stagnation.
principles.quote: If you take a nap, if you encourage everybody else to take a nap, then the great stagnation is never going to end.

principles.text: Ask for something true that few people agree with you on; it is hard to answer because the real answers are things you don't want to say.
principles.quote: “Tell me something that’s true that very few people agree with you on.” This is a terrific interview question.

principles.text: The goal is more good businesses and fewer bad ones, not more startups in the abstract.
principles.quote: My view is we should be starting more good businesses and fewer bad ones. Not more businesses in the abstract, not more start-ups in the abstract.

principles.text: Extreme optimism and extreme pessimism both converge on inaction; a healthy attitude is mild in either direction.
principles.quote: extreme pessimism tells you there’s no point in doing anything. Extreme optimism tells you there is no need to do anything. They converge on doing nothing.

principles.text: Prefer substance over status: chasing respectability softens your edges and dilutes what you say.
principles.quote: I would always be long substance, short status.

sources.title: Peter Thiel on Political Theology: why muddling through fails and one-world totalitarianism is an existential risk
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel on Political Theology
sources.summary: In a live Miami conversation with Tyler Cowen, Thiel argues for big-picture political theology over hyper-specialization and rejects both Calvinism and "muddling through" as distrust of human agency. He names a one-world totalitarian state as an existential risk on par with nukes or AI, and frames AI and tech around centralization and stagnation.

principles.text: A one-world totalitarian government belongs on the list of existential risks, alongside nukes, bio and AI.
principles.quote: In my mind, one other existential risk is a one-world totalitarian government. I find that at least as scary as the others.

principles.text: Assuming we can muddle through is a setup for disaster; it signals people have stopped thinking.
principles.quote: Whenever people think you can just muddle through, you’re probably set up for some kind of disaster.

principles.text: Muddling through, Calvinism and rationalism share one flaw: distrust of human agency and choice.
principles.quote: It’s a distrust in human agency, a distrust in human thought, a distrust in our ability to make choices.

principles.text: Fear of apocalypse can be the route to totalitarianism: the Antichrist rises by selling Armageddon stories.
principles.quote: the Antichrist comes to power by constantly talking about Armageddon and constantly telling us scary millenarian stories.

principles.text: Narrowing "technology" to just IT, then just AI, is itself a symptom of centralizing stagnation.
principles.quote: And it seems to be that this narrowing is a manifestation of the centralizing stagnation that we should be trying to get out of.

principles.text: Whether technology centralizes or decentralizes is not predetermined; people choose its direction.
principles.quote: My intuition is these things are not absolutely written in stone, and it’s up to us to work on making the technologies, having to push it one way or the other.

sources.title: Peter Thiel on PayPal, contrarian truths, stagnation and the education bubble (Kristol, 2014)
sources.originalTitle: Conversations with Bill Kristol: Peter Thiel
sources.summary: In a 2014 conversation with Bill Kristol, Thiel explains how PayPal won through compounding growth, a fraud-fighting technology edge and a long-term plan, and why good businesses avoid competition. He argues conformity drives bubbles, technological stagnation is largely cultural and regulatory, and higher education is a zero-sum tournament bubble.

principles.text: Good businesses avoid excess competition; they are unique, not one of many doing the same thing.
principles.quote: Well, I do think in business one of the critical things is that you don’t want excess competition.

principles.text: Being the last mover matters more than being first, and durability is as important as growth.
principles.quote: In practice, I think it’s more important to be the last mover than the first mover.

principles.text: Most business value lies far in the future, so durability is at least as important as growth.
principles.quote: Durability is at least as important as growth.

principles.text: Have a definite long-term plan rather than iterating randomly; a bad plan beats no plan.
principles.quote: When I was a chess player, an intermediate level chess lesson was always that a bad plan was better than no plan.

principles.text: Ask for a truth few people agree with; conventional thinking is powerful and bubbles come from deferring to others.
principles.quote: Tell me something that’s true that very few people agree with you on.

principles.text: Stagnation outside computing stems largely from regulation and culture; fight it rather than accept or deny it.
principles.quote: I tend to think that we live in a world where bits are quite unregulated, atoms are very heavily regulated.

sources.title: Peter Thiel on Tim Ferriss: Capitalism vs. competition, no trends, and the case against lottery-ticket investing
sources.originalTitle: The Tim Ferriss Show Episode 28: Peter Thiel
sources.summary: In a Q&A-style interview promoting Zero to One, Thiel argues technology matters more than globalization, that capitalism and competition are opposites, and that missions beat trends. He criticizes failure-worship, spray-and-pray investing and the education bubble, and urges starting sooner and thinking for yourself.

principles.text: Capitalism and competition are opposites: competition competes profits away, monopolies accumulate capital.
principles.quote: whereas most people believe that capitalism and competition are synonyms, I think they’re antonyms.

principles.text: Avoid trends; pursue a unique mission that no one else is solving.
principles.quote: You, generally, never want to be part of a popular trend.

principles.text: Failure is overrated: it is over-determined, teaches little, and is a tragedy, not an educational imperative.
principles.quote: I think failure is massively overrated.

principles.text: Don't treat startups as lottery tickets; concentrate and build high conviction before writing any check.
principles.quote: I think the anti lottery ticket approach is to try to be concentrated

principles.text: Never let convention substitute for truth; everyone listening to everyone about the future is the definition of a bubble.
principles.quote: we never want to let a convention be a short cut for truth.

principles.text: Stagnation is the risk, but low-hanging fruit remains and many secrets are left to unlock; innovate or face a bleak century.
principles.quote: There are many great secrets left to be unlocked in the decades ahead.

sources.title: CS183 Class 1: The Challenge of the Future, 0 to 1 vs 1 to n, and why startups
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 1 Notes Essay: The Challenge of the Future
sources.summary: Blake Masters' close-to-verbatim notes of Thiel's first Stanford CS183 lecture. Thiel frames progress as horizontal copying (globalization) versus vertical new things (technology), argues startups are the unit that can do 0 to 1, and offers a contrarian question for finding what to build.

principles.text: Progress is horizontal copying (1 to n, globalization) or vertical new things (0 to 1, technology). Society over-focuses on the former.
principles.quote: Horizontal or extensive progress basically means copying things that work. In one word, it means simply “globalization.”

principles.text: Technology is going from 0 to 1, and it matters even for globalization because 1 to n hits resource limits.
principles.quote: Vertical or intensive progress, by contrast, means doing new things. The single word for this is “technology.” Intensive progress involves going from 0 to 1

principles.text: Innovation can't really be taught: education is imitation, and 0 to 1 is not a statistical problem.
principles.quote: Teaching vertical progress or innovation is almost a contradiction in terms. Education is fundamentally about going from 1 to *n*.

principles.text: Going from 0 to 1 must favor determinism over indeterminism; you need a plan, like Apollo, not a probabilistic spaceship.
principles.quote: Going from 0 to 1 always has to favor determinism over indeterminism.

principles.text: Companies are small for a reason: coordination costs rise with size, so startups can lower internal costs and get things done.
principles.quote: Startups are important because they are small; if the size and complexity of a business is something like the square of the number of people in it, then startups are in a unique position to lower interpersonal or internal costs and thus to get stuff done.

principles.text: Ask the contrarian question: what important truth do very few people agree with you on? Business version: what valuable company is nobody building?
principles.quote: What important truth do very few people agree with you on?

sources.title: Party Like It's 1999? Thiel on the dot-com mania, its lessons, and why "bubble" is the wrong question
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 2 Notes Essay: Party Like it’s 1999?
sources.summary: Thiel's Class 2 lecture recounts the 1990s and the PayPal mania, then argues the world and Silicon Valley drew mostly wrong lessons from the crash (incrementalism, lean, no talk of the future). Bubble and anti-bubble thinking are both social thinking; the truly contrarian move is to think for yourself about what is valuable.

principles.text: Bubbles need widespread, intense belief that is false; today people don't believe in anything, so 'bubble' is the wrong frame.
principles.quote: Bubbles arise when there is (1) widespread, intense belief that’s (2) not true. But people don’t really believe in anything in our society anymore.

principles.text: Bubble and anti-bubble thinking both assume truth is social; merely opposing the herd is equally random.
principles.quote: But if the herd isn’t thinking at all, being contrarian—doing the opposite of the herd—is just as random and useless.

principles.text: The truly contrarian thing is to think for yourself and ask what is valuable, company by company.
principles.quote: To understand businesses and startups in 2012, you have to do the *truly* contrarian thing: you have to think for yourself.

principles.text: The post-crash lessons (anything the market teaches in reaction) were driven by emotion and mostly wrong; people were right about many things in the 90s.
principles.quote: When base emotions are driving, analysis becomes untrustworthy.

principles.text: Silicon Valley's retreat (incrementalism, lean, no advertising, no BD, never discuss the future) was largely an overreaction to be questioned as ironclad rules.
principles.quote: We should be open to idea that some or much of the retreat—however necessary it was generally—was overreaction.

principles.text: Tech looked like the one good bet in the late 90s partly by elimination, since everything else seemed to be failing; proof by contradiction is risky.
principles.quote: There’s still a sense in which tech worked, or was seen as working, because nothing else did, or was.

sources.title: Value Systems: why durable monopolies, not perfect competition, capture value (CS183 Class 3)
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 3 Notes Essay: Value Systems
sources.summary: Great companies create value, last, and capture some of it. Thiel argues tech value sits far in the future, so durability (being the last mover) matters most. Perfect competition destroys profit; monopoly is the real default for valuable businesses, and bigger markets are not better.

principles.text: Great companies create value, last, and capture some of the value they create.
principles.quote: Great companies do three things. First, they create value. Second, they are lasting or permanent in a meaningful way. Finally, they capture at least some of the value they create.

principles.text: Tech value lies far in the future; think 10-15 years, not quarters.
principles.quote: Tech and other high growth companies are different. At first, most of them *lose* money.

principles.text: Being the last mover beats being the first mover; durability is what matters.
principles.quote: More important than being the first mover is being the last mover. You have to be durable.

principles.text: Under perfect competition no one makes money; the really valuable businesses are monopolies.
principles.quote: The really valuable businesses are monopoly businesses. They are the last movers who create value that can be sustained over time instead of being eroded away by competitive forces.

principles.text: Have a decisive advantage over the next best alternative, because even a few competitors make a brutal dynamic.
principles.quote: The takeaway is that it's absolutely critical to have some decisive advantage over the next best service.

principles.text: Bigger market is not better; find or make a small market, excel, and own it.
principles.quote: Maybe it's much better to find or make a small market, excel, and own it.

sources.title: The Last Mover Advantage: why monopoly beats competition and how to build one (CS183 Class 4)
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 4 Notes Essay: The Last Mover Advantage
sources.summary: Thiel argues capitalism and perfect competition are opposites: competition erases profit, monopoly creates it. He shows how companies lie about their markets, names four ways to own one (brand, scale, network effects, proprietary tech), and says to start small, dominate, expand, and enter a frontier late enough to make the last great development.

principles.text: Capitalism and perfect competition are opposites: capitalism accumulates capital, perfect competition destroys profit.
principles.quote: A better one frames capitalism and perfect competition as opposites; capitalism is about the accumulation of capital, whereas the world of perfect competition is one in which you can’t make any money.

principles.text: Intense competition makes people confuse what is hard with what is valuable.
principles.quote: But too often in the race to compete, we learn to confuse what is hard with what is valuable.

principles.text: Monopolies pretend to be in huge markets; non-monopolies shrink theirs. Reality is more binary than rhetoric suggests.
principles.quote: Non-monopolies always narrow their market. Monopolies insist they’re in a huge market.

principles.text: Own a market via brand, scale cost advantages, network effects, or proprietary technology.
principles.quote: For a company to own its market, it must have some combination of brand, scale cost advantages, network effects, or proprietary technology.

principles.text: Build in three steps: find a new market, monopolize it, then expand the monopoly over time. Start small and specific.
principles.quote: find a small target market, become the best in the world at serving it, take over immediately adjacent markets, widen the aperture of what you’re doing, and capture more and more.

principles.text: Enter a tech frontier late enough to make the last great development, after which the drawbridge goes up.
principles.quote: You want to enter the field when you can make the last great development, after which the drawbridge goes up and you have permanent capture.

sources.title: CS183 Class 5: The Mechanics of Mafia - culture, hiring, and avoiding zero-sum fights
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 5 Notes Essay: The Mechanics of Mafia
sources.summary: Thiel's Stanford lecture on company culture: aim between consultant-nihilism and cult, pick non-competitive fields but bring fighters, and surface disagreements fast because companies mostly die from internal blowups. Guest views from Cohen and Levchin on hiring are excluded except Thiel's own PayPal anecdotes and remarks.

principles.text: Good culture sits between consultant-nihilism and cultish dogmatism; if you must lean, lean toward cult.
principles.quote: Picture a 1-dimensional axis from consultant-nihilism to cultish dogmatism. You want to be somewhere in the middle of that spectrum. To the extent you gravitate towards an extreme, you probably want to be closer to being a cult than being an army of consultants.

principles.text: Capitalism and competition are antonyms; do intense work on something others aren't doing.
principles.quote: Generally speaking, capitalism and competition are better seen as antonyms than as synonyms. To compete isn't what you should set out to do.

principles.text: Avoid fights, but where unavoidable, fight and win. Pick a monopoly environment and bring fighters to protect the nerds.
principles.quote: You want to pick an environment where you don’t have to fight. But you should bring along some good fighters to protect your non zero-sum people and mission, just in case.

principles.text: Surface disagreements quickly; lockstep agreement is a red flag, and companies usually die from internal dynamics before external competition.
principles.quote: Everyone moving together in lockstep is a big red flag, not an ideal.

principles.text: Firing is like war: avoid it, but waiting until everyone sees someone should go is far too late.
principles.quote: But the flipside is that if you wait until it’s obvious to everyone that someone should be fired, it’s far too late.

principles.text: Don't compete with Google on money; sell engineers a compelling monopoly narrative.
principles.quote: The first step is to avoid competing on purely financial terms, where you’re likely to lose. You have to have that compelling monopoly narrative that we discussed last week.

sources.title: Thiel's Law: why a startup messed up at its foundation cannot be fixed (CS183 Class 6)
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 6 Notes Essay: Thiel’s Law
sources.summary: Blake Masters' near-verbatim notes of Thiel's Stanford lecture on founding moments, alignment, equity, vesting and fundraising. Thiel argues early structural mistakes are permanent, founder alignment dominates everything, and equity-heavy, low-salary cultures keep everyone rowing in the same direction.

principles.text: Thiel's law: a startup messed up at its foundation cannot be fixed, so get the early structure as right as possible.
principles.quote: A startup messed up at its foundation cannot be fixed

principles.text: Founders should stay in charge while the company is doing 0 to 1; once it shifts to 1 to n, executives should execute.
principles.quote: Founders should arguably stay in charge as long as the paradigm remains 0 to 1. Once the paradigm shifts to 1 to n, the founding is over. At that point, executives should execute.

principles.text: Founder alignment dominates every other factor; fissures in the founding team get amplified and can blow up the company.
principles.quote: If the founders are in sync, you can move on to the rest of the equation. But if they aren’t, it will blow up the company. Nothing will work.

principles.text: Keep CEO pay low: the lower a venture-backed CEO's salary, the better the company tends to do, because it forces focus on equity.
principles.quote: Experience has shown that there is great predictive power in a venture-backed CEO’s salary: the lower it is, the better the company tends to do.

principles.text: Everyone must be fully on the bus or off it; part-timers and consultants misalign incentives.
principles.quote: Being part-time, holding other jobs, or bringing on consultants or advisors to do important work are big red flags because those arrangements are very misaligning.

principles.text: Never have a down round; it makes everyone angry and effectively breaks the company.
principles.quote: Companies are essentially broken the day they have a down round.

sources.title: Follow the Money: Power laws in venture, concentration, and why exponentials are misjudged (CS183 Class 7)
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 7 Notes Essay: Follow The Money
sources.summary: Thiel explains that venture returns follow a power law: the best investment can equal the rest of a fund combined. That implies concentrated portfolios, treating up rounds differently from flat rounds, and judging a company's place on the curve over mere equity percentage. Guests Botha and Graham add views not attributed to Thiel.

principles.text: Venture returns are wildly skewed by a power law, not a bad/mediocre/great bucket model; the best VCs understand that skew.
principles.quote: But that model misses the key insight that actual returns are *incredibly skewed*. The more a VC understands this skew pattern, the better the VC.

principles.text: A VC fund only makes money if its best investment is worth more than the whole fund.
principles.quote: To a first approximation, a VC portfolio will only make money if your best company investment ends up being worth more than your whole fund

principles.text: Because of the power law, be concentrated: about 7-8 high-conviction bets, not 100 lottery tickets.
principles.quote: A better model is to invest in maybe 7 or 8 promising companies from which you think you can get a 10x return.

principles.text: People underestimate exponentials, so up rounds led by smart VCs tend to be underpriced while flat rounds signal trouble.
principles.quote: you should always exercise your pro rata participation rights whenever a smart VC was leading a portfolio company’s up round. Conversely, the test showed that you should never increase your investment on a flat or down round.

principles.text: Where your company sits on the power-law curve can matter as much as your equity stake; this applies to joining startups and life decisions.
principles.quote: given something like a power law distribution, where your company is on that curve can matter just as much or more than your individual equity stake.

principles.text: Inside a business one revenue source tends to dominate; a startup claiming many revenue streams is a red flag.
principles.quote: Making money with A is key. Making money with A through E is terrifying, from an investor’s perspective.

sources.title: Distribution: why great products don't sell themselves and one channel must be nailed
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 9 Notes Essay: If You Build It, Will They Come?
sources.summary: Thiel argues distribution is the most underestimated part of a startup. The best product doesn't always win, sales is hidden and non-rational, CLV must exceed CPA, and most businesses fail by never getting a single channel to work. Pick one optimal channel and nail it, because that can produce a terminal monopoly even with an undifferentiated product.

principles.text: Poor distribution, not product, is the number one cause of startup failure.
principles.quote: Poor distribution—not product—is the number one cause of failure.

principles.text: Great products don't sell themselves; the claim is usually a sales pitch, not fact.
principles.quote: The conventional thinking is that great products sell themselves; if you have great product, it will inevitably reach consumers. But nothing is further from the truth.

principles.text: Find the single best distribution channel; juggling several usually means none works.
principles.quote: If you can get even a single distribution channel to work, you have great business. If you try for several but don’t nail one, you’re finished.

principles.text: Distribution can create a monopoly even when the product is undifferentiated, while differentiation alone gets you nowhere.
principles.quote: Great distribution can give you a terminal monopoly, even if your product is undifferentiated. The converse is that product differentiation itself doesn’t get you anywhere.

principles.text: Match distribution to deal size: customer lifetime value must exceed acquisition cost, and larger deals demand people-intensive sales.
principles.quote: In a world with some friction and uncertainty, you build a great business if CLV > CPA.

principles.text: Viral growth must be inherent to the core use case, and winning the first high-velocity segment locks out followers.
principles.quote: Marketing people can’t do viral marketing. You don’t just build a product and then choose viral marketing. There is no viral marketing add-on.

sources.title: After Web 2.0: Timing the future, working with computers, and avoiding competition (CS183 Class 10)
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 10 Notes Essay: After Web 2.0
sources.summary: Thiel argues the Internet has been a lightly regulated frontier, that being right about the future but wrong on timing is the classic failure, and that the best path is working with computers rather than competing with them or China. Q&A adds his views on paddling early for big waves, small boards, and betting on the single best company.

principles.text: Being right about the future but wrong on timing is a common and costly failure.
principles.quote: Lots of times people get the call right, but the future takes longer to arrive than they thought.

principles.text: Avoid head-on competition; it destroys profits and leaves everyone bloodied.
principles.quote: Competing is too hard. People never really make any money. They just beat each other to bloody pulp.

principles.text: Paddle early for the next big wave; waiting for certainty means missing it.
principles.quote: But you can’t just wait to be sure there’s a wave before you start paddling. You’ll miss it entirely. You have to paddle early, and then let the wave catch you.

principles.text: Don't chase the current wave; building the next social network is already too late.
principles.quote: Trying to start the next great social networking company is current wave thinking. You can paddle hard, but you’ve missed it.

principles.text: The world of bits stayed lightly regulated, which is why computers and finance were the best places to be.
principles.quote: Over the last 40 years, the world of stuff has been heavily regulated. The world of bits has been regulated much less.

principles.text: With power-law outcomes, pick the single best company; the stage matters less than the substance.
principles.quote: If there is indeed a power law distribution in company outcomes, it’s really important to get into the single company you think is the best.

sources.title: Secrets: why important secrets still exist and how to find them (CS183 Class 11)
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 11 Notes Essay: Secrets
sources.summary: Thiel argues the biggest secret is that many important secrets remain, even though society has stopped believing in them. He explains why people disbelieve (incrementalism, risk aversion, complacency, egalitarianism), why that view is wrong, and how to find and use secrets, especially human ones.

principles.text: Secrets are unpopular or unconventional truths; your answer to 'what important truth do few agree with you on' is your secret.
principles.quote: what important truth do very few people agree with you on? To a first approximation, the correct answer is going to be a secret. Secrets are unpopular or unconventional truths.

principles.text: Distinguish hard-but-possible secrets from impossible mysteries; knowing the difference separates lucrative ventures from guaranteed failure.
principles.quote: Intermediate, difficult things are at least possible. Impossible things are not. Knowing the difference is the difference between pursuing lucrative ventures and guaranteed failure.

principles.text: The biggest secret is that many important secrets are left; society's belief in a closed frontier is wrong.
principles.quote: Probably the biggest secret—bigger than monopoly/competition, power law, or distribution—is that there are many important secrets left.

principles.text: Disbelief in secrets comes from incrementalism, risk aversion, complacency, and egalitarianism.
principles.quote: Four primary things have been driving people’s disbelief in secrets. First is the pervasive incrementalism in our society.

principles.text: Those who solve hard problems believe they are solvable; if you think something impossible, you won't try.
principles.quote: If you believe something is hard, you might still think you can do it. You’ll try things, and maybe you’ll succeed. But if you think something is impossible, you won’t even try.

principles.text: Ask what people aren't telling you: human secrets and taboos are the faster path to big secrets, including natural ones.
principles.quote: What aren’t people telling you can very often give you great insight as to where you should be directing your attention.

sources.title: War and Peace: why imitative competition destroys companies and how to avoid it
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 12 Notes Essay: War and Peace
sources.summary: Thiel argues that conflict is mostly Shakespearean, not Marxist: rivals grow alike, obsess over each other and lose sight of the real question. Founders should avoid wars, merge or win fast if forced, and prevent internal fighting by giving each person distinct roles.

principles.text: Competitors converge and become obsessed with each other; fights are Shakespearean, not ideological.
principles.quote: In the great majority of cases, it’s straight Shakespeare. People become obsessed with their competitors. Companies converge on similarity.

principles.text: Choose your enemies carefully, because fighting makes you resemble them.
principles.quote: A working theory is thus that you must choose your enemies well, since you’ll soon become just like them.

principles.text: Manufactured enemies for motivation can turn into real, destructive ones.
principles.quote: The flaw was that creating fake enemies for motivation often leads to real enemies that bring destruction.

principles.text: If you must fight, win quickly with overwhelming force; mainly find ways to avoid war entirely.
principles.quote: But since very often it’s not possible to ensure a quick victory, your primary job is to figure out ways not to have war happen at all.

principles.text: Internal conflict comes from people wanting the same role; give each person distinct, single responsibilities.
principles.quote: People who want very different things don’t fight in well-functioning companies; they just go and own those different things.

principles.text: A bad plan beats no plan; evaluate the hill you're climbing rather than just marching.
principles.quote: A good intermediate lesson in chess is that even a bad plan is better than no plan at all.

sources.title: You Are Not a Lottery Ticket: Determinate vs Indeterminate Futures
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 13 Notes Essay: You Are Not A Lottery Ticket
sources.summary: Thiel argues the luck-vs-skill question can't be settled, but society has swung too far toward luck and indeterminacy (statistics, diversification, process over substance). Founders do better with definite plans and conviction about the future, as Apple's design-led, secret-plan approach shows.

principles.text: Belief in luck is an ineffective truth that stops you from acting; belief in secrets is effective.
principles.quote: Belief in secrets is an effective truth. Belief in luck is an *ineffective* truth; it will stop you from actually doing things.

principles.text: Society has overcorrected toward luck and indeterminacy; the pendulum should swing back toward skill.
principles.quote: All we can do here is point out that we seem to have shifted to the extreme luck side of the spectrum and suggest that it might make sense to dial back the pendulum the other way.

principles.text: If the future is knowable, have firm convictions instead of diversifying across options.
principles.quote: If the future is determinate, it makes much more sense to have firm convictions.

principles.text: Indefinite optimism leaves capital with no ideas: money circulates because nobody knows what to build.
principles.quote: What’s odd about this dynamic is that, at all stages, no one ever knows what to do with the money.

principles.text: Startup A/B testing, iteration and machine learning can become excuses for not thinking about the future.
principles.quote: iteration and machine learning are often excuses for the last two phenomena—not thinking about the future and short time horizons.

principles.text: Companies with a good secret plan are undervalued in a world that doesn't believe in plans, and the plan anchors them against selling.
principles.quote: Any company with a good secret plan will always be undervalued in a world where nobody believes in secrets and nobody believes in plans.

sources.title: Seeing Green: why cleantech failed and what a definite energy bet would need (CS183 Class 14)
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 14 Notes Essay: Seeing Green
sources.summary: Thiel uses the cleantech bust to review his startup checklist: markets, competition, secrets, incrementalism, durability, teams, distribution, timing, financing and luck. He argues energy follows a power law, so a definite, optimistic bet (he sketches thorium) beats the indeterminate portfolio thinking that sank Solyndra-style ventures.

principles.text: Plans beat aspirations: a detailed plan gives mastery over luck; winning without one is hitting a jackpot.
principles.quote: But having a detailed plan is key. To be sure, there are some cases where things work despite the lack of a plan. But there is an awful lot of failure there too. Winning without a plan is hitting the jackpot, and most people do not hit the jackpot.

principles.text: Energy follows a power law: one source dominates, so portfolio thinking is a mistake.
principles.quote: Energy sources are probably not normally distributed in cost or effectiveness. There is probably one that is dramatically better than all others.

principles.text: You need good answers on all 10 startup questions; 8 of 10 is a B-, 5 of 10 is an F.
principles.quote: And, to reiterate, you really do need all 10; 8 out of 10 is sort of a B-, and 5 of 10 earns you an F.

principles.text: Huge, competitive markets breed mimetic competition and tiny profits; companies need a specific mission.
principles.quote: The economic insight is that the battles are so fierce because the stakes so small. Since profits are competed away, people are fighting over scraps.

principles.text: Long-horizon ventures need big secrets, and incremental improvements are not durable enough to win.
principles.quote: Secrets can allow you to escape mimesis and competition in a world of long time horizons, but those secrets need to be pretty big.

principles.text: Avoid investing in companies seeking under $1 million or over $1 billion, since power-law returns need plausible outsized growth.
principles.quote: A good, broad rule of thumb is to never invest in companies who are looking for less than $1 million or more than $1 billion.

sources.title: Back to the Future: Revisiting the Failed Futures of the Past (CS183 Class 15)
sources.originalTitle: Peter Thiel's CS183: Startup - Class 15 Notes Essay: Back to the Future
sources.summary: Thiel argues the failed futures of the 1950s-60s (energy storage, weather, robotics, space) are fertile ground for startups: find where the past went wrong, learn the right lessons, and attack the problem from a radically different angle. He also covers why unique ideas are hard to fund, why enterprise sales must start small with good references, and how to disguise a sale.

principles.text: Revisit failed futures, but don't just copy them: learn from the past and deploy it in a new way.
principles.quote: The goal, then, is to tap into the past, learn all we can, and deploy that knowledge in some new, important way.

principles.text: Underexplored research lines may be worth revisiting if they were dropped for reasons other than merit.
principles.quote: Not everything that has gone underexplored deserves to be lost.

principles.text: Retrofuture: find where the past failed, learn the right lessons, and approach the old problem from a very different perspective.
principles.quote: The retrofuture idea is simply this: think about where the past failed, learn the right lessons, and make it work this time.

principles.text: Computer science is the exception: its visions of the future largely came true, while most other fields went off track.
principles.quote: But in most areas, things got seriously off track. The future didn't work.
