chunks.heading: Why nuclear power stalled: the dual-use theory
chunks.text:
- Official story: Three Mile Island (1979), Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011) killed it.
- Peter's alternate theory: the real cause was India getting the bomb in 1974-75. The US had transferred reactor technology to India, believing it couldn't be weaponized, and it was weaponized easily.
- The consequence: civilian nuclear power is "only one step away" from weapons. That forces a choice between a double standard (the US keeps nuclear weapons, nobody else may have reactors) or effective global governance, "which doesn't sound that good either." The compromise was to regulate so heavily that new plants became too expensive.
- Evidence he cites: even China, which is building the most reactors, has built fewer than expected, because it copies over-safe Western designs. Nuclear was around 4-5% of Chinese electricity in 2013-14 and the share hasn't risen in ten years, since coal is cheaper.
- He believes modern small reactor designs would be much cheaper per kilowatt-hour with no giant containment structure, but they aren't allowed, and the dual-use problem remains.
- His point on energy density: history moved from wood to coal to oil to uranium, with each step more compact and taking up less environment. Solar and wind go backwards by covering deserts and landscapes. So nuclear was supposed to be the 21st-century energy mode.
- The broader stagnation theory: "why" questions are overdetermined (risk aversion, worse education, picked-over low-hanging fruit). One underrated factor is that much science and technology had a "dystopian or apocalyptic dimension" after Los Alamos in 1945 and thermonuclear weapons in the early 1950s.
- He asks whether stagnation is "a feature or a bug." If physicists kept accelerating on supersonics, hypersonic weapons and modular nuclear reactors, "maybe the whole world would have already blown up." He calls it "the stagnant path of the Multiverse" with a partially protective effect, though he still finds it deeply deranged in other ways.

chunks.heading: The deep state, Epstein and Bill Gates: Peter's speculative takes
chunks.text:
- Why the deep state is weaker now: he says the 1940s through 1960s saw crazy secret projects (Manhattan Project, MK Ultra). He doesn't think the CIA does "anything quite like MK Ultra anymore."
- His reasoning: after the Church Commission hearings in the late 1970s, formalization made bureaucracies "a lot less functional." He gives the 2000s torture memos as another example.
- He sees the NSA/FISA process as out of control from about 2003 to 2017-18, culminating in the 2016 Russia conspiracy theories.
- MK Ultra and the 1960s counterculture:
  - He notes that Ken Kesey's LSD trials started at the Menlo Park veterans hospital and that Timothy Leary's work at Harvard began as MK Ultra projects.
  - He suspects MK Ultra was bigger than we realize.
  - He raises "inner space vs. outer space": we landed on the moon in July 1969 and Woodstock started three weeks later. He wonders whether the turn to interiority (therapy, meditation, identity politics, psychedelics) acts as a substitute for changing the outside world rather than the first step to it.
- He says he is a "pretty hardcore libertarian" on drug legalization. On the FDA and MDMA he says: "if it really works you don't need a double blind study," and that the FDA moved the goalposts because people know whether they got the drug or a placebo.
- On Epstein:
  - Peter says Reid Hoffman introduced him to Epstein in 2014, after Epstein's first arrest, and that he was described as one of the smartest tax people in the world. He calls it a moral weakness not to have asked more questions.
  - He thinks the underage-sex angle is "overdone and everything else is underdone," like a limited hangout.
  - He cites Alex Acosta's 2017 testimony that Epstein "belonged to intelligence." The real question is which part of US intelligence he worked for. He dismisses the Israel theory, saying "if you're working for Israel you don't get protected," and cites Jonathan Pollard's 25 years.
  - He suggests the secret-club dynamic: people were not so much compromised as invited into a club where they were "made."
- His Bill Gates theory (explicitly speculative):
  - Gates and Melinda had no prenup, and Epstein reportedly advised on the marriage and on philanthropy structures.
  - Committing the marital assets to the foundation would box Melinda in, since "it's all going to the Gates Foundation anyway."
  - He argues Gates going into overdrive on Covid in 2020 locked this in, because Melinda filed in early 2021 and would look like a "crazy anti-science person" if she resisted.
  - He thinks the left-wing philanthropy structure was a way to control a spouse, and says this fits the timeline well.
  - He adds that Melinda received about a tenth of what a half split would have been.
- On philanthropy: in America it's seen as what a good person does, while in Europe it signals "you must have murdered somebody." He thinks the European intuition is more correct, and that virtue signaling is now more suspect than "vice signaling."

chunks.heading: Birth rates, imitation and why talk substitutes for action
chunks.text:
- Peter's explanation for collapsing birth rates is "overdetermined" (plastics, screens, careers, housing costs). He anchors on social and cultural factors: "people have kids if other people have kids and they stop having kids when other people stop."
- His evidence of the breadth:
  - Every US state is below replacement, even Mormon Utah, and so are Iran, Italy and South Korea.
  - He says Korea's fertility rate is about 0.7, a third of replacement, so each generation shrinks by about two thirds.
  - Israel is the exception.
- Political lock-in: once the pyramid inverts, old voters favor benefits for themselves ("so Grandma can have a spare leg" instead of "so Johnny can read"), and parents get penalized economically. A Japanese demographer's thesis is that once it flips, it doesn't flip back.
- Extrapolation he gives: at one child per woman, each generation halves. 2^33 is about 8 billion, and at 30 years per generation that's about 990 years to one person left. He calls it a very long-term extrapolation.
- Contrast: Paul Ehrlich's 1968 "The Population Bomb" predicted exponential growth, and we flipped to exponential decay. A stable equilibrium at exactly two kids is very hard to hit.
- Imitation theory of humanity: following Aristotle ("man differs from the other animals in his greater aptitude for imitation"), he says humans are giant imitation machines. Imitation explains learning, language and culture, and it also drives conflict (you want the banana because I want it).
- He adds that language is a radical discontinuity from primates, and imitation had to be channeled into ritual and religion. He ties this to René Girard, scapegoats and the origins of kingship.
- Talk versus action: his Korea anecdote has a conglomerate CEO agree "it's a total disaster" and then consider the matter closed. His conclusion: "talking about things is the first step but it also becomes the excuse for not really solving them."
- He applies the same skepticism to therapy, which promises self-transformation but often ends in "self-acceptance." His closing line: "strategy is often a euphemism for procrastination."

chunks.heading: AI risk, China, regulation and the case against the optimists' story
chunks.text:
- Peter says he thinks the scary dystopian AI narrative is "way more compelling" than the Silicon Valley one, and that the Luddite and effective-altruist side is winning the argument this time. He says he doesn't like the effective altruists or the Luddites.
- He frames it as: do you worry about Dr. Strangelove (blow up the world to build bigger bombs) or about Greta (make everyone ride a bicycle)? Today people worry about Strangelove, not Greta.
- Prediction: AI will be "surprisingly" regulated, as "so many other vectors of innovation" have been. Computers progressed over 50 years because they were mostly inert and air-gapped from the real world, which kept regulation light. If the FDA regulated AI, progress would slow a lot.
- On Silicon Valley's pitch (humans merging with AI): he thinks there's maybe a 1% chance it works as advertised, and it's more plausibly "corporate propaganda" where companies say the right things, cut corners and it goes haywire. His critique is that pro-AI people are doing a bad job convincing the average person it will be good for them.
- On global governance: he notes RAND's push for "global compute governance" and says it sounds even worse to him.
- On China: he gives the CCP's best counter-argument, which is that it may regulate AI because it fanatically wants control and AI could undermine party power. He cites the Jack Ma/Alibaba/Tencent crackdown, in which tech leaders went from national champions to enemies of the people over about the last seven to eight years. He doesn't fully trust this and says China could also lose control of its own AI.
- On the military: drones need AI because a human operator can be jammed, so there's a logic to taking the human out of the loop, "but there doesn't seem to be a good end game."
- His rebuttal to the "AI becomes God and aliens are AIs" story: faster-than-light travel implies warp-speed weapons with no defense. So an advanced civilization must be either totally totalitarian (a "mind meld" with no independent agency) or perfectly altruistic, "demons or angels." He argues altruism is hard to reach by evolution, and that status competition is cultural, not just scarcity.
- His PayPal Galaxy Quest anecdote: Star Trek's premise was a post-scarcity world, but a 1999 PayPal event with Star Trek's "Scotty" (James Doohan) hit the "forbidden question" about William Shatner doing Priceline ads. He draws from it that scarcity (only one captain) persists even in sci-fi utopias.
- On UFOs: he is "strangely under-motivated" by the topic. His luggage-at-the-airport argument: waiting 77 years with no progress is like waiting 77 minutes for luggage, at which point "you should stop."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel presents three contrarian answers from Zero to One: all happy companies are different, secrets still exist outside closed fields like geography, and the 21st century needs vertical technology progress rather than copying (globalization). The Q&A covers monopoly policy, themes, the Thiel Fellowship, education, and libertarianism.

chunks.heading: Competition is for losers: monopoly vs. competitive businesses
chunks.text:
- Peter argues all happy companies are different and all unhappy companies are alike, inverting Tolstoy: unhappy companies fail "to escape the essential sameness of competition."
- The Wall Street Journal excerpted the chapter and retitled it "competition is for losers."
- He says the most important and under-discussed distinction in business is that there are only two kinds of companies: competitive ones and monopolies.
- A one-of-a-kind company doing something different is a monopoly, and building one should be every founder's goal.
- He calls capitalism and competition antonyms. A capitalist accumulates capital, and in perfect competition all profits are competed away.
- Bad business example: opening a restaurant, which is super competitive and where nobody makes money.
- Good business example: Google, which has had essentially no competition in search since 2002, when it distanced itself from Microsoft and Yahoo, and has made enormous profits for a dozen years.

chunks.heading: How companies disguise monopoly and competition
chunks.text:
- Monopolists avoid talking about it by pretending to be in a much larger market. Google would never say it is a search engine; it says it is a technology company competing with Apple on phones, Facebook on social, Amazon, Microsoft, and car companies with self-driving cars.
- Competitive businesses do the reverse, pitching a fictionally small submarket to look unique. Example: "the only British food restaurant in Palo Alto." He notes nobody eats only British food, so it still competes with other restaurants, even ones in Menlo Park or Mountain View.
- Result: "the people who don't have monopolies pretend to have them, the people who have monopolies pretend not to have them." The apparent difference is small, the real difference is huge.
- On Google, he notes that despite 20-30,000 talented people, few great companies have come out of it. Insiders are told success comes from talent, so leavers conclude it's just about hiring smart people, and the business strategy (monopoly) gets obscured. People talk about talent when they don't want to talk about monopoly.
- Twitter example: it is a fantastic monopoly-like business built on the 140-character idea, which nobody could catch once it took off. He says such businesses "don't have to be operationally that airtight," unlike a restaurant, which must be operationally tight on everything.

chunks.heading: Why people crowd into competition
chunks.text:
- Psychologically we are taught competition is valuable and feel safety in crowds: if many people want something, it must be good, like joining a long line without asking why.
- He notes that in Shakespeare's time "ape" meant both primate and to imitate, and says human nature is herd-like.
- Competing makes you better at the thing you compete on (SAT prep, swim team), but at the price of losing sight of what is really valuable.
- He quotes Kissinger on Harvard faculty: "the battles in Academia are so ferocious because the stakes are so small." When differences are small, you must fight harder to differentiate, so everyone squeezes through the same tiny door while a huge gate around the corner goes unexplored.
- On social conformity: the socially well-adapted get talked out of original ideas before they're formed, picking up cues like "that's a little too weird." Hence people with Asperger-like traits do well in Silicon Valley, which he frames as a critique of society.
- Harvard Business School studies over 30 years show the largest share of graduates goes into the wrong field because they all ride the last wave: Michael Milken in 1989 (one or two years before he went to jail), internet and tech in 1999-2000 just before the bubble burst, housing and private equity in the last decade.
- His conclusion: "there is no wisdom in crowds," an "anti-Malcolm Gladwell thing," just ferocious competition.

chunks.heading: Secrets: conventions, mysteries, and the in-between
chunks.text:
- Peter's contrarian interview question: "Tell me something that's true that almost nobody agrees with you on." He finds it shockingly hard for people to answer.
- Two reasons it's hard: people are taught truth is whatever everybody agrees on, and an answer people already agree with is by definition the wrong answer, which takes courage to avoid.
- He splits knowledge into three categories: conventions (everyone knows), mysteries (almost impossibly hard to figure out), and secrets (hard to figure out, unknown today, but discoverable with work).
- A secret or idiosyncratic body of knowledge is often at the core of great businesses.
- PayPal example: the team was deeply interested in cryptography and currency on the internet and fantasized about a new world currency (it was on their t-shirt). They failed at that, but the exploration shaped how they built the payment system that worked.
- In the 17th-18th centuries empty spaces on maps were secrets you could explore; in the 19th century basic chemistry let you discover new elements. Geography and basic chemistry are now closed fields, but he says it's a mistake to extrapolate that all fields are closed.
- He sees plenty left in information technology (computers, internet, mobile internet) and thinks many other areas of science and technology have progressed less fast but hold great discoveries and businesses.
- On disclosing secrets: tell nobody and it does no good; tell everybody and it dilutes. He defines a company as "a group of people who have a secret," telling just the right number of people.
- He is skeptical that patent laws, which give legal monopolies on discoveries, work well in practice, though he likes the idea behind them.
- In law, injustice also involves a secret: something unjust persists because most people don't see it. He doubts we've found all injustices and says we're not at the end of history.
- His example guess for 2100's verdict on 2014: many political and business leaders were borderline sociopaths. He also suggests football may be where smoking was in the early 1960s: sensed to be bad (brain damage) but not yet articulated.

chunks.heading: Globalization vs. technology: 0 to 1 vs. 1 to n
chunks.text:
- Peter sees two modes of progress in the 21st century: globalization (copying what works, going from 1 to n, horizontal or extensive growth) and technology (discovering new things, going from 0 to 1, vertical progress).
- He draws globalization on the x-axis and technology on the y-axis to show they are not synonyms, even though they're used interchangeably.
- China is the paradigm of globalization, with a straightforward 20-year plan of copying what works from the US, Western Europe and Japan, skipping steps and avoiding some bad ideas.
- History: the 19th century had both globalization and technological progress. After 1914 (first world war) globalization reversed while technology kept moving very fast. After 1971, when Kissinger went to China, globalization restarted in earnest, but he argues the last 40 years have seen slower technological progress, "a lot in computers, not so much elsewhere."
- The vocabulary changed accordingly. In the 1950s-60s: first world (progress happening) vs. third world (permanently screwed up). Today: developed vs. developing, a convergence theory in which everyone becomes alike.
- He finds "developed world" anti-technological, since it implicitly says nothing new will happen in the US, Western Europe and Japan and that the young should not expect lives better than their parents'.
- His call: resist the label and ask "how do we go about developing the so-called developed world."

chunks.heading: Investing: skeptical of themes, backing one-of-a-kind missions
chunks.text:
- Asked about big themes for the next 5-10 years, Peter says he is skeptical of themes because each contains many undifferentiated companies: "you don't want to be the fourth online pet food company," the 10th thin-film solar company, or the 20th pizza restaurant in Palo Alto.
- He calls education software, healthcare IT, big data, cloud computing and SaaS overwrought themes, noting it's not even clear what "big data" and "cloud" mean.
- What works: one-of-a-kind companies where people are on a mission and the thing wouldn't happen elsewhere if they didn't do it.
- Example: his PayPal colleague Elon Musk, whose SpaceX mission to go to Mars attracted great rocket scientists. Companies going to Mars are not a theme, just one unique thing.
- Airbnb (Peter says they are large investors) is framed by others as a "sharing economy" theme, but he sees a one-of-a-kind company freeing up inventory in housing and expanding the tourism market.

chunks.heading: Good versus bad monopoly, and antitrust
chunks.text:
- Peter says monopolies deserve their bad reputation in a static world where nothing changes, because there the monopolist is just a rent or tax collector that artificially restricts supply.
- A good monopoly invents something new. Apple's iPhone was the first smartphone that worked; Apple had a monopoly on smartphones for years and he argues still does through brand and network effects. That kind of monopoly doesn't create scarcity but a whole new thing, which is why people line up for iPhones.
- The policy question is how static technology is at the moment.
- He thinks government intervention has come too late: IBM was pursued in the 1970s just as computing shifted from hardware to software, and Microsoft in the late 1990s when things were shifting to the internet anyway, with no reason to think Microsoft would have dominated the internet as it did the desktop.
- He is skeptical of the EU's intervention against Google and says Silicon Valley underestimates how much that is building up.

chunks.heading: Substance over status, education, and the Thiel Fellowship
chunks.text:
- A personal resolution he made years ago: value substance over status and prestige.
- Advice to his younger self: he'd probably still go to Stanford and maybe law school, but ask far more why, since too much of his choices was driven by prestige.
- Law firm story: he lasted seven months and three days at a big New York law firm that everyone outside wanted into and everyone inside wanted out of. A colleague told him "it's so reassuring to see you leave Peter, I had no idea it was possible to escape from Alcatraz," when all he did was walk out the front door. People's identities get wrapped up in what they compete for.
- Thiel Fellowship: 20 students get a two-year stipend to stop out of school and work on a business, nonprofit or other project. It was starting its fifth year, with 83 people through the program.
- Results he cites: of the first year's 24, five went back to school after two years; others started successful companies; about $60 million in venture capital raised in aggregate; more applicants each year; peripheral programs such as Summit Series for younger entrepreneurs.
- He rejects being portrayed as against all college. His point is that higher education is too tracked and conventional: "if we say that you go to Yale or you go to jail, that's not the way we want our society to be structured." He cites student debt that limits career choices.

chunks.heading: Founders, alignment, and law lessons for business
chunks.text:
- Peter says law school taught him to think about incentives and alignment: make sure people are aligned both formally (structure set correctly) and informally (natural tendency to work together).
- Founder prehistory question: "how did you meet, what's the prehistory of the company?" A bad answer is meeting a week ago at a business networking event and deciding to start a company because both wanted to be entrepreneurs. That's "like saying I married the first person I met at the slot machines in Las Vegas." A good answer is knowing each other a long time, with complementary skills (for example one technical, one business).
- Non-lawyers in business tend to make one of two mistakes: treating law as irrelevant (breaking lots of laws, getting in trouble fast) or as all-important (getting handicapped and unable to do anything). The right stance is critical but not all-important.

chunks.heading: Technology, government decline, and libertarianism
chunks.text:
- Peter describes himself as libertarian: socially liberal, fiscally more conservative, and temperamentally a "political atheist" who doesn't believe the political system is where problems get solved. He therefore focuses on technology as the way to change things.
- He doesn't treat libertarian ideas as timeless absolutes; he thinks libertarianism is more true today than in the past because of government decline.
- The government used to do much more for science: the Manhattan Project built a nuclear bomb in three and a half years, and a New York Times op-ed days after Hiroshima argued it proved how much faster science moves when the Army orders scientists around, versus letting "primadonna scientists" take 50 years. He says nobody writes op-eds like that anymore.
- He says you couldn't do a Manhattan Project or Apollo program today, and calls for exploring this "decline of competence."
- How to resist conventional thinking: no formula, but awareness of how prone we are to it. A slightly-better-than-average answer admits it is unoriginal; saying "we need more education software companies" is a bad answer, but acknowledging it's unoriginal puts you ahead. Originality is "incredibly hard, incredibly rare," and we underestimate social influence, like thinking ads work on everyone but us.
- Star Wars vs. Star Trek: at PayPal they were pro-Star Wars. Star Trek is the communist series, with transporter technology and no money; Star Wars is the capitalist one, with Han Solo's debts driving the plot. If you're creating a new payment system, you don't want to model it on a Star Trek world.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 2012 Fortune debate, Thiel argues that the developed world has had 40 years of stagnation: flat median wages, no energy progress, and innovation confined to bits because regulation outlawed the world of atoms. He pushes back on Schmidt's techno-optimism, and says cash-hoarding tech giants show they have run out of ideas.

chunks.heading: Peter's view: technological progress has stalled outside computers
chunks.text:
- Peter distinguishes the developed world from emerging markets. In China, India, Africa and Latin America "there's zero need for innovation," because those countries only need to copy things that work.
- He argues technology is "the only way that things get better in the developed world" (US, Western Europe, Japan), so that is where its health matters.
- His headline data point is US wages. Median wages have been stagnant from 1973 to 2012, while from 1932 to 1972 they went up by a factor of six.
- The earlier period matched real technological progress: better cars, aeronautics, supersonic jets, computers.
- He says this stagnation also shows up in socialist countries like France and in Japan, so he does not treat it as only a problem of capitalist countries.
- When Eric Schmidt blames bad politics, entitlements and demographics, Peter answers that technology "should be a large enough force that could power change" even with a somewhat screwed-up political system. In his view, treating everything as politics concedes that technology is no longer a big driver.

chunks.heading: Computers progressed while energy and "the world of stuff" did not
chunks.text:
- Peter simplifies the last 40 years as "incremental but relentless progress on the computer side" and "basically no progress on energy."
- Oil was about $2 a barrel in 1973 and was north of $100 in 2012. He calls this "a catastrophic failure of energy innovation" that was offset by computer innovation.
- His agriculture example: the Green Revolution of the 50s and 60s roughly doubled world food production in line with population growth. It has decelerated dramatically over the last 40 years, which he links to a decade of rising food prices.
- On travel speeds, the Concorde was decommissioned in 2003. Counting low-tech airport security, he says travel speeds are back to about 1960 levels.
- His explanation is government. The FDA charges about $1.3 billion per new drug. Supersonic jets are banned for noise. Nuclear plants, fusion and thorium are not allowed. He says "we've basically outlawed everything having to do with the world of stuff and the only thing you're allowed to do is in the world of bits."
- That is why computers and finance were the two areas of big innovation in 40 years. He expects finance to be outlawed too, leaving only computers.
- He flags the risk that fracking could be outlawed even as Schmidt cites energy independence as an example of innovation.

chunks.heading: Moore's law is good for computers, but is it good for people?
chunks.text:
- Peter says Moore's law is "good if you're a computer," and asks how it translates into economic progress for humans.
- He says he is in favor of the computer companies and wants more of them, but computing is the exception to the rule that there is not enough innovation, and the specific should not be confused with the general.
- He also pushes back on the claim that social media drove the Arab Spring. He says the fundamental driver was food prices rising 30 to 50% in the previous year, which left people facing starvation. Calling it a Twitter and Facebook revolution is, to him, "smug and complacent."
- He notes that Apple, Twitter and Facebook are profitable but do not employ the numbers that General Motors did in the 1950s.

chunks.heading: Google as a monopoly with cash it cannot invest
chunks.text:
- Peter says Google has a "worldclass monopoly" in search. Monopoly is legal as long as it is not used to tie in or oppress other companies.
- He challenges Schmidt that Google holds $30 to 50 billion in cash, has no good ideas for investing it in technology, and so accepts roughly 0% interest. In his words, the cash "gets burned away over time through inflation."
- He argues that with an accelerating technological world and 0% interest rates, a company should be able to invest all its money in things that return it many times over. If it can't, that signals a lack of ideas.
- He credits Amazon as the only big tech company reinvesting all its profits, saying it has "enough of a vision of the future." Google, he says, does more than Microsoft or Apple, citing self-driving cars and asteroid mining.
- His harder charge is that the intellectually honest move would be to say Google is no longer a technology company. The search technology was developed a decade ago, so investing in Google is "a bet that there will be no one else who will come up with a better search technology."
- He compares it to a bank with enormous cash flow that cannot pay a dividend, because returning $30 billion would admit it is no longer a tech company. He says Microsoft and others are hoarding cash for the same reason.

chunks.heading: What Peter would change: imagination, long-term incentives and "vertical" growth
chunks.text:
- Asked how he would improve the technology environment, he says the problem is multifaceted:
  - Regulatory and political issues.
  - "A failure of imagination on the part of people starting things."
  - Incentives that are too short term, so people cannot invest in multi-year projects. He says Google does this relatively better than most tech companies.
- He puts his nonprofit donations into technology projects that are not profitable but could be valuable in other ways.
- He calls taking technology as critical, not being complacent, and continuing to push "an incredible imperative."
- On globalization, he says it is a good trend but has nothing to do with technology. It was happening in the 19th century and is about the spread of ideas, and it would improve China and India.
- What he is interested in is "vertical growth, intensive growth, doing fundamentally new things." He says that needs a change in financial, corporate, cultural and political priorities.

chunks.heading: Finance as a symptom of blocked innovation
chunks.text:
- Asked whether finance has crowded out long-term investment, Peter rejects the premise that there is a trade-off between finance and other innovation.
- He says it is easy to be anti-finance, but the economy became lopsided toward it "fundamentally because people weren't able to do other things."
- His example is why rocket scientists went to Wall Street in the 90s to create new financial products. He says it was because they couldn't get jobs as rocket scientists, since rockets and supersonic airplanes could not be built, not because finance paid too much.
- His analogy is that brilliant people in the Soviet Union became grandmaster chess players because "they weren't allowed to do anything else," not because there was something wrong with chess.

chunks.heading: Education as a bubble and the debt burden on a generation
chunks.text:
- Peter lists a series of destructive bubbles: the tech bubble in the 90s, the housing and finance bubble in the 2000s, and a government bubble now, which he finds strange because government is "so clearly dysfunctional."
- He says that "if there's anything in our society that's a bubble it is education."
- His figures:
  - College costs have tripled or quadrupled, a roughly 300% increase after inflation since 1980.
  - It's not clear quality has gone up at all.
  - The number of years it takes to recoup college debt has been steadily increasing since 2000.
  - College was an increasingly good investment through 2000, but since then the gap between college and high school has been roughly flat because debt kept rising.
- He says Millennials are being turned into "something like indentured servants." Bush rewrote the bankruptcy laws in 2005 so college debt cannot be escaped even through personal bankruptcy.
- He calls education "hyped beyond belief," and says that if education is limited to engineering degrees, it could be cut back by about 90%.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel argues science and atoms-based technology have been stagnant for about 50 years, with only computers progressing, and that LLMs are a breakthrough on par with the internet. He explains why a narrow initial market beats a huge one, why wokeness distracts from stagnation, and why existential risks deserve attention without shutting everything down.

chunks.heading: Where AI and the internet fit in the stagnation story
chunks.text:
- Peter dates the "tech stagnation" argument to about 2008 and says progress in the world of atoms has been limited for roughly five decades, since the 1970s.
- When he was an undergraduate at Stanford in the late 1980s, majoring in mechanical, chemical or nuclear engineering, or in aerospace, was "terrible decisions". Only the world of bits (computers, the internet, mobile internet, software) kept progressing.
- He is unsure how much computing raised GDP compared with the first half of the 20th century. He calls the progress "very unbalanced" even though it produced great companies.
- He sees the situation as roughly unchanged for the last 25 years: decent progress in bits, much slower and harder-to-invest-in progress in everything else.
- The late-90s internet wave was a giant computing wave. He now says LLMs and ChatGPT are "probably a breakthrough" that he would rank "on par with the internet itself".
- Outside computing, he says, we are much further from "the science fiction future of the Jetsons".

chunks.heading: Why science slowed: centralization, risk aversion and the nuclear shadow
chunks.text:
- Peter calls why questions "overdetermined". Some fields have had their easy discoveries made (no new continents, a new element on the periodic table is hard).
- He leans more on cultural explanations: "it's not that nature has run out of things for us" but that society became too risk averse and bureaucratized.
- Centralized government funding could accelerate science once. He cites the Manhattan Project (a New York Times editorial said decentralized scientists would have taken half a century; the Army delivered in three and a half years) and the Apollo program (Kennedy's early-60s speech, a man on the moon by the end of the decade).
- The long-term cost was large bureaucratic institutions and politicized, slower science. He compares it to agricultural monoculture, which boosts output once but is not a healthy ecosystem.
- Military use of science and technology made it ambiguous whether science was more good than bad. He puts the delayed response to Hiroshima at about 25 years: by the early 1970s the reaction was "we can destroy the world 20 times over, what are we doing?".
- That could explain why the smartest physicists stopped being funded to build bigger bombs and scientists in general became regulated: "maybe that's the price you have to pay to stop them from blowing up the world".
- He says Apollo-era risk taking was extreme (Yuri Gagarin died in a test flight years later) and that society then felt things were too dangerous, with too much risk of nuclear war and environmental degradation.
- He does not dismiss existential risks. His line: "we've resulted in a society that was locked down not just during Covid but we've been in a soft lockdown for something like 50 years", and he wants a way out.

chunks.heading: Where he thinks safetyism has gone too far
chunks.text:
- Peter says it is hard to say where the safety line belongs, but gives two examples.
- Real estate: zoning is extremely strict. Looking out his window in Los Angeles he sees office buildings from the 1960s to 1980s and not a single crane on the horizon. For something as important as real estate, that tells him "we've gone way too far".
- Biomedicine: he has thought about it a lot and sees many promising approaches, yet "the barriers are just very, very high".
- His summary: "we're scared of the things that can go wrong but we're not scared enough of the things that will go wrong if we do nothing."

chunks.heading: Wokeness as a diversion from science and economics
chunks.text:
- Peter frames his argument as "anti-anti-woke". The debates on DEI, political correctness and multiculturalism matter on some level, but he worries many are distractions, like a magic show that hypnotizes the audience while a man in an orange monkey suit jumps on someone's back. "Diversity is a diversion from more important things."
- The more important things include economics, science, religion and other political issues.
- Economics: the Marxist critique of cultural Marxism is that focusing on race and gender made people forget class. He also names runaway housing prices as the real problem that gets crowded out.
- He raises a "Marxist conspiracy theory" in which wokeness splits workers by race and gender so they can be paid less. His example is Walmart in the 2000s: under attack for low pay, it rebranded as a green company, which split the left-wing anti-Walmart alliance. A bit of green stuff was cheaper than higher wages, probably good for shareholders, and left the underlying economics unaddressed.
- Science: wokeness focuses on the humanities (English, history) while the real failure is that scientists aren't inventing new things. Research is "corrupt peer-reviewed", incremental, and run by "a stagnant malthusian sociopathic institution".
- He would be "fine with a little bit of wokeness if we were finding a cure for dementia".

chunks.heading: Science needs dogmatism and skepticism in balance; religion and AI simulation theory
chunks.text:
- Peter says science must fight a two-front war against excessive dogmatism and excessive skepticism. Early modern science fought the dogmatism of the Catholic church and Ptolemaic astronomy. Cartesian-style total skepticism is also bad for science.
- His 2023 read: science is "100% anti-skepticism". It fights conspiracy theorists, vaccine, climate, stem cell and Darwin skeptics.
- His test: ask scientists in which fields science is too dogmatic. He says they could not name anything specific, which suggests science "has become as dogmatic as the medieval church was". Non-dogmatic scientists survive in children's books, not in grad school labs, where anyone heterodox gets "thrown off the overcrowded bus".
- On religion, he says God is possibly the biggest question there is, so large that society keeps peace by agreeing not to debate it. He thinks that costs us thinking about the most important things, "maybe at the price of something like a frontal lobotomy" for scientists and the religious.
- On the new atheists (Hitchens, Dennett, Dawkins, Harris), he argues that in 2005 new atheism was a politically correct way to be anti-Muslim, aimed at Bin Laden and Al-Qaeda. In 2023 the main geopolitical challenge is "Xi Jinping thought and the CCP", a consensus-driven "Borg" whose structure resembles East Bay rationalists and consensus scientific thinking, and the new atheists have nothing to say about it.
- He offers two explanations for the AI community's shift from militant atheism to simulation theory:
  - It was a status game in which computer scientists (bits) beat physicists (matter, energy, particles).
  - It partially solved the AI alignment problem. In a multiverse, AGI is in the future and unlikely to be friendly, so "chances are we're all just going to die". In a simulation designed by a super AGI, AGI is in the past and compatibility with humans was already solved, so it can be solved again.
- He says some of this is reasoning, and calls it a quasi-psychological explanation of people grasping for relief from the difficulty of building a friendly AI.
- On naming: if you are insecure enough to call a field a science (political, social, climate science), it often means the opposite. Computer science got the label because it was the major for people not good at EE or math, and it had an inferiority complex. He extends this to adverbs, which often mean the opposite of what they say.

chunks.heading: Existential risk, Pinker, and nuclear deterrence
chunks.text:
- Peter accepts some progress since 250 years ago (e.g. George Washington's wooden teeth) and would not go back even 100 years, but says "something has hit the wall in the last 50 years".
- His specific objection to Steven Pinker is that violence is going down. As a psychology professor who "probably flunked chemistry", Pinker measures only kinetic energy (bombs dropped), while total energy is kinetic plus potential. The potential energy, the number of nuclear bombs and the potential destructiveness, is far higher than 50 years ago.
- He is not complacent that nuclear weapons haven't been used since 1945. He asks how we should treat a North Korean dictator video of a nuke hitting the Golden Gate Bridge, which we dismiss as a cartoon villain.
- On deterrence: it was supposed to work by thinking about nuclear weapons all the time and being scared, which worked during the Cold War (1949 to 1989). Over the last 33 to 34 years we have been "psychologically exhausted" and stopped thinking about it.
- He thinks JFK, LBJ or Nixon could have launched, but doubts Trump could have pushed the button after the 2020 election, and he is not sure nuclear weapons are completely unusable now.
- He says "I'm not a Luddite", you can't turn the clock back, and other existential risks are real: AI and environmental issues beyond climate change.
- On AI risk, he says Eliezer Yudkowsky has "gone kind of crazy" but his arguments "are not that bad", and Silicon Valley has no great rebuttals. The answer is to talk about the risks seriously without minimizing them like Pinker, and also without shutting everything down.

chunks.heading: Debt, US vs the world, polarization and taxes
chunks.text:
- Debt: the US has about $32 trillion in federal debt. Warnings since the 1980s that debt would squeeze the private sector seemed wrong for about 40 years because of a bond bull market. Rates fell from about 20% in the early 1980s to roughly 0% after 2008, with mostly zero rates from 2008 to 2021.
- Servicing cost was about 1.6% of GDP in 2021 versus 3.2% in 1991. Now rates and inflation have spiked, and "I think we're headed for a very, very challenging decade" because "once the rates are above zero the crisis is here".
- The US reserve-currency status let it run bigger deficits for longer, which both helped and hurt.
- US vs the world: despite US problems, "almost everything else seems worse". His metric: companies founded since 1990 worth over $100 billion. There are 17 in the world, 11 in the US, 6 in China, and none anywhere else. He calls Europe's failure extraordinary and says a CEO of one of the 17 would now much rather be in the US than China.
- Polarization: parties look extremely polarized but differ little on his priorities (faster tech innovation, cutting the deficit, more housing). He uses Romeo and Juliet: families fight because there are no differences, which he calls "90% Shakespeare and maybe 10% Marx".
- Inequality and mobility: he thinks both are problems but anchors on stagnation. At 3% GDP growth, "everybody would be better off" and the problems would matter less. At 0 to 1% growth they become zero-sum and hard to solve.
- Tax view: billionaires pay a lower effective rate (maybe about 15%, mostly deferred capital gains) than millionaires on ordinary income (50% in California). Raising capital gains taxes would make billionaires not sell, so the Laffer curve effect would cut revenue. He thinks the US is near the maximum on billionaires.
- His libertarian answer, which he calls outside the Overton window: cut taxes massively on the middle class and millionaires. A bigger government that collects more would need a Western Europe-style structure, where the 50% rate kicks in at about $70,000 in Austria versus $1 million in California, which reduces mobility.

chunks.heading: Courage, conspiracy thinking and conventional wisdom
chunks.text:
- Peter says courage is in shorter supply than genius. Heterodox, think-for-yourself thinking is harder than 50 to 70 years ago, partly because anything put on the internet stays forever.
- His example: he started the Stanford Review in 1987, and it was wildly heterodox, obnoxious and even cruel. It moderated in 2002, the exact point when articles started going online, because everything written would follow you for life.
- His "conspiracy" example is the ESG explanation for the oil majors. Oil demand is highly inelastic (about 100 million barrels a day; cutting 1 million barrels raises price roughly $10 a barrel). If Exxon, Shell, Chevron and BP CEOs agreed to cut output 30% and collude with OPEC, they would break Section 2 of the Sherman Act.
- Hiring ESG consultants who tell them to put half their profits into solar and windmills, which "don't really work", gets the same result: lower supply, higher prices and profits. He doesn't claim it is a deliberate plot, only that the market feedback rewards more of it either way.
- He gives a similar example: the late-1990s US tobacco settlement effectively cartelized the industry, turning tobacco into a tax source and a set of monopolies that "printed money".
- Closing question on bad conventional wisdom: almost all of it. There is no one-size-fits-all or cookie-cutter advice, and advice that works for everyone isn't differentiating. He is not interested in "timeless eternal truths" but in what makes sense to do "in 2023, right here, right now".
- He says "it's probably not a good idea to go around killing people", but that does not get you far in planning your life.

chunks.heading: Total addressable market and monopoly dynamics, including in venture
chunks.text:
- Peter says a market is a necessary component of a startup, but people overstress TAM. A very large TAM probably means a lot of competition.
- Examples: the restaurant business has an enormous TAM and is "a terrible business to go into". Energy functions in a nearly commodified way, so it is hard for startups to find a differentiated niche.
- His preferred narrative is a tight, fairly narrow initial market plus a way to expand. "Build a fortress" there, then expand from that base.
- PayPal: the initial TAM was power sellers on eBay, about 20,000 people in early 2000. PayPal reached 30 to 40% market share in about three months. Expansion paths included payments on and off eBay, eBay's own growth, and gaining share on eBay.
- Crossing the chasm to the off-eBay market turned out to be quite hard, so PayPal sold to eBay in 2002. The strong initial TAM and expansion capability probably "got us to an m&a exit".
- For VCs, he applies the same monopoly layers: companies are layer one, investors are layer two. You want companies without too much competition "red in tooth and claw", and you don't want to compete too much with other VCs.
- Monopoly sources for VC firms parallel those for companies: brand, network effects, economies of scale, unique technology. Founders Fund had a founder-friendly brand from 2005, as the firm was started by founders. By 2023 many others claim it, so it is more cluttered.
- Network effects give idiosyncratic deal flow, but he says advantages must often be reinvented deal by deal.
- His poker rule for investing: "what do we understand about this that other investors do not understand?" If you can't answer, you are the sucker, like the poker player who can't tell who the mark at the table is.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Post-election 2024 conversation with Barry Weiss. Thiel argues the Democratic "machine" and identity politics collapsed, that stagnation made "Make America Great Again" a powerful pessimistic frame, and that science and institutions have grown dogmatic. He also covers trade, nuclear proliferation, and why a future world war would look more like WWI.

chunks.heading: The 2024 election as the collapse of liberalism and the "machine"
chunks.text:
- Peter did not expect a close race. He thought the polls still had not corrected their 2016 and 2020 errors, and he expected a solid Trump win. He calls the result a "collapse of liberalism" and of the Democratic party, not just the failure of "a somewhat senile Biden" and "a somewhat goofy Kamala Harris."
- 2016 was Trump against the Bush Republicans, and Hillary Clinton did not take him seriously. In 2024 the Democrats gave it their all. They spent two to three times as much in the final months, prosecuted him and tried to get him off the ballot, and still lost.
- He argues the result refutes "demographics is destiny" and identity politics. Millions of people changed their minds between 2016 and 2024, which means arguments can still move voters. Trump and Vance made a case. The Democrats had "zero substance," so there was nothing to differentiate from Biden.
- His historical claim is that identity politics last worked in 2008, in a pre-internet world, when Obama could tell black voters he was black and white voters he was post-racial. That tailoring no longer works. Making "diverse" concrete means picking one person and alienating everyone else, and the Democrats now seem able to elect only old straight white men.
- On "retroactive continuity," he says a Harris win would have made 2016 the fluke. In his reading, 2020 was the fluke, one last Biden-era win for an old regime.
- He calls the Democratic party a "machine" rather than a cult, because a cult has a leader and this has no individuals. He cites the 2020 primary (Biden fourth or fifth in Iowa and New Hampshire, then rammed through South Carolina) and Harris's replacement of Biden as extremely non-democratic. He feared a Harris win would have made the machine unbeatable and turned the country into a one-party California, worse because people can leave California but not the US.

chunks.heading: Why the elite pipeline stopped producing strong Democrats
chunks.text:
- He traces a decline in credentials: Clinton (Yale Law, Rhodes), Obama (Harvard Law) and Hillary Clinton (Yale Law), then Biden (University of Delaware), Harris (Howard, UC Hastings), Walz ("even more mediocre"), Newsom (Santa Clara), Shapiro (Georgetown Law). "There is nothing Elite left."
- He can believe the elite schools are corrupt and still select very smart people. His twist is that a conservative who survives Yale Law, one of perhaps five in a class of 170, is well trained to understand what is wrong with liberalism. A liberal graduate would not defend liberalism any better.
- He suggests Democrats may avoid a truly smart nominee like Pete Buttigieg because a smart person defending the deficits, inflation and open border would be more embarrassing than Harris's word salad.
- He says there is no room for individual thought on the left. In the 1980s and 90s Stanford and Hollywood were liberal but had eccentric professors and candid private conversations. He says that is gone, including "in small groups at dinners behind closed doors."
- He thinks celebrity has lost its mystique, because celebrities now read as left-wing "ditto heads" who are not allowed to say anything individual.
- On the Democrats' prospects, he says "you go bankrupt gradually then suddenly." The 20th-century order (New Deal liberalism, political correctness, the university) lingered as a zombie into the 2000s and 2010s before unraveling.
- He started the Thiel Fellowship in 2010 to pay kids to drop out of college. In 2019 he heard an MIT president recite the same bromides as 2005 and thought nothing would change. He says five years later the collapse has been large.

chunks.heading: The Silicon Valley preference cascade
chunks.text:
- He describes a preference cascade. If everyone knows they are lying and knows everyone else knows, the equilibrium is unstable and can flip fast. The Butler assassination attempt and Elon Musk's endorsement gave people cover.
- He says Elon was "incredibly important" and "incredibly courageous," and asks what would have happened to him had Trump lost. Peter has known Elon for almost 25 years, and says for the first 20 he was left of center. Tesla was a clean-energy company and the Republicans were the people who did not believe in climate change.
- His explanation for the shift is that the left's "intellectual straight jacket" is not what Musk, Tulsi Gabbard, RFK Jr. or others signed up for. He says it is never enough to agree with 80%, and you must be 100%.
- His metaphor is the Empire versus a ragtag Rebel Alliance, uncomfortably heterogeneous, with a "teenage Chewbacca," a Princess Leia type and an "autistic C3PO policy wonk."
- He says much of the tech shift was prosaic corporate governance. Founders told him privately how hard it was to manage ideologically deranged millennial employees. In 2017 one big San Francisco founder said he might not be able to take more money from Peter because Peter supported Trump. By 2019 that company's hiring goal was to move headcount out of the Bay Area as fast as possible, because anywhere else is "less woke and less crazy and more productive."
- He explains the ambiguity of failing wokeness. For years the instinct was "a little bit more" wokeness. At some point it was exhausted.
- On his own role, he did not give money to the Trump campaign this time, and says the money would not matter (Trump was "insanely outspent" and won). At Aspen he deliberately said Trump would win by a big margin, which that liberal audience heard as scandalous because "the actual is the ideal" and predicting a win sounds like saying Trump deserves one.

chunks.heading: Stagnation, "Make America Great Again," and the second Trump term
chunks.text:
- His fantasy in 2016 was that Trump would force a conversation about stagnation. He calls "Make America Great Again" the most pessimistic slogan any presidential candidate had used in a hundred years, because it starts by saying we are no longer a great country. The first step is to admit that, and then perhaps the country can become great again.
- He lists stagnation problems: slow progress, a broken intergenerational compact, young people finding it much harder to get their footing, and an economy doing worse. He doubts the country was ready for the conversation, least of all the Democrats.
- He had worried about the first term as "crazier and more dangerous" than he expected: prosecutions, people going to jail, a circular firing squad and "uncompensated volatility" for those involved.
- On staffing, he thinks the second term will have a stronger bench. He blames the first term's hires, not just Trump's firings, citing Mattis (a general sitting on Theranos's board) and Bolton, who was picked for agreeing on Iran and disagreed on everything else. Trump, he says, is better prepared and the buck stops with him.
- He cautions that elections are "relativistic" (which candidate do you hate less) and governing is "absolute," so Trump will fall short of the pedestal. He expects problems to be harder than eight years ago: the border, Russia-Ukraine, Iran, China-Taiwan. He says the world feels like it is "sleepwalking to Armageddon."

chunks.heading: Trade, tariffs, immigration and the Georgist housing problem
chunks.text:
- He thinks tariffs are directionally a good idea, with nuance. Free trade theory assumed comparable labor standards, regulation and free flow of capital and implied near-equilibrium trade, so a chronic deficit signals something off.
- He argues the deficit has sectoral winners. Wall Street banks are effectively "long the trade deficit," because the dollars China earns get recycled into US assets. In 2006 the roughly $800 billion current account deficit required about $800 billion of "fake" financial products, and the correction fed the 2008 crisis. Losers include Rust Belt swing states (Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin), and fixing that is what JD Vance needs to do to win in 2028.
- He also gives a game-theory case. Threatened tariffs pressure partners to open up. He never wants trade deals negotiated by ideological free traders, who think they need to negotiate nothing.
- On 60% tariffs on China, he thinks it would badly hurt Chinese companies and be only mildly bad for US consumers, since production would shift to places like Vietnam or India rather than back to the US. The iPhone cannot be built economically in the US. A shift to Vietnam, "an evil communist country but not bent on world domination," would suit US geopolitical interests.
- On immigration, he doubts the 11 million deportation figure will literally happen. He is himself an immigrant, born in Germany, and his parents came to the US in 1968. He says Europe's immigration problem is cultural, while the US is still good at assimilation and its challenge is economic.
- He uses Henry George to argue that real estate is inelastic. Add 10% to a city's population and house prices might rise 50% while salaries do not, so the GDP grows but it is a windfall to boomer homeowners and landlords and a hit to young people and the lower middle class. He calls the Anglosphere experience "a Georgist real estate catastrophe" and says rent matters more than the price of eggs.
- His "cloning" thought experiment: 100 clones of Barry Weiss with competing talk shows might be ethically debatable, but the economics are the point. A Bangladeshi Uber driver in New York should not want many more Bangladeshis. He notes that public schools in Los Angeles have to teach in 30 languages and that the open border strained the social fabric (fentanyl, cartels).

chunks.heading: Universities, student debt and bankrupt blue states
chunks.text:
- He supports eliminating the Department of Education but says to pick battles. A concrete lever is the overhead charged on NIH grants, which can be reset by executive order. The aim is more money to scientists, less to the "woke administration" and diversity bureaucracy, without defunding universities.
- On student debt, he says it rose from about $300 billion in 2000 to approaching $2 trillion. Graduates of 1997 had mostly paid off by 2009. For the 2009 cohort, the median student with debt owed more in 2021 than at graduation. Debt grew faster than the economic value of degrees, outside a few fields such as computer science. It takes about 12 years to realize it is not working.
- He is somewhat sympathetic to forgiving the debt as realistic level-setting, but not a taxpayer bailout. The hit should fall on bondholders and the colleges. If colleges were liable for unpaid debts, most would go out of business.
- He expects an implosion without Trump needing to act. Illinois, Chicago, New York and possibly San Francisco and Los Angeles are close to bankrupt. COVID spending in 2020 and 2021 was in part a bailout of failed blue cities and states. Trump only has to "sit on his hands," as Ford did with New York City in the 1970s, which was popular with voters. He says "good money after bad" is the thing to refuse.

chunks.heading: Foreign policy: Iran, the two world wars and appeasement
chunks.text:
- On Ukraine, he thinks NATO's relentless expansion may not have been a good idea (the US would not want Russian troops in Cuba or Mexico), but that in 2024 the US cannot simply retreat without a route, and Trump does not want a repeat of Afghanistan.
- He distinguishes isolationism, the utopian Bush 43 neocon approach (the 2005 second inaugural was Fantastical) and a realistic middle. He says if the US deferred to Israel on the Middle East it would have a saner and more realistic policy, since the Israelis are realists about Syria and Saudi Arabia and see Iran as the one problem. When he first met Netanyahu in January 2009, a month before he returned as prime minister, the only thing Netanyahu wanted to discuss was Iran.
- His argument against an Iranian bomb is about proliferation and impunity. After the Soviets got the bomb in 1949, the Korean War started in 1950. After China got it in 1964, the Vietnam War exploded in 1965. In both cases the nuclear power could back proxies with impunity, and he fears the same from Iran backing Houthis, Hamas and Hezbollah. He adds that Israel and the Saudis had misgivings about the Iraq War because weakening Iraq strengthens Iran.
- He expects Rubio, Waltz and Stefanik to be hawkish on China and to prioritize China more than Biden or the Europeans would.
- His history of the 20th century: the two world wars teach opposite lessons. World War II says do not appease. World War I says do not have entangling alliances with hair-trigger escalation. To avoid World War III you must learn both. His contrarian weighting is about 60-70% World War I and 30-40% World War II, because we always fight the last war, and a World War III would look like gradually escalating conflagration that could happen overnight.
- Pre-1914 was also a deeply connected, globalized world. Norman Angell's bestselling 1910 book The Great Illusion argued that a world war made no sense economically, as little as London invading Hertfordshire, and it happened anyway. He says to ask where Angell was wrong and why the "great illusion" was not one.
- Asked about the far-right revival of Buchanan-style revisionism around World War II, he says he would never defend Hitler and thinks it is mostly a left-wing talking point. He adds that a self-fulfilling nihilism is a bad bet for any individual, since a white supremacist who believes white people are all losers will "eat a lot of donuts and move into a trailer."

chunks.heading: Science, skepticism, populism and the internet
chunks.text:
- His framework: science began as a two-front war against both excessive dogmatism and excessive skepticism. Today scientists can list the Skeptics (on climate change, vaccines, Darwin) but cannot name one place science is too dogmatic. He says that shows lost balance and that "science" in scare quotes is now more dogmatic than the 17th-century Catholic Church.
- On vaccines, he does not believe they lead to autism, but doubts current science could find it out if they did, because results would be suppressed. Autism has risen dramatically with no good explanation, and the question should be askable. He thinks it was a mistake to suppress COVID skepticism prematurely, since the Skeptics were right on the lab origin and the bat-market "politically correct Theory."
- He admits there is a point where skepticism goes too far, but says directionally institutions have been very unhealthy. He sees RFK Jr. and Joe Rogan as fresher than the consensus echo chamber, even if not right about everything.
- His NSA analogy: the DMV and post office are transparently dysfunctional, but the NSA is more likely badly mismanaged because no one can see in. He applies this to science: humanities corruption is visible, and the esoteric sciences (no progress curing cancer in 50 years, string theory) may be worse. He cites the fired Stanford president Marc Tessier-Lavigne's alleged decades of fraud as harder to see than Harvard's plagiarism case.
- On populism, he calls populism and democracy a "Russell conjugate": synonyms that are emotional antonyms, where it is democracy if people vote right and populism if they vote wrong. He says he shares concerns about both, since rampant majoritarianism tramples minorities and property. The US checks it with republicanism and the Constitution.
- His revision is that the US is not too populist. It has become less of a constitutional republic, replaced by an unelected technocratic bureaucracy or "deep state," which an advanced technological society with secrets partly requires.
- On the internet, he is hesitant to make everything about tech, since making it omnipotent makes it a scapegoat. He thinks it made things transparent and that markets get more efficient with transparency while scapegoating works less. Trump was "the first internet president" because the internet exposed how fake other politicians were.
- He argues no science fiction anticipated the internet's small-packet, 140-character modality, which hints at a deeper change in human consciousness. He still doubts how much it added to GDP, and says people are "embedded in the atomic world," so a shiny iPhone does not replace a decrepit subway.
- He recommends Martin Gurri's The Revolt of the Public, which predicted the dynamics without mentioning Trump. He cites Fukuyama's The End of History as the book that got it wrong. He says history did not end, with 9/11, the rise of China and Xi becoming president for life in 2017, and that human agency still matters.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel restates the stagnation thesis (progress in bits, not atoms since the 1970s) and argues AI may be bigger than the internet and could reaccelerate growth. He warns that a zero-growth "safe" world is not peaceful, that societies fray when progress stops, and that Europe is far behind in AI and in building new scalable companies. He also covers contrarianism as independent thinking, generalism, and longevity.

chunks.heading: Stagnation thesis: slowdown in atoms, progress only in bits
chunks.text:
- Peter has argued for about 20 years that since the 1970s progress slowed broadly. Progress came in the world of bits (computers, internet, mobile internet, software) but not in the world of atoms.
- Engineering fields tied to atoms (mechanical, chemical, aero-astro, nuclear) were already "a bad idea" for students to pursue by the 1980s.
- He calls it "not total stagnation but this broad slowdown," hard to measure because progress has many dimensions.
- The internet was an important growth driver in the late 1990s, bigger than anything else then, but perhaps not big enough to take civilization to the next level.
- He now thinks AI is perhaps bigger than the internet and has the potential to re-accelerate growth, "with all the good and bad things that come with that."
- His defense of the thesis today: now that AI exists, nobody disagrees that the prior decades were stagnation. It was proven in retrospect.
- He has "changed his mind to some extent" only in that AI may end the stagnation.

chunks.heading: Why stagnation deranges society: zero-sum politics and the broken intergenerational compact
chunks.text:
- When progress slows, "there's a loser for every winner," so society becomes zero-sum and politics polarizes.
- The middle class in the US and Europe expects its children to do better than themselves. The intergenerational progressive compact (material, health and social progress from one generation to the next) is what holds society together.
- When that breaks down, "the whole society starts to derange in very strange ways."
- Common misconception: people picture the alternative to AI as a peaceful, social democratic zero-growth world. He says that is not true, and the no-progress alternative "is also far from neutral."
- Democracies and liberal societies are in trouble because they lack a broad growth story of the future. People no longer think things are getting better.
- AI is not a panacea, but without growth, zero-sum parties on the extreme right and left will keep gaining ground.
- Europe and the US are "gerontocracies," societies run for old people. Young people find it very hard to get ahead.
- His first step on tech stagnation: "I don't have a comprehensive solution but the first step is you have to talk about it."

chunks.heading: AI risk, slowing down, and the China competition
chunks.text:
- On scenarios where a far-smarter-than-human system escapes control, he doesn't think probabilities are very high, but notes that even 5 or 10% "seems pretty bad."
- He rejects the conclusion that you should therefore always go slower. Doing nothing carries its own risk, and "you can never just turn the clock back."
- Slowing AI globally would need real, forceful one-world government. His classical liberal side calls that "a frying pan into fire... a cure that's worse than the disease."
- The realistic alternative is "fake global government": many conferences and empty statements, with a risk that the West slows while China does not.
- He says the Pope's AI encyclical works for the Communist Party of China: the CCP won't listen to the Pope, but people in the US might. He called the Pope "a useful idiot" for the CCP, while saying he is not claiming he is an agent.
- Asked about Chinese-spread anti-AI content on American social media, he is inclined to believe it but thinks it is not the main factor. "It's mainly what we're doing to ourselves," and he warns it is too easy to blame China.
- He wants the rivalry with China taken very seriously and is a "very tough critic of China."
- He pushes back hard on any moral equivalence between the US and China. He says it would be best for Europe to be a reliable ally.

chunks.heading: Moralizing technology: good vs. evil vs. bad
chunks.text:
- Peter says society moralizes far too much and asks for the antonym of "good." The moral antonym is evil. The functional antonym is "bad."
- Examples: a Ferrari is an "evil" car (poor miles per gallon) but competent. A Trabant is a "bad" car: it doesn't work.
- "If you're evil, you're at least competent... you're at least getting something done."
- Marlowe's Faust (a fake scientist, bad science, straight to hell) versus Goethe's Faust (pact with the devil, dubious means, but it works out for the best and he is redeemed).
- He says it is better to be good than evil, but "I prefer Goethe's Faust."
- The real problem to discuss: in a world where "99% of businesses, companies, people, political leaders, business leaders are totally incompetent," badness, not evil, is the issue.

chunks.heading: Europe's decline: far behind in AI, and the fear-of-success hypothesis
chunks.text:
- In his telling, the US is where AI is happening, China is a fast follower, and Europe is "extremely far behind," and it is extremely hard to catch up.
- Evidence from Palantir: sales to US corporations have accelerated tremendously in recent years because of urgency to transform companies for the AI age. Europe has much less urgency, with the attitude "don't do tomorrow what you can save for the day after."
- Two historical analogies:
  - Concorde: supersonic flight began in the US (Chuck Yeager, 1947), Europe was behind but caught up and overtook it. Not a free-market program, but something the US should support.
  - French Minitel (1990s): the internet was supposed to be French, and Europe dug itself into a deeper ditch.
- His assessment: on AI in 2026, Europe is further behind than Minitel was.
- Germany's usual explanation is a fear of failure. He pushes a different dimension: perhaps also a "fear of success," meaning not scaling something that works to an extreme degree like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg, but selling or exiting.
- Stat he cites: of the 50 wealthiest people in the US, only 12 are Gen X or younger (born 1965 or later), and 9 of those 12 made their own money. In Germany, 20 of the 50 wealthiest are Gen X or younger, but all 20 inherited it. Not one built a large new scalable company.
- Each such founder creates thousands of millionaires and tens of thousands of jobs. Germany once built great new businesses (late 19th and early 20th century, and after 1945), but this "really broke down since 1995."
- He says he has no answer, but it is the question to think about hard.
- From an American perspective, it is in the US's interest for Europe to get its act together, build industry and be part of building the future. Where Europe is far behind, it should work with America much more closely.

chunks.heading: Debt, deficits and drift in Western politics
chunks.text:
- Welfare states are very large, taxes "feel pretty high," and deficits are big. They might be sustainable at 0% interest rates, but rates are no longer zero, so there is "a compounding runaway deficit problem."
- Three choices: massively cut spending (the Milei answer), massively hike taxes (which would "completely shut down our societies and all growth"), or keep borrowing and kick the can down the road.
- For close to 20 years, since the 2008 crisis, the answer has been number three. He thinks that is close to ending, pushing countries toward socialist-level taxation or really tough austerity.
- He criticizes Merz: "the best idea Mertz has is just borrow more." He expects drift to continue for a long way because replacements lack answers either.
- Centrist leaders "systematically underestimate the scale of the problem." In Britain there have been seven prime ministers in 10 years, none with a plan to turn the society around. Each thinks becoming prime minister is the hard part.
- On Argentina and Milei: people are fascinated because "their past is our future," a century of subpar growth. He thinks Milei will be re-elected because the situation is so existential. He rejects the accelerationist Leninist idea that "the worse things get, the better," and worries things have to get a lot worse before they turn around.

chunks.heading: US politics: Trump, the Democratic establishment, DSA and 2028
chunks.text:
- On Trump, he says to ask him in 10 years. His 2016 support reflected the establishment's failure to deal with long-term problems: growth, globalization and endless Middle East entanglements.
- On the two administrations making opposite mistakes: the first brought in people who couldn't agree, producing internal fighting. The second overcorrected with loyalty tests, staffing the government with "not very smart but very loyal people."
- He worries the exhaustion that hit the Republican establishment (the Bush family, 2016) is about to hit the Clinton-Obama center-left establishment. Pattern he cites: 2016 Trump won the Republican primary and Hillary barely beat Bernie Sanders, then the establishment won in 2020 and 2024, and it may not in 2028.
- The Democratic Party is the establishment party, so a Democratic Socialist takeover is a much bigger deal, "like, I don't know, the end of America." He does not want it and calls it "a real danger."
- Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) data: created in 1982 as a fringe fusion, about 5,000 members. After the 2016 Sanders campaign, membership rose from 5,000 to 50,000 and median age fell from 66 to 33. He says it has energy and charisma while establishment Democrats "are all lame."
- 2028 forecast: if Republicans get wiped out in the midterms, Democrats will think they win no matter what and won't pull out all stops to block a Democratic socialist. He puts the chance of a DSA-type winner in 2028 at about 50%, and says he argued this with Fukuyama, who answered "No way. Can never happen." Peter: "I don't think history works like that."
- He says he is "still a Vance partisan" but thinks the key question is who the Democratic candidate will be. He backed JD Vance because he thought he was thoughtful, open-minded and charismatic, and says he helped him financially in the 2022 Senate race.

chunks.heading: The 2009 "freedom and democracy" quote and the AfD/Linke discussion
chunks.text:
- On his 2009 line that he no longer believed freedom and democracy are compatible: he says he typed the essay one night, asked a colleague whether it was controversial, and was told no. In retrospect, he says he should have been more careful and issued a correction two weeks later.
- His actual argument was for "depoliticization, a de-intensification of politics," aimed at libertarians who put too much faith in politics. He says he said nothing Montesquieu or John Stuart Mill wouldn't have said, and that he does not think voters' rights will be taken away.
- Weimar lesson: in 1932 the Nazis and the Communists together got over 50% of the vote. Once over half vote for parties that want to end democracy, "it's almost too late."
- On Germany: the Linke got 25% in Berlin, but 47% among 16-24 year olds, a very bad trend since those voters will decide things eventually. He makes the "pro argument" only to show that you must take young people's issues seriously (rents too high, impossible to build, hard to get ahead). He says the Linke has no solutions but at least talks about the problems nobody else does.
- On the AfD: it reflects the failure of centrist parties to find an inclusive economic future for Germany. He says they don't know how to balance the budget, and he thinks the AfD is wrong on Ukraine, China and Israel, even though he wants reasonable debate on all three.
- On why he cares about politics: "it's both toxic, but it's the air we breathe." He thinks he is not electable, and says it might be healthier and more profitable to ignore politics and focus on a business.

chunks.heading: Contrarianism, generalism, longevity and the Antichrist answer
chunks.text:
- On contrarianism: "the point is not to be contrarian for its own sake," since that just puts a minus sign in front of consensus. "The real goal is always to try to think for oneself."
- He grew up in Silicon Valley, and says founders combine an outsider and insider dynamic. He says people exaggerate the outsider piece, which tends to become playing the victim. He credits Alex Karp (Stanford Law insider, Jewish outsider element) and Max Levchin (left Ukraine at 16, grew up in a poor part of Chicago, straight-A student, "incredible drive") as examples.
- He explains his independence by broad interests: history, politics, economics, science fiction, the future, psychology. Against the Adam Smith pin-factory specialization of late modernity, he says "there has to be room for at least one generalist." He still plays too much chess online and was a scholastic player, calling it beautiful and "somewhat dangerously addictive."
- On kids: having four young children changes his time horizons. His oldest daughter "will be 81 years old in 2100," so he wonders what the 22nd century will be like.
- On longevity: early-modern optimists like Condorcet, Francis Bacon and Benjamin Franklin thought death and all diseases could be cured. He calls the abandonment of that "a shocking social decline" and asks why we won't even try to cure Alzheimer's.
- Cancer example: Nixon declared war on cancer in 1971 and said it would be cured in 5 years. It is now 55 years later, with only some progress.
- He suggests if biology is understood as an information science, in theory processes could be reversed, but he rejects mind uploading: "I wouldn't find it acceptable to be uploaded... I don't think it would be me," and holds a physical, Christian-informed view of identity.
- He says transhumanism's problem is not that it is too extreme but "that it didn't go far enough" compared with Christianity's eternal body. On boredom with eternal life, his answer is that it beats the alternative.
- His target for the years ahead: dementia, finding a way to slow or reverse declines in people's brains. He says biotech investing is "surprisingly difficult."
- On the contrarian-truth interview question: he gave his speeches about the Antichrist three years ago, thinking the view was extremely unconventional. He now says it is less contrarian than he thought: most people think something like the Antichrist is right around the corner and that there is incipient totalitarianism worldwide. His meta-level conclusion: people call the idea crazy but "they actually secretly agree with me."
