The money was largely squandered on white elephant projects, and often ended up in Swiss bank accounts held by Third World dictators.
- The deeper failure: the blow came from upper-middle-class, college-educated Saudis, not from "the favelas of Rio de Janeiro" or "Tibetan yak herders." Bin Laden inherited a fortune now worth an estimated $250 million, and "had he been born in America, bin Laden could have been a Rockefeller."
- He concludes that economically motivated political thought, "from The Wealth of Nations on the right to Das Kapital on the left," is incomplete, and that the essay's agenda is to reexamine the foundations of modern politics.

chunks.heading: Why the modern West abandoned the question of human nature
chunks.text:
- Peter says Enlightenment political philosophy abandoned the older questions: what is a well-lived life, what does it mean to be human, how do culture and religion fit in. "The death of God was followed by the disappearance of the question of human nature."
- If humans are approximated as rational economic actors (he notes even Adam Smith and Karl Marx agree), then people who seek glory for God or country look odd. But if such people are commonplace and can assert themselves with explosive force, that account of politics needs reexamining.
- The older tradition (Augustine's Christian virtues, Machiavelli's pagan virtues) saw humans as potentially evil or at least dangerous. It split into two incompatible streams, Athens and Jerusalem, which he describes via Pierre Manent as two "millstones" that wore each other down, producing the modern "individual" who defines himself by refusing all sacrifice.
- The early modern era tried to force agreement through violence: the Reformation, Counter Reformation, and the Thirty Years' War, which by some estimates killed well over half the population of Germany.
- The Peace of Westphalia (1648) is his date for the birth of the modern era. Questions of virtue and religion became private, and polite people learned not to discuss them. Hobbes boasted of running away from a religious war, and "Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori" came to be seen as an old lie.
- The Enlightenment was therefore "a major strategic retreat": the question of human nature was dropped "because it is too perilous a question to debate."

chunks.heading: Locke and the American compromise: capitalism fills the vacuum
chunks.text:
- Peter argues that economics and capitalism filled the vacuum, with John Locke as the main proponent and the United States as the greatest practical success. He says one exaggerates only slightly in calling Locke America's definitive founder.
- He reads Locke as understated and cautious: in The Reasonableness of Christianity he denounces atheists while quietly teaching that honoring parents does not apply to "unnaturally careless" parents, that wives may separate, and that self-preservation is "the first and strongest desire God planted in men." Avarice stops being a mortal sin and infinite accumulation of wealth becomes acceptable.
- Locke reduces human nature to power (following Hobbes) and leaves an unknowable "X" in place of human nature. That unknowability grounds classic liberalism: freedom of religion, speech, property and commerce, because nobody is in a position to challenge another's desires. He quotes Milton Friedman: "Capitalism is simply what humans do when they are left alone."
- He says America gradually shed Christian religiosity while keeping its outward appearances, with no catastrophic war on religion as in France or Russia, and that conservative moralists never realize the drift "had been a part of that original conception."
- Locke's blind spot is origins. He says there is little value in the state of nature, so we can ignore how property was first acquired and look forward. Peter counters with oil: most of its value exists in nature and the labor added is proportionately small, yet it is a large share of world wealth. The original expropriation of oil built as many as half of the greatest fortunes of the twentieth century. He cites Balzac's "behind every great fortune there lies a crime" and says the Rockefellers "had forgotten their own family history."
- Since 9/11 the West must "awaken from that very long and profitable period of intellectual slumber and amnesia that is so misleadingly called the Enlightenment." He concedes that in the long run power may go to those who follow Locke's capitalist rules, but "none of this will matter if we are all dead in the short run."

chunks.heading: Carl Schmitt: the persistence of the political and the problem of choosing enemies
chunks.text:
- Peter presents Schmitt as the extreme alternative to Locke. Schmitt agrees with Westphalia that there will never be agreement on religion, virtue or human nature, but says humans are equally condemned to be divided by those questions and forced to take sides.
- Politics is the choice between friend and enemy. "The high points of politics are the moments in which the enemy is, in concrete clarity, recognized as the enemy"; the enemy is "our own question as a figure."
- Schmitt argues you cannot escape politics unilaterally. A population that declares it no longer recognizes enemies "joins their side and aids them." Examples: the Kellogg Pact of 1928, and the pre-revolutionary Russian and French aristocrats who sentimentalized the goodness of the people while 1793 was coming. A world state is a logical impossibility, since it would end the friend/enemy distinction.
- Applied to 2001: Islam retains a strong religious and political conception of the struggle (more important than life and death), while the West is confused about what it is fighting for. Bin Laden could quote Cromwell and Pope Urban II "requiring almost no changes at all." The West prefers to see police actions against a few criminal sociopaths and no longer believes in a "Gott mit uns in heaven."
- Peter's challenge to Schmitt: a side that, like Hobbes, values earthly life above all will run away, and running from an enemy who keeps fighting means losing. But a Schmittian response, a new crusade, would be a Pyrrhic victory that destroys what distinguishes the West from Islam. "One must choose one's enemies well, for one will soon be just like them."
- He concludes that on Schmitt's premises the West must lose the war or lose its identity, and that after 1945, in a world of nuclear weapons, Schmitt's drastic solutions are impossible.

chunks.heading: The opposite danger: the end of politics, Kojève, and the Antichrist
chunks.text:
- Peter considers the inverse of Schmitt: a worldwide abandonment of politics rather than a world state. Kojève's end of history means humanity reverts to animal-like "conditioned reflexes," with no philosophy and no wisdom.
- Schmitt's version: what remains is "culture, civilization, economics, morality, law, art, entertainment." Peter sketches it as violent video games instead of wars, amusement park rides instead of heroic feats, soap-opera "intrigues" instead of serious thought, "a world where people spend their lives amusing themselves to death."
- Schmitt asks "upon whom will fall the frightening power implied in a world-embracing economic and technical organization" and says it cannot be assumed things would administer themselves. Such a world needs a "religion of technicity" with faith in unlimited power over nature.
- In Schmitt's medieval-Christian frame this "Babylonian unity" can be brought about only by the Antichrist, who seduces people with "peace and security." Peter quotes: "God created the world; the Antichrist counterfeits it... the age of security dawns; everything has been taken care of, a clever foresight and planning replace Providence."
- He links this to the self-administering world of Snow Crash and The Matrix, and warns the price of abandoning yourself to an artificial representation of reality is always too high "because the decisions that are avoided are always too important." The Antichrist swindles people out of their souls by making them forget they have them.

chunks.heading: Leo Strauss: esoteric writing and an exceptional framework for security
chunks.text:
- Peter frames the impasse: the Enlightenment never became global and came at a high price of self-stultification, while a return to the older tradition is too violent. He offers Leo Strauss as an attempted synthesis.
- Strauss holds that even in the most liberal regimes there are deeply problematic truths, so great thinkers of the past wrote esoterically, addressing "trustworthy and intelligent readers only." His thought experiment is a historian in a totalitarian state who publicly defends the official line but writes "three or four sentences" between the lines that arrest "young men who love to think." Strauss notes esoteric writing has the advantages of both private and public communication without the downsides, namely a small audience and "capital punishment for the author."
- Peter says Strauss therefore escapes relativism and nihilism: there is a truth about human nature that can in principle be known, and the great writers agreed on it more than their exoteric disagreements suggest. He notes the Straussian open agenda is only "reading the Great Books for their own sake."
- Recurring Straussian themes: the city and humanity, founding and origins, and religion and the best regime. He highlights that Strauss hints even America's greatness owes something to "her occasional deviation" from freedom and justice, and that there are politically incorrect taboos even in America.
- On action, Strauss holds "a universally valid hierarchy of ends, but there are no universally valid rules of action." In extreme situations there are no limits that can be defined in advance on just reprisals, and it is best to leave "these sad exigencies covered with the veil."
- Peter's own policy conclusion: America's checks and balances ("setting ambition against ambition") frustrate ambitious people, and merely political careers end in failure, but there are domains outside the conventional legal system. He quotes Strauss that "the most just society cannot survive without 'intelligence,' i.e., espionage." Instead of the United Nations, "filled with interminable and inconclusive parliamentary debates," he points to Echelon, the secret coordination of the world's intelligence services, as "the decisive path to a truly global pax Americana." He agrees with Tennyson on ends and differs only on means.
- He flags the self-referential risk: awareness of the city's problems makes unreflective defense of it impossible, so the Straussian project may become "a hastener against its will" (in Schmitt's terms, failing to preserve the katechon).

chunks.heading: René Girard: mimesis, the scapegoat, and the apocalyptic end of the Straussian moment
chunks.text:
- Peter turns to Girard as the thinker who may show the Straussian moment to be brief. Girard also believes there is a disturbing truth about the city and humanity that the Enlightenment whitewashed, and predicts a post-Darwinian "Origin of Religions" that will transform the sciences of humanity.
- Core claim: following Aristotle, "Man differs from the other animals in his greater aptitude for imitation." Human brains are "gigantic imitation machines," and the independent human self is a modern myth. Imitation extends to desire: "keeping up with the Joneses" escalates into rivalry. Envy, the mortal sin closest to mimetic rivalry, remains a cultural taboo even among avant-garde postmoderns. Humans have no instinctual brakes strong enough to limit mimetic rivalry.
- Girard calls the social contract the "fundamental lie of the Enlightenment." Instead, the war of all against all ends in a war of all against one: a scapegoat whose death unites the community and brings a limited peace. That murder is the secret origin of religious and political institutions, concealed by myth that the victim was guilty. Myth turns victims into gods, rituals reenact the founding murder through sacrifice, and every king is a sort of living god (the tomb is "the first pyramid").
- The cat is now out of the bag: we know the scapegoat was not as guilty as the community claimed, so archaic rituals no longer work. The myths that distinguished legitimate from illegitimate violence are unraveling, which may leave humanity without "limited and sacred violence" to protect it from unlimited, desacralized violence.
- Peter's applications: nuclear weapons are a dilemma, and mimesis could drive many states to acquire them "for the mimetic prestige they confer," so the situation is never static. He defines a "liberal" as someone who knows nothing of the past and still believes in natural human goodness, and a "conservative" as someone who knows nothing of the future and thinks the nation-state can contain unlimited violence. The risk is a synthesis of violence and globalization with all boundaries abolished (geographic, civilian/combatant, children, even self versus other, as in suicide-murderers). "Terrorism" is the word for this unbounded, apocalyptic violence.
- "Apocalypse" originally meant unveiling. Girard's version is "the end of the world, the Christian apocalypse, the bottomless abyss of the unforgettable victim."

chunks.heading: Strauss versus Girard on timing, and what the Christian statesman should do
chunks.text:
- Peter says the key dispute between Strauss and Girard is when the disturbing knowledge will burst into general awareness. Strauss, like Nietzsche's madman ("I come too early"), thinks the truth of mimesis and the founding murder is so shocking most people will never believe it, so it can stay with a philosophical elite. The danger is its popularization. Pierre Manent attacks Girard on this ground: Girard would bring "the destruction of humanity in the fallacious guise of non-violence."
- Girard's reply: there will come a day when no esoteric knowledge is left. Events will be "infinitely more eloquent than whatever we write," and the truths will become "simpler still; they will soon be accessible to anyone." Peter explains the difference as historicism: for Girard the Judeo-Western revelation is slow but irreversible.
- Peter ends with the individual choice between Jerusalem and Athens, citing Thomas More: Christ wept and left no example of laughter, while Socrates left no example of weeping.
- His prescription for the Christian statesman: no return to the archaic world or to Schmitt's robust political, no accommodation with the Enlightenment ("so many of its easy bromides have become deadly falsehoods in our time"), and no retreat into Bible study awaiting the Second Coming, which would end one's role as a statesman.
- Unlike Strauss, the Christian statesman knows the modern age is not permanent and that "all will be revealed, that all injustices will be exposed."
- His rule of thumb: "in every close case," side with peace. There is no formula for what counts as a close case. The cumulative decisions may decide whether the postmodern world is "the limitless violence of runaway mimesis or the peace of the kingdom of God."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 2015 conversation with Tyler Cowen, Thiel argues stagnation is concentrated in the regulated world of atoms rather than bits, and that the future depends on human agency, not automatic progress. He also covers conformity, the contrarian interview question, why to start good businesses rather than more of them, and why extreme optimism and extreme pessimism both lead to doing nothing.

chunks.heading: Stagnation is a story of atoms, not bits
chunks.text:
- Peter says the stagnation is a failure in the world of atoms, not bits. Computers, the Internet and mobile have seen heavy innovation; supersonic travel, space, new energy and new medicine have not. He calls it a "two-track" pattern of innovation.
- Core explanation: "bits were unregulated and atoms were regulated."
  - A software company costs maybe $100,000 to start.
  - A new drug through the FDA costs on the order of a billion dollars.
  - If the FDA regulated video games, they would need double-blind studies to show games aren't addictive.
- He says it is overdetermined, with many causes. His own response is not lobbying regulators to be reasonable; it is helping people "succeed at the margins."
- He also points to hysteresis: a history of failure discourages people, so failure begets failure. "No halfway sane parent would encourage their kids to study nuclear engineering today," while software draws people in because of past success.
- Signal successes in other fields could set precedents and turn a vicious cycle into a virtuous one.

chunks.heading: How the stagnation ends: human agency, not an automatic trend
chunks.text:
- His most natural hope is technology at the boundary of bits and atoms, with information technology broadening out to affect the physical world. Self-driving cars are his example of a significant innovation that would change a decent amount at the margins.
- Views on specific fields:
  - AI "feels slightly overhyped."
  - Biotech could see a lot happen but is heavily regulated.
  - He thinks AI is further away than the consensus believes, and that its story is "happening more slowly."
  - Self-driving cars might replace at most 1 percent of the workforce and raise productivity by a few percent; phased in over a decade, that would not be that transformative.
- He rejects the premise of asking for an indicator that the stagnation has ended. He does not think the future is a fixed thing that just exists, and he disagrees with Kurzweil's accelerating-chart vision where you "sit back, eat popcorn, and watch the movie of the future unfold." If everyone takes a nap, "the great stagnation is never going to end."
- His overarching agenda is to find some way out of the stagnation "by literally helping people to start companies that will change the world."

chunks.heading: Government has lost the capacity to do big things
chunks.text:
- Peter is pessimistic that government is where the stagnation gets reversed. "A letter from Einstein to the White House would get lost in the mail room today. You could not even do Apollo."
- Expectations have fallen: in the 1980s the SDI debate was first-strike weapon versus great defensive technology; today people say it was fiction that would never have worked.
- He thinks the 1930s and 1940s had real technocratic competence, and that the Manhattan Project and Apollo would be unthinkable now. The 1970s were when institutions started working much less well, and Nixon's war on cancer was "the first signal one that really went wrong."
- Government is a poor investor in technology because it lacks the ability to evaluate it. By his count, no more than about 35 members of the House and Senate have technical degrees, and two-thirds are lawyers.
- Solyndra example: a cylindrical panel has 2πr the surface area of a flat panel of width 2r, so it is 1/π as efficient, which ninth-grade geometry shows. The Energy Department, run by Nobel laureate Steve Chu, couldn't use that. The Republican critique blamed process and kickbacks, the Democratic defense pointed to a portfolio process; he wants focus on substance, not process.
- Private-sector coordination at scale is the alternative: Silicon Valley start-ups, and larger companies like his PayPal colleague Elon Musk's SpaceX and Tesla, which require complex coordination of many pieces. This is "not as big as we could do" with a well-functioning government, but he says that isn't realistic.
- On democracy: he now says it is unclear the US is a democracy at all. It is a representative republic modified by courts and largely superseded by unelected technocratic agencies. Many are "deeply sclerotic," yet the alternatives (for example Congress dictating Fed policy) seem worse.

chunks.heading: Conformity, original sin, and how Peter selects people
chunks.text:
- Peter places "original sin" in society more than in individuals: society is real and powerful but on the whole problematic.
- He says many successful Silicon Valley entrepreneurs seem to have a mild form of Asperger's, "missing the imitation, socialization gene." That is a plus for innovation, but it is also an indictment of society: everyone else gets "talked out of our interesting, original, creative ideas before they are even fully formed" and ends up opening the safe restaurant everyone understands, which is hypercompetitive.
- His own path: highly tracked in Northern California (an eighth-grade yearbook note predicted Stanford), then Stanford, Stanford Law, and a big Manhattan law firm. "From the outside, it was a place where everybody wanted to get in. On the inside, it was a place where everybody wanted to get out." He left after seven months and three days, and a colleague said it was like "I had no idea it was possible to escape from Alcatraz." He calls this a quasi-conversion experience: the value system was deeply corrupt and needed to be questioned.
- Two routes to challenging convention: being oblivious to it, or becoming aware of how conventional conventions are and thinking for yourself.
- He worries conformity is more acute than in the 1950s and 60s; the eccentric scientist or professor is going extinct because research universities leave less room for them.
- What he looks for in people is combinations of near-opposites ("Zen-like opposites... like 175 degrees"):
  - Really stubborn and really open-minded.
  - Idiosyncratic and different, but able to work in teams.
  - For founding teams, ask about the company's prehistory: how they met and how long they have worked together.
- He prefers mild versions of attitudes. Extreme pessimism says there's no point in doing anything and extreme optimism says there's no need to; "they converge on doing nothing." He credits German pessimism (his family spoke German at home for his first 12 years, no TV) as a corrective to Silicon Valley's "optimistic and somewhat desperate" culture.

chunks.heading: Contrarian questions, monopoly, and the Straussian reading of Zero to One
chunks.text:
- His interview question: "Tell me something that's true that very few people agree with you on." It is hard to answer not for lack of ideas but because the answers aren't things people want to say.
- He gave "the education system is badly broken" as a now-uncontroversial example (a TechCrunch piece drew about 350 comments, roughly 70 percent in his favor). The idea that every successful business aims for a monopoly is on "the border" of what he'll say; "the really good ideas are way more dangerous than that."
- The Straussian reading of Zero to One is that "perhaps you should not be an entrepreneur." He is skeptical of "entrepreneur" as a goal, calling it a vague, empty term like "I want to be rich." If the core advice is to build a monopoly, that discourages people who don't have such an idea. "We should be starting more good businesses and fewer bad ones," not more start-ups in the abstract.
- He said he did not think the tech scene was in a bubble like 1999-2000 (as of this conversation), because the public as a whole wasn't involved the same way.
- Vertical versus horizontal progress:
  - Horizontal progress is globalization, copying what works from 1 to n, and has something like a formula.
  - Vertical progress is technology, going from 0 to 1, and has no formula.
  - Every moment in the history of science, technology and business happens only once: "The next Mark Zuckerberg won't start a social network, the next Larry Page won't start a search engine."
  - He suggests being passionate about something you are good at that other people are not doing.
- Nonprofits: the contrarian nonprofit question is which great causes are deeply unpopular. He only wants to fund unpopular causes and asks "Why is your cause popular? Why is your cause unpopular?" Keep a counterfactual sense of mission: if you weren't doing this, nobody else would be. "Social" can mean good for society or good as seen by society, and the second tends to dominate, yielding "lemming-like, sheep-like clones."
- Advice to an institution: "I would always be long substance, short status." Chasing respectability means softening the edges.

chunks.heading: Globalization, geography and company names
chunks.text:
- Bet against globalization: 2007 was likely the peak of both the finance boom (a 25-year boom from 1982 to 2007) and globalization, "like maybe 1913." Be in places and industries not levered to globalization.
  - Long California, short New York.
  - Long Texas, short Virginia (DC and New York are centers of globalization; California and Texas are inward-focused).
  - Relatively long Japan; skeptical of London and New York.
  - Smaller countries are underrated for adaptability; New Zealand is attractive as far from the Middle East as you can get.
- Japan: he suggests it is now perhaps the least conformist, least imitative country, no longer the Meiji or 1950s copying Japan. It no longer thinks it can gain much by copying the West, and this is a critique of the West.
- Brazil: inward-looking, with four false dawns of bullishness over about 150 years, each tied to globalization hopes. Facebook's international spread was a proxy for inward-versus-outward focus; Brazil was harder to break into than the rest of Latin America. Example: OGX's founder, worth $30 billion in 2011 and about -$1 billion later, held offshore oil concessions but there were no Brazilian oil service companies to develop them.
- China: hard to evaluate; he suspects it is underestimated but hard to invest in, since you would need to be a well-connected Communist Party member.
- Fracking: roughly $450 billion went in over four or five years, and it is unclear whether it earns a return at $50 oil. The fortunes made in fracking were much smaller than in IT, which suggested it was a more marginal innovation.
- Company names are "often very predictive of future failure or success":
  - PayPal was a friendly name, "the friend that helps you pay"; Napster ("you nap some music, you nap a kid") was a bad name, and regulators shut it down within a few years.
  - Airbnb sounds like an innocent virtual bed and breakfast; Uber sounds like a bad German name from the 1930s ("What are you exactly above? Maybe the law?"), worse from a regulatory view.
  - Facebook beat MySpace: reading dominates writing over time, Facebook was about real identities at Harvard, and MySpace started among wannabe actors writing fictional narratives about themselves. "The whole product arc was implicit in the names."

chunks.heading: Science, money, inequality, longevity and careers
chunks.text:
- Science has gone "dramatically for the worse." Government money in the 1930s-60s accelerated research but politicized it. A good scientist is nearly the opposite of a politician (scientist interested in truth; politician has "a very troubled relationship with the truth"). A Gresham's law applies: grant-writing experts drove out eccentric scientists. Extreme specialization lets expert communities obscure this from the public. "When you use the word science it's often a tell, like in poker, that you're bluffing": we have political science and social science, but physics and chemistry are not called "physical science."
- Money: microregulations matter more than monetary policy. He would rather abolish most regulation and keep the Fed than keep zoning laws and other crazy rules and switch to PayPal, Bitcoin or gold. He thinks money should be linked to something real, citing the gold standard's discipline.
- Inequality: separate whether it is rising (probably in the US, unclear globally), why (he blames globalization more than technology, and it is overdetermined), and what to do (many remedies are worse than the disease; higher marginal rates incentivize loopholes). The real issue is stagnation, not inequality. In San Francisco housing costs are the biggest variable, and he'd break the "unholy alliance between urban slumlords and pseudo-environmentalists" that blocks urban development.
- Security versus privacy is a fake dichotomy of doing more with more or less with less; real innovation is doing more with less.
- Longevity: life is worthwhile in itself, and death is "kind of a bad thing." Wanting to live longer needs no special mission; the acceptance-and-denial attitude toward mortality converges on doing nothing. His straight-line forecast uses life expectancy rising about 2.2 to 2.5 years per decade since 1840, putting him in his early to mid-90s, plus perhaps 10 more years for an upper case of 100-110.
- Careers: he distrusts abstract general advice, since if everyone followed it, it would be wrong. Software still has too few people, and petroleum engineering is another underexplored field. Vocational careers like plumbing can pay about what the average doctor makes but are seen as uncool. Smarter people are often more prone to trendy thinking because they pick up cues more easily.
- Private cities: he'd be interested if one could be started for around $50 million rather than $50 billion, and thought Romer's African charter-city idea was prohibitively expensive.
- Chess: he always opens e4 even though d4 may be marginally better, because below world-champion level he enjoys the added risk and volatility.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a live Miami conversation with Tyler Cowen, Thiel argues for big-picture political theology over hyper-specialization and rejects both Calvinism and "muddling through" as distrust of human agency. He names a one-world totalitarian state as an existential risk on par with nukes or AI, and frames AI and tech around centralization and stagnation.

chunks.heading: Why Peter wants political theology back
chunks.text:
- He says late modernity is Adam Smith's pin factory "on steroids": hyper-specialization leaves people as "ever smaller cogs in an ever bigger machine," unable to see the big picture.
- Political philosophy and political theology integrate the facets of life. The Enlightenment set them aside because the questions seemed too hard or a "fool's errand," or too dangerous and divisive. Religion was settled by the 1648 Treaty of Westphalia, and "you're not supposed to have debates about religion."
- He calls that a reasonable 18th-century compromise, but argues that in the 21st century it is "maybe more dangerous not to think about things."
- He starts at human scale (politics, economics, society, culture) rather than micro or cosmic scale, which he calls a Socratic move.
- He sees a link between the university and the universe, and between the failing "multiversity" and the "crazed multiverse." His view is that you have to fix what went wrong with the university before you can make sense of the universe.

chunks.heading: Why he is neither a Calvinist nor a rationalist
chunks.text:
- Tyler argues that "religious but not spiritual" makes Peter a natural Calvinist. Peter replies that he is "still mostly a libertarian."
- On the five points (total depravity, unconditional election, limited atonement, irresistible grace, perseverance of the saints), he doesn't know if he agrees with even one.
- Girardian argument: gods and scapegoats are deeply linked. Calvinism is "an extreme form of scapegoating," where "Mr. God did everything, he determined everything." He says to be deeply distrustful of scapegoating God for everything.
- Intellectual argument: if you are too depraved to think, "we shouldn't be having a conversation."
- Medievals trusted the intellect and distrusted the will; moderns reverse this. Effective altruists and East Bay rationalists are "much closer to Calvinism." Outwardly they are pure and rational, inwardly "it's all just spaghetti code," and "you can never be right about anything. Maybe you can be a little bit less wrong."
- His shared diagnosis of Calvinism, rationalism and "muddling through" is distrust of human agency, human thought, and our ability to make choices.
- Against Catholicism, his "two-word rebuttal" is "Pope Francis." He grew up Lutheran and says the Reformation had to come from outside, since a centralized church could not reform itself. He thinks the Protestant project lines up more closely with a libertarian view, but admits he is "not a perfect Lutheran."

chunks.heading: Old Testament, victimhood and the woke
chunks.text:
- He holds a fairly orthodox Christian view of continuity between the Old and New Testaments. The Christian God is "maybe the original progressive," the first time the new is better simply by being new. Exaggerating the difference ends in saying the two Gods differ, and he says the progressive 19th-century higher criticism was "deeply anti-Semitic."
- The Girardian reading: the Bible repeatedly tells stories from the victim's side. Cain and Abel (founding of the first city, told from Abel's view) mirrors Romulus and Remus (told from Romulus's view). The Exodus is told from the Israelites' view, not the Egyptians' ("troublemakers and we got rid of them").
- On Tyler's pitch that history is bad so we should side with the woke, Peter agrees history was very bad and says conservatives err by whitewashing it ("happy slaves" is "a loser argument").
- He lays out three options:
  - Christian: history is terrible, so find a way to forgive.
  - Woke: history is terrible, forget the forgiveness.
  - Right-wing Nietzschean (Bronze Age Pervert): forget the history, "sick of this guilt trip."
- He thinks the in-between Christian position is the most tenable.
- Victimhood: he doesn't want a blanket rule against claiming it (he jokes he is "a poor and persecuted Peter person"), but absolutizing it is unhealthy. His test from the Harvard talk: "You can't say that you're a greater victim than Christ."
- His other canon is the Western great books (Shakespeare, Cervantes, Goethe), read with near-semi-divine seriousness, though he calls them less holy than the Bible.

chunks.heading: Carl Schmitt, Weimar and why history isn't cyclical
chunks.text:
- Schmitt belongs to the 1920s Weimar thinkers, after Germany lost WWI, when neither throne and altar nor liberal democracy was viable. They reopened political theology questions set aside since the Enlightenment. Peter notes Schmitt got entangled with the Nazis, which was "very bad judgment."
- His image: the dwarves of Moria who "dwelled too deep" and woke the Balrog.
- He sees parallels between the US in the 2020s and Germany in the 1920s: liberalism exhausted, democracy perhaps exhausted, questions to be asked "very far outside the Overton window." He adds that he doesn't think we are in a cyclical world.
- The Schmitt insight he values is from *The Concept of the Political*: politics is defined by friends and enemies.
- His example is the Reagan coalition. A millionaire, a general and a priest have almost nothing to talk about at dinner, yet the coalition worked because they shared an enemy, anti-communism. When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, the coalition disintegrated. Anti-communism was his own formative political idea as a teenager in the late '70s and early '80s.
- Where Schmitt goes wrong: politics may be a scapegoating machine that only works if you don't look into the sausage-making. His example is accusing a random elderly woman of witchcraft to unify a village, which "doesn't really work if you're that self-aware." Schmitt's optimistic Enlightenment rationality, describing politics as an arbitrary friend/enemy split, likely accelerated its disintegration.
- On cyclical history, he stresses what is "one-time and world-historical." He favors the Judeo-Christian linear view over the Greco-Roman one.
  - Thucydides' peace-then-war pattern is cyclical, and none of the details matter (he made up the speeches).
  - Daniel's succession of four kingdoms is unique and unrepeatable. Peter calls Daniel the real first historian, and says "Thucydides isn't even close."
- Science and technology give history a progressive character. We have nuclear weapons now, and "I don't know how you unlearn all the knowledge we've gained, even since 1900." He rejects Tyler's analogies to 17th-century England and the Roman Empire.

chunks.heading: The Antichrist, existential risk and the katechon
chunks.text:
- Apocalyptic dangers today come from a nonreligious place: science and technology (nuclear weapons, bioweapons and the Wuhan lab question, climate, AI). Girard noted that the Church stopped Advent sermons on the end times after 1945, so people wouldn't link nuclear weapons to Armageddon. The first nuclear test was named Trinity.
- He wants one more risk on the list: "a one-world totalitarian government. I find that at least as scary as the others."
- Biblical frame: you are supposed to worry about Armageddon and also the Antichrist, "maybe more" since "the Antichrist comes first." The path runs between "the Scylla of all these existential risks and the Charybdis of this political totalitarian catastrophe."
- Fiction: the best Antichrist novels are pre-WWI (Robert Hugh Benson's *Lord of the World*, 1908; Solovyov, 1900). Their Antichrist takes over by hypnotic speeches ("daemonium ex machina"). A post-1945 version would be *One World or None*: the Antichrist rises "by constantly talking about Armageddon and constantly telling us scary millenarian stories."
- The Antichrist's slogan in 1 Thessalonians 5:3 is "peace and safety." He argues we've moved toward peace-and-safety rather than chaos. After 9/11 we got the Patriot Act and tracking of money flows, not chaotic terrorism, and it is now hard to have an illegal Swiss account or exit the US.
- He is more worried about the humans trying to stop AI than AI: "A force that's powerful enough to stop the AI is probably a force that's powerful enough to destroy the world, too."
- He cites a 2019 Bostrom essay on stopping AI risk (culture change so nobody has heterodox ideas, global policing, global compute governance), which "sounds to me at least as scary as the AI." Dr. Strangelove versus Greta: if everyone has to ride a bicycle, "that requires some real, real enforcement."
- Katechon: the mysterious restraining force that holds back the Antichrist. He doesn't put too much stock in it, because it is provisional and you can't identify it with an institution ("if you're not supposed to immanentize the eschaton, you're also not supposed to immanentize the katechon").
- The Girardian risk is that the katechon is mimetically entangled with what it opposes and can become the Antichrist. Examples:
  - Claudius restrained Nero, but both were Roman emperors.
  - Anti-communism (about 1949 to 1989) was the katechon of the 20th century, violent and hard to justify morally, yet it stopped communism. It then morphed into neoliberalism and Bush 41's "new world order."
  - Greta presents herself as a katechon stopping climate change.

chunks.heading: Why "muddling through" is a formula for disaster
chunks.text:
- Tyler asks what variables he tracks for whether the West muddles through. Peter says it's not really empirical, and that granting the frame "you've already won half the argument."
- Post-Cold War globalization was the "you don't need to sweat the details" story, and he thinks the US-China relationship went differently than Fukuyama and others envisioned. Alarm bells would have gone off sooner without the muddle-through assumption.
- Globalization could lead to a neoliberal paradise or to the totalitarian state of the Antichrist. Libertarians weren't critical enough of the latter over the last 20 to 30 years and "didn't believe their own theories."
- "Whenever people think you can just muddle through, you're probably set up for some kind of disaster."
- Parallel to *Zero to One*'s chapter "You are not a lottery ticket": an investor who sets up a desk on South Beach and writes checks to everyone has a formula for losing all their money. He calls muddling through anti-intellectual: "It's not thinking about things."
- His default is that the default is really bad: "muddling through isn't good... You don't get to muddle through with Greta on her bicycle." This is why he favors AI even if the Luddites turn out to be right.

chunks.heading: Human agency, Girard, Shakespeare and Strauss
chunks.text:
- On agency in the Bible: Girard called Christ "the first political atheist." Caesar Augustus, son of the divinized Caesar, was not simply Son of God, so the Roman Empire was not divinely ordained. That opens room for a less unitary order, and for the individual, over many centuries.
- He calls Ayn Rand "a pretty good Christian in this way": "you just can't sacrifice the individual... your mind... your reason."
- Shakespeare as proto-Girardian: Marx says conflict comes from objectively different class interests, but Shakespeare shows conflict is most intense when people don't differ at all (*Romeo and Juliet*: two houses "alike in dignity"). So Shakespeare would distrust extreme ideological differences.
- *Julius Caesar* shows reenactment as a trap. Brutus is pulled in by his ancestor who overthrew Tarquin in 509 BC. John Wilkes Booth, a Shakespearean actor, reenacted it with "Sic semper tyrannis."
- Peter notes Lincoln's 1838 Lyceum address, which describes a Caesar or Napoleon figure who would "enslave all the white people or freed all the slaves," and suggests Lincoln was speaking of himself. He says we should want to transcend cycles of reenactment.
- Strauss and Girard agree that some truths are disruptive when unveiled. The apocalypse means "unveiling," and unveiling the social order may deconstruct it.
- Girard: "To see Satan is to see Satan fall," so Satan appears only at the end of the world.
- Libertarian reading: in the temptation in the desert, Satan offers all the kingdoms of the world, implying governments are "more satanic than divinely ordained."
- He favors truth over utilitarian reasons for religion, as in the case of Ayaan Hirsi Ali's conversion.

chunks.heading: AI, centralization and the questions Silicon Valley doesn't ask
chunks.text:
- He says Silicon Valley is bad at talking about AI: questions are "way too narrow" (will the next transformer improve 20 percent?) or "too cosmic" (the simulation theory). He wants the in-between questions.
- Wordcels versus math: he guesses AI is "much worse for the math people than the word people." Contacts told him that within three to five years models could solve all US Math Olympiad problems.
- His history of math bias:
  - The French Revolution favored math testing because verbal ability was thought to run in families, and math to be spread across the population, which made it meritocratic and egalitarian.
  - In the Soviet Union, honoring chess grandmasters and number theorists may have been a control mechanism, since they were "singularly clueless."
  - Silicon Valley today is "way too biased toward the math people."
  - His own late-'80s chess bias was undermined by computers in 1997. "Isn't that what's going to happen to math? And isn't that a long-overdue rebalancing of our society?"
  - On medical school: he doesn't want a neurosurgeon "doing prime number factorizations in their head."
- Questions he wants asked:
  - How much will AI raise GDP versus inequality?
  - Is it centralizing? His old riff: "if crypto is libertarian, why can't we say that AI is communist?"
  - Returns to scale on AI are so big that "even San Francisco will survive."
  - What does it do to US-China?
- On China: it may deploy AI faster and train it on all its people. But the US may be ahead, and Chinese models must be nerfed (e.g., can't say who Winnie the Pooh is). He asks whether a US edge, and a volatility-increasing technology China can't match, could accelerate China's timetable toward invading Taiwan "in the next year or two."
- He doubts the claim that AI is the only technology that matters. In the 1960s "technology" meant computers, medicines, spaceships, supersonic planes and the Green Revolution. Narrowing it to IT, then to AI, is "a manifestation of the centralizing stagnation that we should be trying to get out of."
- Centralization of computing is not predetermined. Late-'60s computers were imagined as centralized (2001, *Star Trek*'s Planet Beta supercomputer), the late '90s as decentralized (*The Sovereign Individual*, which influenced him), and the late 2010s as centralizing again (crypto excepted). He says "it's up to us" which way to push the technology.
- On open-source AI, he doubts it is the main variable, citing the Linux versus Microsoft precedent.
- Crypto: he is hopeful Bitcoin is on net on the "anti-one-world-order side," but notes physical cash may beat it for anonymity and that the crypto-anarchist utopia of the late '90s didn't happen. As a one-time way to move money outside a government's control, it is "still extremely good."

chunks.heading: Other views from the Q&A
chunks.text:
- **World order:** He wants "a libertarian world order of many nations" where you can move between them, with a transnational layer not strong enough to control the nations. He notes the globalization paradox that people confuse a Hegelian synthesis with "a superposition of the thesis and antithesis." Bostrom and communism both reach one-world government through Enlightenment rationality and optimism about human nature.
- **Scaling the Thiel Fellowship:** Scaling means automating and turning it into a "cookie cutter," which deranges at scale, "like some kind of Mao's Little Red Book." Advice like "think for yourself" can't be formulized.
- **Personal path:** Highly tracked as a kid (Stanford, law school, a top Manhattan firm that "everybody wanted to get in" and "on the inside... everybody wanted to get out"), then a mid-20s quarter-life crisis. His lesson is to avoid the worst mimetic competition, though he doesn't think awareness of it fixes anything.
- **DEI:** He is "very against it," though not always the most important issue. His 1990s book *The Diversity Myth* described campus culture wars, but he calls the arguments ineffective because drivers were on a different level. He calls DEI a distraction from the economy, science and tech and religious questions, and says "a real Marxist would be much preferable to a diversity person." Walmart was the "proto-woke company" of the 2000s, using green rebranding to split the anti-Walmart coalition.
- **Biotech:** The FDA has a "global stranglehold." Most governments won't loosen below it, so there's less regulatory arbitrage than it appears. US pricing means for a biotech drug it is "US or bust."
- **Miami:** He is pro-Miami, mainly as an anti-New York story where finance doesn't have to be centered in New York. He worries about a Georgist outcome, where all value is captured by real estate owners as in San Francisco, New York and London.
- **Next learning:** He is a hedgehog (versus Tyler the fox) coming back to "the wonderful and terrible history of the world that we're living through as Christianity's unraveling our culture" and how to get to the other side.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a 2014 conversation with Bill Kristol, Thiel explains how PayPal won through compounding growth, a fraud-fighting technology edge and a long-term plan, and why good businesses avoid competition. He argues conformity drives bubbles, technological stagnation is largely cultural and regulatory, and higher education is a zero-sum tournament bubble.

chunks.heading: Founding moments, durability, and building for the long term
chunks.text:
- Peter left a tracked career (Stanford law, a big New York law firm, a bank) after a "rolling quarter-life crisis". His test: do something where "if you wouldn't do it, it wouldn't happen", not a career where "a hundred other people" would take your place.
- He argues the frontier is not as wide open as in the 19th century, and technology is where a small group can still start something new with a big impact.
- He prefers "founder" to "entrepreneur". "Entrepreneur" is overused and sounds like "I want to be rich, I want to be famous". A better mindset: there are important problems to solve, and a new business is the form in which you solve them.
- He favors a long-term plan over the "random walk" of iterating with no overarching vision. From chess: "a bad plan was better than no plan".
- Most value comes late. A PayPal financial model from March 2001 (27 months in) put about 80 percent of the company's value in profits in 2011 and beyond. So "durability is at least as important as growth".
- Founding moments carry a degree of freedom that later disappears. He compares the Constitutional Convention: Alaska has the same number of senators as California, which has 50 times the people, and that will not change. The key company DNA is set early.
- On teams: talent often beats experience, because experienced people have "anti-theories" about why things can't be done. At PayPal the team ignored advice that fraud would be overwhelming.
- Team members must work together, not just be brilliant. He asks how long the founders have known each other and how often they have worked together. Starting a company with someone met a week earlier is like "getting married to the first person you met at the slot machines in Las Vegas".

chunks.heading: PayPal: compounding growth, one-way payments, and being the last mover
chunks.text:
- The core insight: only about 3 million US businesses could accept credit cards, but 150 to 200 million people had email. Linking money to email lets anyone with an email receive a payment, which solved the usual counterparty problem of needing both sides signed up at once.
- Growth: 24 people (the company's own staff) in October 1999, compounding about 7 to 10 percent daily. About 1,000 by mid-November, 2,000 by December 31, 100,000 by February 3, 2000, and 1 million by mid-April. Today about 120 million users (as of the 2014 taping).
- He wants positive feedback and snowballing, not "trench warfare on the Western front" where each step gets harder.
- It took off on eBay. eBay's own competing service was "a giant store that couldn't get its own cash register machines to work".
- On competition: "you don't want excess competition". The 20th person selling pet food online, or opening a restaurant in DC or San Francisco, has a terrible business. Good businesses have an "extremely unique character".
- The original plan was first-mover exponential growth so copycats could never catch up. In practice, "it's more important to be the last mover than the first mover". He cites Capablanca: to begin, study the endgame, because the last mover wins.
- That usually needs a technological edge. At PayPal it was fraud. The fraud problem deterred big banks, whose consultants said "too much fraud". Citigroup's competing effort failed because smarter people inside sensed it would not work and avoided it. Large corporations are "quite dysfunctional" with many bureaucratic levels and internal politics.

chunks.heading: The "political approach" to contrarian truth, and psychosocial bubbles
chunks.text:
- His interview question: "Tell me something that's true that very few people agree with you on." He admits he is not sure it is a good question, since people answer poorly. Typical answers are a conventional truth claimed to be even more true (worry about climate change even more) or trivial, esoteric truths.
- He stresses it has two parts: something others don't believe and that is true. "Brilliance is hard, courage is in even shorter supply than brilliance."
- He sees powerful psychosocial forces homogenizing thinking: an Internet bubble in the 90s, a housing and finance bubble in the 2000s, and in his view a "government bubble" in the 2010s, all marked by deferring to others' supposed answers. There was a big bubble in the 1720s and 1920s, but four or five of similar size in the last 30 years. Like an EKG with repeated spikes, "it might be a mistake to say that everything is normal".
- Two ways to find unconventional truths: a natural/metaphysical approach (work out fundamental truth) and a political approach (ask what people can't say or think). He prefers the political approach as more straightforward, "a shortcut".
- Example, clean tech: from 2002 to 2008 venture capitalists mainly invested in next-generation Internet companies (mostly worked) or clean tech ("an unmitigated disaster"). Evaluating each technology on its merits would have been extremely hard. The political approach saw intensely held conventions, social status ("it seemed cool"), and no interest in whether it made sense. That is why roughly ten times as much good money was thrown after bad in 2005 to 2008.
- He notes that many Silicon Valley founders have mild Asperger's traits or social awkwardness, which he reads as an indictment of American society: well-adjusted people are deterred from unconventional thoughts quickly.
- The worst founder profile is the Harvard MBA: extroverted people without strong convictions who look to each other and ride the last wave. He cites a Harvard Business School study: in 1989 they all wanted to work for Mike Milken (a year or two before jail), technology only in 1999 to 2000 (the two worst years), and 2005 to 2007 private equity, hedge funds and real estate.
- He worries that a more transparent, connected world makes people self-censor more than 50 years ago. He cites Nietzsche: madness is rare in individuals but the rule in nations and crowds.

chunks.heading: Human-computer complementarity (PayPal fraud and Palantir)
chunks.text:
- Two conventional fraud approaches both failed. One was human investigators (20 of them) hunting a needle in millions of transactions. The other was a "super-duper computer" that figures everything out, which would need general AI that does not exist.
- The winning paradigm was a hybrid: the computer flags somewhat suspicious things and trained people visualize the transactions. Getting the division of labor right was "extremely powerful".
- Palantir (started 2004) applies the same idea to counterterrorism. The pure-human model is characteristic of the CIA (no one knows what anyone else is doing). The pure-computer model is characteristic of the NSA (collect all the data, no idea what you have). The hybrid is "vastly more powerful".
- Palantir has a backend that combines databases that do not connect, and a front-end visualization engine for trained analysts to spot suspicious patterns. He says it helped connect dots in identifying bin Laden, and in SEC insider trading cases.
- His view: computers and humans are "fundamentally complementary", good at very different things. The dominant narratives (Luddite, or utopian where computers replace us) are wrong. "We have not asked the question enough of how can people work better with computers." A computer smarter than a human in every respect is "somewhere between science fiction and science fiction fantasy".
- On government technology: bureaucratic incentives work against sustained effort. He blames the DC contractor subculture, with billing by the hour and long, complex projects so "nobody really has responsibility". As a libertarian he was still shocked the Obamacare website failed: "this is not the Manhattan Project".

chunks.heading: Facebook: why he invested and why real identity won
chunks.text:
- He and Reid Hoffman invested about half a million dollars in Facebook in summer 2004, after Zuckerberg launched at Harvard in February 2004 and was already on about 20 campuses. It was a good sign that the only thing it needed money for was more computers, because demand was so high.
- Others were too negative on social networks after earlier ones came and went. Peter looked at intensity of usage, time spent and network effects. He initially thought it could be a media channel reaching all college students, not that it would get this big.
- Why it beat earlier efforts: 1990s social networking assumed fictional alter egos (pretending to be a cat or dog in an AOL chat room). People wanted real identities. Starting at Harvard helped because people represented themselves accurately.
- MySpace (Los Angeles) was about narcissistic self-presentation and writing. Facebook was about learning about others, and over time "reading dominates writing". He says the names themselves were suggestive.
- It opened beyond college in late 2006 or early 2007, after two years of college-only. Later additions included multiple languages, age groups, and the newsfeed.

chunks.heading: Technological stagnation: specific success masking general failure
chunks.text:
- Facebook is probably worth about as much as all other Silicon Valley companies started since 2000 combined. His framing: there are "specific successes that may be symptomatic of general failure". Facebook and Twitter are great businesses, and not to blame; the problem is that so few others are being built.
- Founders Fund's tagline: "They promised us flying cars and all we got was 140 characters." It is a dig at Twitter, which he says will last decades but is "probably not enough to take our civilization to the next level".
- Over 40 to 50 years there was big innovation in information technology (hardware, software, Internet, mobile) and much less in everything else. His reason: "bits are quite unregulated, atoms are very heavily regulated". Bill Gates in 1975 had no government checking his code; biotech and rockets face massive regulatory barriers.
- "STEM" is an abstraction. Only computer science and maybe petroleum engineering have been good careers for 40 years. Electrical engineering was mediocre in the 80s, and nuclear and aerospace were "catastrophic decisions for very talented people".
- Gadgets "distract us from the ways in which our larger surroundings are strangely old": phones in a 19th-century New York subway, a decrepit 50s and 60s San Francisco housing stock. "Bits making progress, atoms are strangely very stuck."
- Natural explanation (low-hanging fruit picked) versus cultural one. He is "very heavily on the cultural bias": a culture more risk-averse and less ambitious. People prefer the natural explanation because it exonerates them from responsibility. Evidence: the regulatory double standard, and SDI, which in the 1980s everyone assumed would work, while now it is assumed it never will, even though Israel's Iron Dome works remarkably well.
- Macro signs: wage stagnation since the early 1970s, most Americans believing the next generation will be worse off. Cultural sign: recent science fiction films (Terminator, Matrix, Avatar, Elysium) show dystopian technology; Star Trek retreads are a 60s throwback and The Jetsons a reactionary aesthetic.
- Energy: nuclear is still "the energy of the future" because of energy density, versus windmills and solar panels, which are less energy intensive and "retrograde". We could build much safer, cheaper reactors with political will and belief.

chunks.heading: Accept, deny, or fight stagnation
chunks.text:
- Peter says there are three responses to stagnation: accept, deny, or fight. Culture is dominated by acceptance (Democrats: an era of limits, lower expectations) and denial (Republicans, especially the Bush 43 era: growth is automatic, fix one or two policies). Both tell you "there's nothing to worry about, there's nothing you can do". What is needed is to fight it.
- "Technological stagnation" is not meant to demotivate: "there's a problem and we could be doing a lot better".
- Belief is a necessary precondition: "thinking you can do something is a necessary precondition for being able to do it." Example: Andrew Wiles worked eight years alone on Fermat's last theorem after 358 years of attempts; if he hadn't thought he could, he never would have.
- Hysteresis: Nixon declared war on cancer in 1970, promising victory by the 1976 Bicentennial. Forty-four years later no president would declare war on Alzheimer's, though about one-third of Americans at 85 have some dementia.
- Where it can break through: space (some deregulation under Bush 43 enabled SpaceX), Uber and Airbnb (technology outpaces politics, then tens of thousands depend on it so it is not shut down). But medicine is hard without a less onerous FDA. Things needing political cooperation up front are "quite hard to change".
- Globalization is implicitly anti-technological: splitting the world into developed and developing nations treats the developed world as where "nothing new is going to happen". His question: "how can we develop the developed world?"
- Politicians lack concrete visions. The last such speeches he recalls: Martin Luther King's "I have a dream" and Reagan's Berlin Wall speech. Obama's slogan shifted from "hope and change" to "the change we need" because change poll-tested badly. Pessimism in Japan and Western Europe is "somewhat un-American", leaving an opening for an optimistic story.
- He wonders if the US constitutional system can work without growth: legislating works when the pie grows (a bit for you, a bit for me). The 1930s strained all democratic systems.
- He is bullish on Silicon Valley (the most charismatic place for talent) and bearish on New York, the tracked, overly financialized path. Since 2008, tracked jobs (lawyer, banker, consultant) work less well.

chunks.heading: The higher education bubble
chunks.text:
- Peter calls education "perhaps the most anti-technological aspect of our society": if technology means doing more with less, it gives the same at higher prices. Real costs have gone up about 400 percent since 1980, after inflation, with no clear quality gain.
- He says we have an education bubble: things cost more than they're worth, with psychosocial dynamics and "abstractions away from reality". "Education" is "incredible abstract filler". Drill down: engineering, rigorous humanities, or education in the abstract?
- Investment vs consumption: people think they are investing by consuming, like buying a house with a pool as a frugal investment. His better frame is insurance against falling through the cracks. In reality it is a "zero-sum tournament masquerading as general insurance", where a third-tier diploma is "a dunce hat in disguise".
- Value is mostly selection and signaling, with little value-added learning. Test: if Harvard's education were as good as claimed, it would grow enrollment (say 1,600 to 3,000 over 20 years). Instead the only product that limits access this much is "a nightclub". Doubling enrollment would draw uniform opposition from alumni, students and faculty.
- Law schools: the top three (Harvard, Stanford, Yale) are very good, the next four are pretty good, 8 to 14 only for the top half, and for roughly 15 to 200 it is unclear whether it adds value for the bottom 90 percent.
- The college premium stopped widening around 2000 while costs kept rising, so years to pay off debt are rising and the relative premium has declined for 14 years. 2008 was a watershed as tracked jobs dried up.
- Reform: top universities, with rich endowments, resist outside influence. He compares the university system to "the atheist church": 2014 is like the Catholic Church in 1514, with a priestly class, indulgences in the form of debt, and a Reformation that will come from outside. He expects online alternatives to gain traction, and the non-elite colleges to change first.
- Elite schools dampen ambition: a Yale dean told incoming students "you're set for life". Peter says ambitions get "beaten out of them" and notes Caltech students convinced they can only be line engineers at Lockheed. His career version of the contrarian question: "what are you really good at that other people aren't that good at?" He wants a return to many paths, not a single track.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a Q&A-style interview promoting Zero to One, Thiel argues technology matters more than globalization, that capitalism and competition are opposites, and that missions beat trends. He criticizes failure-worship, spray-and-pray investing and the education bubble, and urges starting sooner and thinking for yourself.

chunks.heading: Startups, monopoly and the capitalism vs. competition distinction
chunks.text:
- Peter argues most people treat capitalism and competition as synonyms, but "I think they're antonyms." A capitalist accumulates capital; under intense competition, "all of the capital is competed away."
- Example: the San Francisco restaurant industry is "incredibly competitive but not very capitalistic because no one ever makes any money at it."
- Counter-example: Google is "a very capitalistic company" that has made enormous profits for about a dozen years and has had no real competition since it definitively distanced itself from Yahoo and Microsoft around 2002.
- He advises against joining popular trends: "You do not want to be the fourth online pet food company in the late '90s. You do not want to be the twelfth thin panel solar company in the last decade."
- Once something is a trend, many people do it, so there is lots of competition and little differentiation.

chunks.heading: Mission over trends
chunks.text:
- Peter prefers a sense of mission to a tech trend: working on a unique problem that people are not solving elsewhere.
- Example: when Elon Musk started SpaceX, the mission was to go to Mars. Whether or not you agree with it, the problem would not be solved outside SpaceX, and everyone there knew it, which motivated them tremendously.
- He says unique missions beat trends because "every moment in technology happens only once." Each is a unique constellation of technologies and people where the time is right for a new kind of thing.

chunks.heading: Contrarian thinking and convention vs. truth
chunks.text:
- Peter's high-level contrarian answer: technology matters far more than globalization. People focus on globalization (copying things that worked) and not enough on technology (doing new things). He wants technology seen as the main driver of progress in the 21st century.
- He calls "What do you believe that very few others do?" a harder question than it sounds.
- The core philosophical question, in his view: what do people agree on merely by convention, and what is true? "We never want to let a convention be a short cut for truth."
- His indirect version of the question: "tell me something that's true that very few people agree with you on."
- Silicon Valley is "laden with conventional thinking," possibly more than the rest of society, because the future is uncertain and there are few markers. When people are uncertain, they look to what others say about the future.
- When "everybody, simply, is listening to everybody else," that is "the definition of a bubble or of a mass psychosocial insanity." Thinking for yourself and breaking through convention matters even more there.

chunks.heading: Investing: concentration over "spray and pray"
chunks.text:
- Peter says investors spray and pray not because of portfolio theory but because they lack conviction and are too lazy to work out which companies will ultimately work.
- He objects to treating companies, and especially founders, as lottery tickets. It is morally bad and also bad investing.
- His reasoning: "small number times big number normally equals a small number." Thinking in lottery-ticket terms means you write checks without thinking and lose money.
- The alternative is to concentrate. A small number of positions (he cites five to seven companies per fund at Founders Fund) forces high conviction before writing a check of any size.
- He says Founders Fund's approach is the anti-lottery-ticket approach.

chunks.heading: Failure, success and relentlessness
chunks.text:
- Peter says failure is "massively overrated." Most businesses fail for more than one reason, so failure is over-determined. You think it failed for Reason 1 but it failed for Reasons 1 through 5, so the next business fails for Reason 2, then 3, and so on.
- Conclusion: people don't learn much from failure, and it is damaging and demoralizing. The death of every business "is a tragedy," neither a Darwinian nor an educational imperative.
- When asked who he thinks of as successful, he names Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk (a serial entrepreneur who has built multiple mega-billion-dollar companies), and also Jeff Bezos.
- What they share: they are relentless. "Every day, they start over, do more, get better at it."
- He rejects the "Facebook was a fluke, right place at the right time" story: the more you know founders like Zuckerberg, the less plausible it is, because of how hard they work, how much planning there was, and how much vision there was from the beginning.

chunks.heading: Don't wait; competition's hidden cost
chunks.text:
- Looking back 20 to 25 years, Peter wishes he had known "there was no need to wait." He went to college and law school and worked in law and banking, and only with PayPal did he fully realize you don't have to wait to start something.
- His test: if you have a 10-year plan, ask why you can't do it in 6 months. Sometimes the 10-year path is real, but check whether it's just the story you're telling yourself.
- On what he'd improve in himself: his younger self was "insanely tracked, insanely competitive." Being very competitive makes you good at the thing you compete on, at the expense of other things.
- A competitive chess player gets very good at chess but neglects other things because they focus on beating competitors rather than on something important or valuable.
- He says he has become more self-aware about the problematic nature of competition and rivalries, and doesn't claim to have extricated himself. His framing: "how do I become less competitive in order that I can become more successful."

chunks.heading: Growth, technology and unemployment
chunks.text:
- Peter gives a micro and a macro answer on unemployment. Micro: no one-size-fits-all; look at why people are unemployed (e.g. a rust belt factory job that no longer exists vs. a 20-something with a poorly advised major and a mountain of debt).
- Macro: the economy needs more growth. At 4 percent annual US growth, he thinks these problems would broadly get solved, but growth has been 1 to 2 percent for 7 or 8 years, which is not enough to overcome structural unemployment.
- He holds that technology is the key driver of growth, especially in a developed nation like the US, so accelerating technological progress and innovation increases growth and opportunity.
- Zero to One has an alarmist and a hopeful side. Alarmist: if we don't innovate more, "we will have a bleak and stagnant century ahead of us." Hopeful: the great ideas have not all been found, the low-hanging fruit has not all been picked, and "there are many great secrets left to be unlocked in the decades ahead."
- He frames the issue as cultural: what we need to do "to get back to the future."

chunks.heading: Fighting death, education and Bitcoin
chunks.text:
- Peter says the problem he is most passionate about is making real, continued progress against aging and death. About 100,000 people a day die, mostly from diseases linked to old age.
- He says people are in denial ("not a problem") or acceptance ("nothing you can do"), which are opposite extremes with the same passive effect. He wants an active mode: "there is nothing more natural for us than to fight death."
- On education, he dislikes the abstraction and favors learning over credentialing. He asks whether college is a four-year party (consumption), an investment, insurance, or a tournament, and compares elite universities to an exclusive nightclub like Studio 54.
- He sees engineering as "the opposite of education" because it is a specific skill. He expects less one-size-fits-all education, with big institutions "delivering less and less and charging more and more."
- Quoting a friend, he compares education today to the Catholic Church on the eve of the Reformation: people believe salvation requires a college diploma, and his answer is that "you're going to have to figure out your salvation on your own."
- He defends going to Stanford for undergrad and law school as not hypocritical because he never claimed one size fits all. The oddity is a society where the most talented all get tracked to the same elite colleges, subjects and careers. If doing it over, he'd ask whether he was doing it for prestige or from passion for the work.
- On Bitcoin: PayPal created a payment system but never quite a new currency, while Bitcoin created a new currency but not yet a new payment system. People speculate on it as a store of value rather than transact, so it must become a payment system too.
- His daily habit: sustained conversations with smart friends and long-time colleagues, not "an MTV approach where you talk to a new smart person every day."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Masters' close-to-verbatim notes of Thiel's first Stanford CS183 lecture. Thiel frames progress as horizontal copying (globalization) versus vertical new things (technology), argues startups are the unit that can do 0 to 1, and offers a contrarian question for finding what to build.

chunks.heading: Retail sanity, wholesale madness: the "0 to 1" framing of progress
chunks.text:
- Peter describes the world as having "retail sanity, but wholesale madness": details are well understood, the big picture is not. The challenge in business and life is to integrate micro and macro into one coherent narrative.
- He notes humanities majors learn about the world without career skills, while engineers learn technical detail without knowing why, how, or where to apply it.
- The best students, workers and thinkers join those questions into a single story.

chunks.heading: Horizontal vs. vertical progress: globalization vs. technology
chunks.text:
- Peter splits progress into two kinds. Horizontal/extensive progress means copying things that work; its one-word name is "globalization". Vertical/intensive progress means doing new things; its one-word name is "technology".
- Intensive progress is going from 0 to 1, as opposed to the 1 to n of globalization.
- Example: in 50 years China will be a lot like the US now. Cities, cars and rail systems get copied, maybe with some steps skipped.
- Most people focus on globalization over technology. Speaking of "developed" vs. "developing" nations is implicitly bearish about technology, because it assumes convergence on the "developed" status quo. Society believes in a technological end of history "almost by default".
- The two interact. If 1 to n is blocked by resource constraints (not everyone can have a car without environmental catastrophe), only 0 to 1 solutions help. Technology matters "even if all we really care about is globalization".

chunks.heading: Technological stagnation after the 1960s
chunks.text:
- Peter says that for most of recent history, from the late 17th-century steam engine to about the late 1960s, technological progress was tremendous, perhaps relentless.
- The industrial revolution changed how people make money: from taking it from others (plunder) to trade. Of perhaps 100 billion people ever born, most lived in essentially stagnant societies where success meant claiming value, not creating it.
- The 1960s were the peak of optimism: people believed in and thought about the future, and were confident the next 50 years would bring unprecedented progress.
- With the exception of computers, it didn't happen. Per capita incomes still rise but the rate is decelerating, and median wages have been stagnant since 1973.
- He compares the result to Alice in Wonderland: people run harder (longer hours) just to stay in place.
- Computers are the exception: Moore's/Kryder's/Wirth's laws held, and hardware plus agile development are a model for other industries. That is why CS is the logical place to start recapturing progress.

chunks.heading: Why 0 to 1 can't be taught, and the limits of case studies
chunks.text:
- Peter argues that teaching innovation is almost a contradiction in terms, because education is about 1 to n: observe, imitate, repeat. Infants learn existing languages rather than invent new ones.
- Crossing T's and dotting I's (incorporation, pitching VCs) gets you maybe 30% of the way. Then you must do something important and do it right, which can't be taught.
- Echoing Tolstoy: all successful companies are different, having solved 0 to 1 in different ways; all failed companies are the same, having botched it.
- Case studies of PayPal and Facebook are of limited use because it's hard to know what was path-dependent. The next great company may not be an e-payments or social network company. The business school case method is "more mythical than helpful".
- Exceptionalism is a problem for anyone doing something new, who must ask "am I sane? Or am I crazy?" Example: some 20,000 people move to Los Angeles each year to become famous actors, and very few do. Startups are probably less plagued by this than Hollywood, but not immune.

chunks.heading: Determinism vs. indeterminism: the calculus metaphor
chunks.text:
- In 1 to n you can analyze statistically. In 0 to 1 it isn't a statistical question: "the standard deviation with a sample size of 1 is infinite."
- Society thinks about the future statistically and probabilistically, as random. If markets follow a random walk, there's no point out-calculating them.
- Peter offers calculus as the alternative metaphor: figuring out exactly what will happen. Apollo had to know where the moon would be and whether the rocket had enough fuel. "No one would want to ride in a statistically, probabilistically-informed spaceship."
- Startups are like the space program: going 0 to 1 has to favor determinism over indeterminism.
- The practical problem: people who claim to know the future are called prophets, and "in our society, all prophets are false prophets". Steve Jobs finessed the line; people sensed he was a visionary but he didn't go too far, and he "probably cut it as close as possible (and succeeded accordingly)".
- Separating luck from skill is difficult or impossible and invites fallacious reasoning. Entrepreneurs should at least have a handle on the question.

chunks.heading: Four theories of the future of intensive progress
chunks.text:
- Convergence: growth rose quickly after the industrial revolution, then technology decelerates and growth becomes asymptotic.
- Cyclical: advances and retrenchments repeat. Probably true historically, but hard to believe now; losing all accumulated know-how "strains credulity".
- Collapse/destruction: some technological advance does us in.
- Singularity: technological development produces an AI or intellectual event horizon.
- People overestimate the likelihood and explanatory power of convergence and cyclical theories, and so probably underestimate destruction and singularity.

chunks.heading: Why companies, why startups: coordination costs and small teams
chunks.text:
- Peter applies the Coase Theorem: companies exist because they optimally balance internal and external coordination costs. As an entity grows, internal costs rise and external costs fall.
- Totalitarian government is the extreme: external coordination costs are zero, but internal coordination is hard (Hayek and the Austrians showed central planning doesn't work). Independent contractors are the opposite extreme: zero internal costs, but paralyzing external costs. Firm size is finding the right mix.
- Above about 100 people, employees don't all know each other, politics matter, incentives change, and signaling work can matter more than doing it. These costs are almost always underestimated.
