- Red flags: professional investors should and do reconsider before investing in companies with more than one office; even a multi-floor office can cause coordination problems. Hiring consultants and outsourcing key development are also serious red flags.
- Path's limit of 150 "friends" is illustrative, and ancient tribes apparently had a natural size limit near that number.
- If a business's size and complexity scale like the square of the number of people, startups are uniquely positioned to lower internal costs and get things done.
- A computer couldn't model all of a company's costs even if it modeled the economics, since it would have to model human irrationality, emotion and interaction.

chunks.heading: Why do a startup, the costs of failure, and where to start
chunks.text:
- Peter's negative answer: you can't develop new technology in existing entities. Big companies, governments and nonprofits can't recognize financial needs (the federal government over- and under-compensates), and can't give personal recognition, respect or fame. Anyone on a 0 to 1 mission needs to be surrounded by others who want the same, which happens in startups.
- On motives: money alone is a weak reason. Research shows happiness rises with income only up to about $70,000 per year. Fame is questionable. A better motive is a desire to change the world (he points to the US in 1776-79 as a startup of sorts). Culture matters: in Japan entrepreneurs are seen as reckless and the respectable path is lifelong employment. He raises the line "behind every fortune lies a great crime" and asks whether founders are criminals.
- Financial losses from a startup's lower pay aren't that high. Non-financial costs are higher: a failed startup may teach nothing useful, or teach you to fail again and become more risk-averse. "You aren't a lottery ticket," so failure isn't just 1 of n tries.
- A failed 0 to 1 startup has low financial and low non-financial costs; you'll learn a lot. A 1 to n startup has especially low financial costs but higher non-financial ones. Example: if "Groupon for Madagascar" fails, "it's not clear where exactly you are."
- Three starting questions: What is valuable? What can I do? What is nobody else doing? In academia the cardinal sin is plagiarism, not triviality; in business, valuable output is what counts.
- Intellectual version: "What important truth do very few people agree with you on?" Business version: "What valuable company is nobody building?"
- Test: an answer like "our educational system is broken and urgently requires repair" is wrong because many agree with it. Right answers take the form: "Most people believe in X. But the truth is !X."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel's Class 2 lecture recounts the 1990s and the PayPal mania, then argues the world and Silicon Valley drew mostly wrong lessons from the crash (incrementalism, lean, no talk of the future). Bubble and anti-bubble thinking are both social thinking; the truly contrarian move is to think for yourself about what is valuable.

chunks.heading: "Late to the party": why Peter says you must know the 1990s to understand startups today
chunks.text:
- Peter treats history as an "extended dinner conversation" that each generation is born into. A toddler in 1969 technically lived through the 1960s but missed the civil rights and Vietnam debates.
- He argues today's students (2012) are in the same position relative to 1999. To join the conversation about startups, you have to know the history of the '90s. He says it is questionable whether you can understand startups without knowing Webvan or recognizing the Pets.com mascot.
- History often turns out different from what people living through it thought. Even '90s entrepreneurs struggle to piece it together, and why things happened is harder than what happened.
- Most of the 1990s was not the dot-com bubble. The mania started in September 1998 and lasted about 18 months.

chunks.heading: Why money flowed into tech: the 1990s as a proof by elimination
chunks.text:
- The decade started with the Berlin Wall falling (Nov 1989), then 2 months of euphoria, then a long, drawn-out recession (first such post-WWII). Technically it ended March 1991, but through the end of 1994 it still felt like recession. Manufacturing never fully rebounded.
- Culture reflected hopelessness (Nirvana, grunge, heroin). NAFTA and competitiveness worries fueled Ross Perot's third-party run. George H.W. Bush became the only one-term President in 30 years.
- In the late 1980s Stanford felt disconnected from the Valley, Japan seemed to be winning the semiconductor war, and focusing on tech was idiosyncratic.
- Netscape's August 1995 IPO made the public aware of the Internet. It was unprofitable, priced at $14, doubled before trading, doubled again on day one, and hit $160 within 5 months. Netscape poked Microsoft (posters on the Redmond campus), Gates redirected Microsoft to the Internet, IE followed, and Netscape's antitrust claims were what let it sell to AOL for over a billion dollars.
- Xanadu had the two-way network idea in 1963 but needed everyone to adopt at once. It kept attracting venture funding for about 29 years and died in 1992.
- Yahoo IPO'd in 1996 at a $350M valuation, Amazon in 1997 at $460M. NASDAQ was about 1400 in late 1998, only about 400 above August 1995.
- Meanwhile everything else was failing: Greenspan's "irrational exuberance" speech (1996), the 1997 East Asian crises, the 1998 Russian ruble crisis (banks bust and currency worthless: "Zero times zero is zero"), the LTCM blowup ("picking up nickels in front of a bulldozer," needing a multibillion Fed bailout), and a Euro that lost value after its January 1999 launch.
- His conclusion: old economy, emerging markets, Europe and leverage all looked broken, so "by the late '90s, a process of elimination left only one good place to put money: in tech."
- Caveat he flags: proof by contradiction is dangerous ("even if something's not A, B, C, or D, it doesn't necessarily follow that the truth is E"). But he says indirect proof had real purchase here.

chunks.heading: The mania (Sept 1998 to March 2000): what it looked like
chunks.text:
- Peter says the best way to convey it is crazy stories, and that surfaces matter: "quite often, the surface of things is actually the heart of things." Themes: extremely social, irrationally exuberant, money everywhere, lots of sketchy people.
- Examples: 40-year-old Stanford grad students starting dozens of companies at once; billionaires from Idaho flying in to fund anyone with a polished pitch; broke founders paying $1,000 dinner bills in shares; an exclusive email list ranking the day's launch parties.
- Business models where the more you sold, the more you lost (the SNL pennies-at-the-bank skit): "It's okay... we'll make it up in volume." Adding ".com" to a name roughly doubled value overnight.
- Yahoo replaced Netscape as the most hubristic company. In 2000 it told PayPal to think about who it sold to, because a stock-for-stock deal needed a sound buyer; Yahoo considered itself one because its stock, it said, "always goes up."
- VA Linux: Larry Augustin nearly closed it in 1997. It IPO'd at $30 in 1999, traded to $300 on day one (biggest first-day gain ever), making his 10% stake about $1B. Six months later, at the end of lock-up, it was down 90%, then fell another 90%. He ended with $5-6M.
- Filtering the sketchy: Max Levchin's "aura test." Listen to someone for 15 seconds, decide if the aura is good, and walk away if not. Peter implies companies that did something like this were likelier to survive.

chunks.heading: PayPal in the mania: hiring, pivots, and growth by giving away money
chunks.text:
- PayPal started December 1998, late in the boom. Founders agreed they couldn't afford to hire sketchy people, "So they just hired their friends instead."
- The original idea was beaming money over Palm Pilots, voted one of the 10 worst business ideas of 1999. One angel only wanted to know who else was investing, then consulted a fortune cookie, which said invest.
- Nokia Ventures put in $4.5M, but mobile Internet didn't work yet, so PayPal announced a pivot at the first post-investment board meeting to account-based payments to any email address. It felt too easy, so 1999 was frantic: move fast or fail.
- Ads were too expensive. BD deals with big banks went nowhere (the HSBC London meeting, where Luke Nosek and the team concluded over Häagen-Dazs that "BD didn't work"). They needed organic, viral growth, so they gave people money: $10 for signing up, $10 for each referral. They paid $20 per new customer.
- Result: 7 to 10% daily growth and 100 million users (his wording), but no revenue and an exponentially growing cost structure. Peter says it worked out but "does not mean it's the best way to run a company. Indeed, it probably isn't."
- Valuation by press: a Feb 16, 2000 WSJ piece gave a back-of-envelope $500M valuation, and the next round's lead accepted it as authoritative. In March 2000 a South Korean firm wired $5M to PayPal's law firm with no documents and refused to say where to return it ("You have to take it"). PayPal closed a $100M round on March 31, just before the crash.

chunks.heading: The crash and the schadenfreude era
chunks.text:
- The collapse came in waves: marketing-driven e-commerce in the first half of 2000, B2B in the second half, telecoms in 2001. Military defense stocks were at the lowest in March 2000 (nobody believed in war) and then rose for most of the next decade.
- Hubris gave way to schadenfreude ("we were right all along") and cultural depression.
- PayPal broke even in 2001, fixed fraud and customer service problems, and filed its IPO in late September 2001, the first company to file after 9/11. The "Earth to Palo Alto" article ridiculed it, saying the US needed PayPal "as much as it does an anthrax epidemic."

chunks.heading: Lessons the world and Silicon Valley took, and why Peter says they were overreactions
chunks.text:
- World's lessons: tech was a bubble; go from "clicks" back to "bricks" (housing, emerging markets); Buffett-style avoidance of tech; only profit matters; globalization over technology; the future is indeterminate and "all prophets are false prophets."
- Peter says these are "probably all wrong," driven by "hubris, envy, and resentment against the '90s." "When base emotions are driving, analysis becomes untrustworthy." People were right about much in the '90s, and March 2000 "was still a peak of clarity as well" as a peak of insanity.
- Silicon Valley's post-bust rules:
  - Incrementalism; grand visions out.
  - "Lean": don't know what you'll do, experiment and iterate.
  - Zero advertising: "If your growth isn't viral, it's fake."
  - Anti-social as the new social (Google as the iconic product for people who'd rather interact with computers).
  - Product over BD: smart non-engineers did BD in 1999, product in 2001; Larry Ellison-style salesperson CEOs gave way to Steve Jobs-style product CEOs.
  - Distrust rapid monetization; longer growth phase, later IPO, reinvest profits.
  - Don't discuss the future, or you look weird and crazy.
- His verdict: a "strategic retreat" that was necessary in part (why IPO early into a hostile market?) but "probably overblown." He asks whether you should really never advertise, never do BD/sales, or never talk about the future, and says "we should be open to idea that some or much of the retreat... was overreaction."

chunks.heading: Are we in a bubble? Why he calls it the wrong question
chunks.text:
- In 2012 many said yes. Peter says the bubble-vs-no-bubble debate is the wrong question, and some froth (more Stanford CS majors than in '99, rising valuations) doesn't prove the thesis.
- His definition: a bubble requires "(1) widespread, intense belief that's (2) not true." But "people don't really believe in anything in our society anymore," so there can't be a bubble without intense belief. The bubble narrative comes from people "looking for a bubble," which is more overreaction to the pain of the '90s than analysis.
- Anti-bubble thinking ("everything will work, buy houses and tech stocks") is probably somewhat truer, but he says to resist it too. Both hold that truth is social.
- On contrarianism: "if the herd isn't thinking at all, being contrarian—doing the opposite of the herd—is just as random and useless."
- The truly contrarian move is to "think for yourself." The better question is what is valuable, then specifically: is company X valuable, why, and how do we figure that out. He says the next class takes this up.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Great companies create value, last, and capture some of it. Thiel argues tech value sits far in the future, so durability (being the last mover) matters most. Perfect competition destroys profit; monopoly is the real default for valuable businesses, and bigger markets are not better.

chunks.heading: Value comes from durability and capture, not just creation
chunks.text:
- Peter says great companies do three things: they create value, they last, and they capture some of the value they create.
- Creating value is necessary but not sufficient. Disk drive companies of the 1980s created a lot of value with better drives, but were all replaced by others.
- Capturing value is separate from creating it. Isaac Newton created immense value and captured little of it. Airlines create value for the public and employ many people, but "have never really made any money."
- On first mover advantage: a first mover can fade away. He argues "more important than being the first mover is being the last mover."
- He cites Capablanca: to succeed, "you must study the endgame before everything else."
- Last movers build non-commoditized, relationship-driven businesses that create value, last and make money.

chunks.heading: Valuation: multiples, PEG and why tech value sits 10-15 years out
chunks.text:
- Multiples and comparables "sort of" work, but Peter warns that social heuristics substitute for rigorous analysis. If everyone at an incubator invests at a $10M cap, the company gets deemed worth $10M.
- Software companies are often valued around 10x annual revenue. Guy Kawasaki's joke formula: pre-money valuation = ($1M x engineers) - ($500k x MBAs).
- P/E ratio = market value per share / earnings per share. It ignores growth.
- PEG = P/E divided by annual earnings growth. He says PEG should be less than one, and is a good indicator to watch while growing a business.
- Real valuation sums discounted future cash flows (time value of money), because money today is worth more than money later and the future carries risk.
- In a growth model you want growth rate g above discount rate r. Growth must eventually decline, otherwise the company approaches infinite value.
- Old Economy businesses in decline hold most value in the near term. If a company can maintain present cash flows for 5 or 6 years, value investors see a good investment.
- Tech and high-growth companies usually lose money at first. A typical model could see about 2/3 of the value created in years 10 through 15.
- He argues startup culture wrongly thinks in months and quarters, in "Old Economy mode," and "pointedly ignores, and even resists, 10-15 year thinking."

chunks.heading: PayPal and LinkedIn as long-horizon valuation examples
chunks.text:
- PayPal: 27 months in, its growth rate was 100%. The team expected deceleration but a rate still above the discount rate. The plan was for most of the value to arrive around 2011.
- That horizon undershot. The discount rate came in lower than expected and growth was still a healthy 15%, so most of PayPal's value now looked likely to come around 2020.
- LinkedIn: market cap around $10B and a P/E of about 850. Discounted cash flow makes it make sense: about $2B of value expected between 2012 and 2019, and the other $8B reflects 2020 and beyond.
- His conclusion on LinkedIn: the valuation only makes sense if the company is durable, "around to create all that value in the decades to come."

chunks.heading: Perfect competition vs monopoly
chunks.text:
- In perfect competition no firm makes economic profit. Profits attract entrants and erase themselves; losses force exits. The firm is a price taker whose scale is negligible against the market.
- A monopoly owns its market and is a price setter.
- Peter says economics textbooks spend most of their time on perfect competition and treat monopoly as a small exception. He asks whether monopoly is instead "a valid alternative paradigm in its own right" and perfect competition only the default in textbooks.
- Most great tech companies have one decisive advantage, such as economies of scale or uniquely low production costs, that makes them monopoly-esque. A drug company with a patent can charge above its production cost.
- "The really valuable businesses are monopoly businesses": last movers whose value is sustained instead of eroded by competition.
- His point about intensity: "the more intense the competition, the less likely you'll be able to capture any value at all." Under perfect competition you "compete hard, but you can never gain anything for all your struggle."

chunks.heading: The case for and against monopoly
chunks.text:
- Cons he lists: lower output and higher prices than competitive markets, price setting, price discrimination (capturing more consumer surplus), and complacency that stifles innovation because profits arrive either way.
- The counter-argument: monopoly can incentivize innovation. If a company builds something dramatically better than the next best thing, the gap between its price and marginal cost is "the creators' reward for creating the new thing."
- Monopolistic firms can do better long-term planning and fund deeper projects because of durability. Under perfect competition, profits are zero and that durability does not exist.
- Adam Smith's view, quoted: "People of the same trade seldom meet together... but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices." Peter says the idea that monopoly is bad is usually accepted as a given and deserves questioning.
- Legal and measurement tools he walks through: the Sherman Act ("monopoly power will not be found unlawful unless it is accompanied by an element of anticompetitive conduct") and three DOJ tests.
  - Lerner index = (price - marginal cost) / price; 0 is perfect competition, 1 is monopoly. Hard to compute externally, but tech companies know their own numbers and should watch it.
  - Herfindahl-Hirschman index: sum of squared market shares of the top 50 firms. Under 0.15 is competitive, 0.15 to 0.25 concentrated, over 0.25 highly concentrated and possibly monopolistic.
  - m-firm concentration ratio: sum the shares of the 4 or 8 largest firms; over 70% means a concentrated market.

chunks.heading: Why people overvalue competition, and why small markets win
chunks.text:
- Peter says people are biased toward perfect competition because it is easy to model, efficient in a static world and politically salable. The name itself, "perfect," is normative.
- He calls it irrelevant in a dynamic world: if there is no equilibrium, you can capture some of the value you create, which perfect competition prevents.
- Competition is overrated and taught unquestioningly: high school, college, grad school, then the "rat race." His example is Big Law, where young lawyers work insanely hard for partner odds that "aren't in your favor." He concludes "winning by a large margin is better than ruthless competition, if you can swing it."
- Globalization starts from "the world is flat," which frames work as crazed competition and a race to the bottom. Technology starts from the idea that the world is Mount Everest and much of it is unique.
- "The bigger the market, the better" is, in his words, "utterly, totally wrong." The restaurant business is a huge market and "not a very good way to make money."
- Better to find or make a small market, excel and own it. In a huge, well-defined market it is hard to be number one and hard to see where the predators are.
- He returns to the question to keep asking: what valuable company are other people not building?

chunks.heading: PayPal's decisive advantage and the value of networks
chunks.text:
- Payments had considerable economies of scale, so PayPal could not compete head-on with big credit card companies. It had to undercut them through technical and product innovation.
- Technical problem: fraud. There was far more of it than expected and it was hard to stamp out. Enemies included "Carders World" and a hacker named Igor. PayPal's fraud software was named "Igor."
- Product innovation: cheaper funding sources. Getting users' bank account information drove down blended costs. By modeling how much money sat in an account, PayPal could make advance payments, largely bypass the Automatic Clearing House system, and make payments instant from the user's perspective.
- His takeaway: it is "absolutely critical to have some decisive advantage over the next best service," because even a few competitors quickly create a very competitive dynamic.
- On venture capital: VCs rely on a discrete network of people, not a large pool of business. The network is the core value proposition and is driven by relationships, so VC is "anti-commoditized," personal and idiosyncratic, like great businesses.
- The "PayPal network" is a set of friendships built over a decade that became a sort of franchise.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel argues capitalism and perfect competition are opposites: competition erases profit, monopoly creates it. He shows how companies lie about their markets, names four ways to own one (brand, scale, network effects, proprietary tech), and says to start small, dominate, expand, and enter a frontier late enough to make the last great development.

chunks.heading: Why competition is a trap and monopoly is the goal
chunks.text:
- Peter argues the common view that capitalism and perfect competition are synonyms is wrong. He frames them as opposites: capitalism is about accumulating capital, while in perfect competition "you can't make any money."
- Competition is deeply embedded in American culture and education as character-building. Peter's concern is that people keep competing forever when the optimum is to stop competing, "to become a monopoly and enjoy success."
- Perfect competition can be fine for people who don't need to make money (just keep the lights on), and some fields like sports and politics are inherently competitive. He notes it is easier to build a good business than to become the fastest person alive or get elected President.
- He treats competition as appropriate for learning, and credentials as sometimes reflecting real accomplishment, but warns about chasing credentials as a habit.
- Competition also demoralizes. Top students reach elite universities, find the bar has been raised, and compete harder instead of questioning the bar. He says Harvard "sends its students into the eye of the hurricane" while Stanford is the farthest of the top schools from perfect competition (structured heterogeneity of engineering, humanities, athletics).
- On Stanford vs. Berkeley: asking which grads started the most valuable company in each of the last 40 years, Stanford "probably wins by something like 40 to zero." He calls that "monopoly capitalism, far away from a world of perfect competition."
- War is the perfect picture of competition ("everyone just kills everyone"). If life is war, you spend all your time preparing for it or doing it. Peter asks whether "life is war" is "just a strange lie we're told" and suggests sometimes you should run away and find something else to do.

chunks.heading: Confusing difficulty with value: the Supreme Court clerkship story
chunks.text:
- After graduating from Stanford Law in 1992 and clerking a year on the 11th Circuit, Peter was among a handful of clerks who reached the interview stage with two Supreme Court Justices. He didn't get the clerkship.
- Years later, after building and selling PayPal, an old law school friend asked, "So, aren't you glad you didn't get that Supreme Court clerkship?" Peter's reading: winning would probably have meant more insane competition, and no PayPal.
- The wry version: Rhodes Scholars "all had a great future in their past."
- Core lesson: "in the race to compete, we learn to confuse what is hard with what is valuable." Intense competition makes things hard, so intensity becomes a proxy for value, but value is a separate question.
- He cites Kissinger's line about academia: the battles are so fierce because the stakes are so small.
- The question he poses: at what point does it make sense to step out of competition and shift your life trajectory toward monopoly?

chunks.heading: Why companies lie about monopoly and competition
chunks.text:
- Monopolies have an incentive to hide it. A CEO bragging about a great monopoly invites antitrust audits and scrutiny, so the incentive is to "shout from the rooftops that you're not" a monopoly, even if you are.
- Non-monopolies have the opposite incentive: they want investors, but in a world of perfect competition investors shouldn't invest because no company can make a profit. So they pretend to be unique.
- Result: monopolies pretend they aren't, non-monopolies pretend they are, and rhetoric shrinks the apparent range between them. Peter concludes reality is "probably more binary—monopoly or competitive commodity business—than we think."

chunks.heading: How to spot market-definition lies (intersection vs. union stories)
chunks.text:
- Really big markets tend to be very competitive, so a competitive business is tempted to rhetorically shrink its market.
- Example: a British-food-only restaurant in Palo Alto. The relevant market might be restaurants generally, or include Menlo Park and Mountain View. The incentive is not to ask, and to tell a story about why you're different when a bearish investor cites that 90% of restaurants fail within 2 years. Peter asks whether people who eat only British food in Palo Alto, the only ones you'd have pricing power over, even exist.
- PayPal vs. Castro Street in 2001: Mountain View had many lunch places (Indian, Thai, Vietnamese, American, with sub-splits like South Indian, cheaper vs. fancier). PayPal was then the only email-based payments company in the world and employed fewer people than the restaurants did, yet from a capital formation perspective was worth more than all the restaurants' equity combined.
- Movie pitches work the same way: "Andrew Luck stars in a cross between 'Hackers' and 'Jaws'" (a college football star joins elite hackers to catch the shark that killed his friend) is unique, but "query whether that intersection would be any good."
- The rule: **non-monopolies narrow their market and tell intersection stories** (British food ∩ restaurant ∩ Palo Alto). **Monopolies insist they're in a huge market and tell union stories** about tiny fish in big markets.
- Google as worked example, depending on how the market is defined:
  - Search engine: Google 66.4%, Microsoft 15.3%, Yahoo 13.8%. By the Herfindahl-Hirschman index, 66% squared is well over 0.25, so a monopoly.
  - Advertising company: U.S. search advertising $16b, U.S. online advertising $31b, U.S. advertising $144b, global advertising $412b. Google then has under 4% of global advertising.
  - Tech company (robotic cars, TV, Google Plus, Android): consumer tech is a $964b market.
- Eric Schmidt's line fits the union story: "The Internet is incredibly competitive, and new forms of accessing information are being utilized every day." Peter's subtext: we have to run hard to stay in the same place, no different from the pizzeria in downtown Palo Alto.

chunks.heading: Reading cash and margins as monopoly signals
chunks.text:
- Cash on balance sheets (as cited in 2012): Apple about $98b, growing about $30b a year; Microsoft $52b; Google $45b; Amazon $10b.
- In perfect competition you'd have to reinvest all that cash just to stay where you are. Growing $30b a year makes you question whether things are really that competitive.
- Gross margins cited: Apple around 40%, Google about 65%, Microsoft around 75%, Amazon 14% (still huge for a retailer; grocery stores are probably around 2%).
- In perfect competition marginal revenue equals marginal cost, so high margins suggest a company is two businesses combined: a core monopoly (search, for Google) plus side projects (robotic cars, TV). Cash piles up because the monopoly piece is cheap to run and it doesn't make sense to pump it all into side projects.
- Amazon reinvests just 3% of its profits, which Peter describes as "more easy jog than intense sprint."

chunks.heading: The four ways to own a market
chunks.text:
- A company must have some combination of **brand, scale cost advantages, network effects, or proprietary technology**.
- **Brand**: the hardest to pin down; Peter calls it "a classic code word for monopoly." It means people don't see products as interchangeable and pay more. Example: most people strongly prefer Coke or Pepsi, so both generate huge cash flows. If you build a brand, you build a monopoly.
- **Scale cost advantages**: apply with high fixed costs and low marginal costs, where you get more efficient as you get bigger (Amazon online, Wal-Mart in retail).
- **Network effects**: the nature of the product locks people into a particular business.
- **Proprietary technology**: technology no one else can use.
- Apple, "probably the greatest tech monopoly today," has all four: building both hardware and software gives it the whole value chain; Foxconn scale gives cost advantages; developers and millions of repeat customers give network effects; and the brand is "something extra that's hard to define." An otherwise identical product from another company would have to be priced lower.

chunks.heading: The three-step recipe: pick, monopolize, expand
chunks.text:
- Steps to a valuable tech company: (1) find, create, or discover a new market; (2) monopolize it; (3) expand the monopoly over time.
- **Goldilocks principle** for the first market: not too small, not too big. Too small means no customers; PayPal's original idea of beaming money on Palm Pilots meant "no one else was doing it, which was good. But no one really needed it done, which was bad." Too big is too competitive and hard to get a handle on.
- Choosing the market is "not a rhetorical exercise." It is about the objective truth of the market, not intersection or union framing.
- The scaling story takes one form: "find a small target market, become the best in the world at serving it, take over immediately adjacent markets, widen the aperture of what you're doing, and capture more and more." Once large, network effects, technology, scale or brand should make it hard to follow. If there's no compelling narrative of how the market scales, "you haven't yet found or created the right market."
- You can't get the future exactly right, but thinking about it improves the narrative and the odds. Example: Bell's telephone market started tiny, was easy to own, then expanded until network effects made it hard to break into.
- The best way to fail is to invert the recipe by starting big and shrinking (Pets.com, Webvan, Kozmo.com). Failure paradigm: not being honest about objective market conditions; "you can't succeed by believing your own rhetoric over reality except by luck."

chunks.heading: Case studies: Amazon, eBay, LinkedIn, Twitter, Zynga, Groupon
chunks.text:
- **Amazon**: started as an online bookstore (cataloguing every book is hard but manageable in scale), with the vision of scaling to the world's general store from the outset. The name, evoking the diversity of the Amazon, was elastic enough to cover every *thing* later.
- **eBay**: started small as a platform for the unexpected; first Pez dispensers, then beanie babies. Marketplaces tend toward natural monopoly: buyers go where sellers are and vice versa (why companies list on one stock exchange). In 2004 it became clear auctions suited unique goods with intense demand and limited supply (coins, stamps), not commodity products sold by Amazon, Overstock and Buy.com. It's "still a great monopoly business," just smaller than expected.
- **LinkedIn**: 61 million U.S. users and 150 million worldwide, pitched as a network for everyone but largely used for headhunting. Peter notes a joke long/short idea: short companies whose staff are joining LinkedIn to post résumés, go long the ones suspiciously quiet. Key question: is the business network the same as the social network? If it is fundamentally discrete, LinkedIn likely owns that market for a long time.
- **Twitter**: began as a small niche product (anyone as a microbroadcaster) and scales into a media distribution center. Monetization is an open question, but on durability it's hard to beat: "you can copy it. But you can't *replicate* it"; at 141 characters you break SMS compatibility, at 139 you're missing a character.
- **Zynga**: Mark Pincus's line, "Not having clear goal at outset leads to death by a thousand compromises." Zynga executed well (Farmville, aggressive copying of what worked, best-in-class monetization of in-game perks). Its durability question is whether it's a creative business, which would make it like a Hollywood studio whose fortunes rise and fall. The better narrative is "hardcore psychometric sauce": "we know how to make people buy more sheep, and therefore we are a permanent monopoly."
- **Groupon**: started small and scaled aggressively; claims brand as its moat. The bear case is no proprietary technology and no network effects, so if the brand is weaker than claimed, long-term trouble.

chunks.heading: Finding the tech frontier and timing entry
chunks.text:
- Peter argues the "disruptive tech" story is overdone: "Disruptive companies tend not to succeed. Disruptive kids get sent to principal's office." Napster was disruptive, probably too much, and broke too many rules. Better to find a frontier and go for it.
- **Fog-on-the-water framework**: you're in a boat on a foggy body of water that could be a pond, lake or ocean. The longer you've been out, the longer your expected remaining journey; time passing means you're likely crossing an ocean. The frontier is temporal, not geographical: it's about *when* things happen.
- **Timing**: building a car company in the 19th century was too early, and it's far too late now (some 300 companies were built in the 20th century, a few survive). The best time to enter may be much later than conventional wisdom's "early," but not too late. You want to make "the last great development, after which the drawbridge goes up and you have permanent capture." In his phrasing: go long on tech, succeed, then short tech.
- Examples of "last" companies: Microsoft is probably the last operating system company; Google is the last search engine company (algorithmic approach was a quantum improvement that can't be much improved on).
- Fields assessed:
  - Lithium batteries: probably past the time to start; innovation may be too slow and the technology too set.
  - Aerospace: seemingly terminal markets sometimes aren't; SpaceX thinks it can cut launch costs 70-90%. If nothing has happened in an industry for a long time and you dramatically improve something important, "chances are that no one else will come and do that again, *to you*."
  - Bioinformatics: promising, but hard to know where it will be in 15 or 20 years; avoid fields moving too fast, like the 1980s disk drive companies.
  - Artificial intelligence: "probably an underrated field." People are burned out because it was overrated for decades, but progress is increasingly relentless (chess improving; computers probably beating humans in Go in 4 or 5 years). No one knows how far it will go.
  - Mobile internet: ask whether it's a gold rush and whether to dig or sell shovels. Google and Apple already sell the shovels, there may not be much gold left, and the market is too big and too competitive. Maybe you can own a valuable niche, but be skeptical.

chunks.heading: The test for a good frontier: why should the 20th employee join?
chunks.text:
- Peter's test: "Why should the 20th employee join your company?" A great answer means you're on the right track; the question is deceptively easy.
- Your indirect competition for talent is companies like Google, so the sharper version is why the 20th engineer would join you rather than Google for more money and prestige.
- The right answer must be that you're creating a monopoly business. Early companies are driven by the quality of their people, so you need a compelling monopoly story to attract the best.
- You can't out-recruit a great monopoly business unless you have a powerful narrative that you're becoming one too. He advises not competing with Google at its core monopoly of search.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel's Stanford lecture on company culture: aim between consultant-nihilism and cult, pick non-competitive fields but bring fighters, and surface disagreements fast because companies mostly die from internal blowups. Guest views from Cohen and Levchin on hiring are excluded except Thiel's own PayPal anecdotes and remarks.

chunks.heading: Culture sits between consultant-nihilism and cult
chunks.text:
- Peter says everyone knows culture matters, but it is hard to say what makes a good one. The early Microsoft team "clearly got something right."
- He describes a 1-dimensional axis from consultant-nihilism to cultish dogmatism and wants a company somewhere in the middle.
  - A cult is a culture that fails: crazy and idealistic in a bad way, with members "fanatically wrong about something big."
  - Anti-culture is the dominant paradigm. Consulting firms are the classic case: people are mercenaries and nihilistic.
- If a company must lean to one extreme, he prefers being closer to a cult than to an army of consultants.
- Homogeneity alone is not enough. A robust culture is one where people share something that "distinguishes them quite sharply from the rest of the world." If everybody likes ice cream, that doesn't matter. A relevant, unique shared philosophy about something important does.
- Differences matter only when they go to the core mission. A key person on an ice-cream-only diet is quirky but irrelevant. Different kinds of problem-solvers on one team can strengthen the culture.

chunks.heading: Capitalism and competition are antonyms, but be ready to fight
chunks.text:
- Peter says capitalism and competition are "better seen as antonyms than as synonyms." Don't set out to compete.
- That is no excuse to slack off: you probably need to work intensely, but on something others aren't doing, an area that is not zero-sum.
- Monopoly is the theoretical ideal to always pursue. You won't always find a non-competitive, cornucopian world, though, and may land in zero-sum situations. You must be prepared to handle them.
- He quotes Gandhi's advice to let yourself be slaughtered rather than owe allegiance to Hitler and Mussolini, and says Gandhi "probably would not have been a great startup advisor." His rule: try to avoid fighting, but where you must, "fight and win."

chunks.heading: Nerds, athletes and the 2x2 matrix
chunks.text:
- Peter dichotomizes two extreme types.
  - Nerds (engineers, STEM people) are highly intelligent, good at problem solving, and naturally non-zero-sum.
  - Athletes are highly motivated fighters who think you only win if the other guy loses.
- A company of only athletes is biased toward competing. They like competition because they've historically been good at it, so they jump into crowded fields.
- A company of only nerds ignores that sometimes you have to fight, and gets "crushed by their own naiveté."
- His 2x2 matrix has zero-sum vs non-zero-sum people on one axis, and warring, competitive environments vs peaceful monopoly/capitalist environments on the other.
  - Examples of warring environments: Indian food joints on Castro Street, art galleries in Palo Alto.
  - Most startups are run by non-zero-sum people who believe the world is cornucopian. That is good, but they often pick competitive fields anyway because they don't know better, and "don't realize that they've decided to fight a war until it's all over."
- The optimal spot is monopoly capitalism with a tailored mix of zero-sum and non-zero-sum people. Pick an environment where you don't have to fight, but bring good fighters to protect the non-zero-sum people and the mission, just in case.

chunks.heading: Founders Fund and the cleantech cap table
chunks.text:
- Founders Fund is a picky VC firm with maybe 20 dogmas of the form "Never invest in x" (mobile internet, cleantech and so on). Sometimes it seems impossible to invest in anything.
- Being contrarian, they tried a new strategy: find the best company in or for each dogma. Peter calls it more useful as a thought experiment than as a strategy.
- It led them to a cleantech company they would normally have skipped. The space is extremely competitive and no one really makes money, but this one looked good: run by scientists, great engineers and technology, everyone passionate about the mission. Term sheet talk began.
- Then the cap table showed the founders and employees owned about 20% and other VCs 80%, at a $35m valuation, still early stage.
- The founders' response was nonchalant: "We are so committed to making the technology work that we didn't care about the equity." Peter calls that noble but "also pretty bad."
- It killed the deal because of the questions it raised.
  - With such passivity, what will they do about competitors?
  - Can they build a sales team?
  - If they got run over so hard by investors, how will they fare against the entire world?

chunks.heading: Firing, and why companies die from the inside
chunks.text:
- An early PayPal goal was to never fire anybody. The founders hired friends they could trust, but eventually had to hire more people they knew less.
- They hired an outside sys admin who showed up at 6pm on his first day and had poor hygiene. The "never fire" rule silenced objections.
- A couple of months later PayPal's systems crashed and the sys admin had made no backups. Luckily an engineer had secretly backed up everything daily, outside his job description. Order was restored and the sys admin was fired.
- Peter's takeaway: firing is like war, and war is bad, so try not to do it. But "if you wait until it's obvious to everyone that someone should be fired, it's far too late."
- Surface issues quickly. Details matter and people will disagree often. Concealing disagreements out of discomfort "doesn't fix things," they just sit and do damage.
- "Everyone moving together in lockstep is a big red flag, not an ideal." If disagreements aren't surfacing, key things are being covered up.
- The standard view is that external competition destroys companies. Peter says that may hold in the long run, but most failures happen in the short run, from internal blow-ups during a down period. Companies are "complex entities with complex dynamics," and those dynamics usually blow up before an outside predator strikes.

chunks.heading: Hiring and paying engineers and salespeople
chunks.text:
- Salespeople: check how much they've sold, but apply a discount rate because they don't always tell the exact truth. Scott Bannister of IronPort asked sales candidates to submit their W-2s; exaggerators couldn't survive a simple test of what they'd earned in past commissions.
- Value is built over a long term. When eBay bought PayPal, all the PayPal engineers left. eBay had to hire them back as consultants at roughly 3x their old salaries because it couldn't manage the codebase without them. So target people who will stay a long time.
- Pay transparency thought experiment: emailing everyone what each person is paid is "the surest way to blow up a company." He says not to try it. But ask how upset people would be, whether that would be justified, or whether they could be persuaded the pay is reasonable.
- Engineering pay is hard because you compete with Google's prestige and money. Avoid competing on purely financial terms, where you're likely to lose. You need the compelling monopoly narrative from the previous class.

chunks.heading: Keynes, and vertical over horizontal search
chunks.text:
- Peter cites Keynes: "When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do?" But you don't want every new fact to call what you're doing into question.
- Searching for a great business, he asks whether your search space is broad but shallow (every possible business) or focused on one area and drilled deep.
- A super-broad, horizontal search is perhaps fine when first deciding to start a company. Returning to it at later stages is counterproductive. His example: "An internet company talking about being a cleantech company is lost."
- People overrate horizontal search and underestimate the sheer size of the search space. Better to do vertical search and value depth over breadth.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Blake Masters' near-verbatim notes of Thiel's Stanford lecture on founding moments, alignment, equity, vesting and fundraising. Thiel argues early structural mistakes are permanent, founder alignment dominates everything, and equity-heavy, low-salary cultures keep everyone rowing in the same direction.

chunks.heading: Thiel's law: a startup messed up at its foundation cannot be fixed
chunks.text:
- Peter states "Thiel's law": a startup messed up at its foundation cannot be fixed.
- Beginnings are qualitatively different from later life, like the origin of the universe or of a country. The US Founders got most things right, but the ones they got wrong, such as Alaska having 2 senators like California despite roughly 1/50th of the population, can't really be fixed.
- This is the logic behind the Founders Fund name. If you focus on the founding and get it right, you have a chance. If you don't, you'll be lucky at best.
- At Google, a debate is settled by "The Founders have scientifically determined that x is true." Peter's point is that all the science is done at the founding moment.
- He ties the founding to 0 to 1 (technology) versus 1 to n (globalization). The founding may last as long as the company's technical innovation continues. Founders should arguably stay in charge while the paradigm is 0 to 1. Once it shifts to 1 to n, the founding is over and executives should execute.
- Rules can't prevent every breakdown, but the early stuff should be as right as possible.

chunks.heading: Trust and alignment: the 2x2 and the founding team
chunks.text:
Peter's matrix crosses high-trust or low-trust people with low-alignment or high-alignment structure:

- **High trust, low alignment (anarchy):** Google from 2000 to about 2007, where talented people worked on all sorts of projects with few constraints.
- **Low trust, high alignment (totalitarianism):** Foxconn. People are "sort of slaves", the company installs suicide nets, yet it is very productive and "sort of works".
- **Low trust, low alignment (dog-eat-dog):** an investment bank is the example. Avoid it.
- **High trust, high alignment (the ideal):** people trust each other and share a good culture, with a structure that has them "rowing in the same direction, and not by accident".

One factor dominates all others: whether the founders are aligned with each other. If they aren't, "it will blow up the company" and nothing else will work.

- Investors should focus on how well founders know each other, how they interact, and whether skills and personalities are complementary. Any fissure in the founding team is amplified later.
- Example: in 1998 Peter made an early investment in a company Luke Nosek started with someone he met at a networking event. Luke was a chaotic, brilliant thinker and the other founder was a "by the books" deliverables person. It was doomed and went poorly.
- Choosing co-founders is like marriage. Marrying the first person you meet at the slot machines in Vegas might hit the jackpot, but chances are it won't.
- The founding team is "the single most important question in assessing an early startup", including how founders split equity and how well they work together.

chunks.heading: Set up as a Delaware C corporation
chunks.text:
Peter's answer is categorical: a startup should be a Delaware C corporation.

- Incorporating separates personal and company affairs, lets others in, lets you sell equity, and adds legitimacy. "Larry Page and Friends" might work today but would not have in 1997.
- **S corps:** one class of shareholders only (no preferred vs. common), no stock options, a cap on shareholder count, and no IPO. They only suit companies that won't scale past a point.
- **LLCs:** similar to C corps, but issuing preferred stock, granting options or going public gets problematic. Specially drafted agreements can do it in theory, but in practice "it doesn't work so well".
- **Double taxation is the C corp's cost:** on $100 of income at a 39.2% corporate rate, $39.20 goes to the government, leaving $60.80. Taxed at 35% on the top personal tier, that is $21.28 more, leaving $39.52.
- That is why consulting and law firms aren't usually C corps. But C corps are easier to take public or sell, and acquirers (usually C corps themselves) value you as if you were double taxed anyway, so being an LLC doesn't make you a more attractive target.
- Over 50% of C corps incorporate in Delaware because its business law is clear and well understood, its chancery courts are fast and predictable, and its judges are good. There is also signaling value, since everybody does it.

chunks.heading: Ownership, possession and control
chunks.text:
- Peter separates three things:
  - **Ownership:** who has equity and how much.
  - **Possession:** who operates the company day to day (job titles).
  - **Control:** who formally controls it, meaning the board, "most of whom really don't know your business that well".
- The DMV analogy: as a voter you indirectly control the DMV, but the window clerks and managers in possession decide whether they help you. Telling them they are your boss under representative government won't work. That gap between control and possession is misalignment.
- In many parts of the world these three can't be separated. If the majority owner also has exclusive control, minority shareholding has no benefit, so there are no minority shareholders and viable businesses are hard to build.
- Separating them creates its own misalignments, between and within the groups.
- A sole founder has 100% of all three and is fully aligned. Even one co-founder adds imbalance, though with two people it is still mostly aligned. Employees get lots of possession, small ownership and minimal control. Investors complicate it further.
- The founder's job is to prevent misalignment and fix it where it arises.

chunks.heading: Equity, salaries and vesting as alignment tools
chunks.text:
- Equity is the classic alignment tool because everyone benefits from a higher share price.
- Cash salaries and bonuses create opportunities for misalignment. Founders Fund's rule of thumb is that **no CEO should be paid more than $150k per year**.
  - The lower a venture-backed CEO's salary, the better the company tends to do.
  - If diligence were reduced to one question, it would be the CEO's salary. If it's more than $150k, do not invest.
  - A low CEO salary makes the CEO believe the equity will be worth a lot, and it effectively caps everyone's pay, creating an equity-focused culture.
  - At $300k a year, when something goes wrong the CEO's incentive is to keep the well-paying job rather than fix things.
- "Either on the bus or off the bus" (Ken Kesey). Part-time work, other jobs, and consultants or advisors doing important work are big red flags because the equity matters less to them.
  - Exception that proves the rule: Peter passed on YouTube in summer 2005 because the founders were working on it part-time. Things then took off and Sequoia got the investment.
  - Never hire consultants. Their cash or immediately vesting equity gives bad incentives, and they break the bus metaphor.
- **Vesting standard:** 4 years, 25% at a 1-year cliff, then 1/48th per month for the remaining 3 years. Someone who leaves before a year gets nothing, though people who didn't cause trouble often keep what they earned.
- Founders need vesting too. A fully vested founder can quit and leave the co-founder "working for 2 people". Typically 20-25% vests immediately as credit for work before the first financing, and the rest vests over time.

chunks.heading: Equity mechanics: what actually matters
chunks.text:
- **Common stock** is a fraction of ownership. The share count is meaningless without shares outstanding: 200k/10m equals 20m/2bn, and "2% is 2%".
- **Options** are the right to buy at an exercise price set at grant. It is set at or above fair market value to avoid an immediate tax event, so options are worth zero on day one. If FMV is $20 and the option is priced at $10, the $10 gap is taxable compensation.
- **ISOs** expire 10 years after grant or 3 months after an employee leaves, which locks employees in. They have favorable tax treatment. Any option that isn't an ISO is an NSO, where gains until exercise are ordinary income.
- **Restricted stock** is sold to an employee at a heavy discount, and the company can buy it back at that price. It is a mirror image of an option grant because the buyback right shrinks over time (a reverse vest).
- The takeaway: "What matters is your share of the company." Share count, share price and option pool share are irrelevant. This is 3rd grade arithmetic, and many smart technical people fail to divide, perhaps from anchoring that makes 1m/1bn look better than 1k/1m.
- "The surest way to blow up a company is to circulate a spreadsheet listing everyone's equity stake." Equity is keyed to when you join, not only what you can do. At eBay, secretaries who joined three years earlier may have made 100x what their Stanford MBA bosses did. Later, more important hires see that as unfair, and you can't please everyone.

chunks.heading: Fundraising math, convertible notes and Series A
chunks.text:
- Angels must be accredited (net worth over $1m or income over $200k). Investors get preferred stock with protective rights, while founders and employees hold common. As a rule of thumb, common is priced around 10% of preferred at a Series A.
- **Angel math example:**
  - Two founders hold 1m shares each, bought at $0.001 per share.
  - An angel invests $200k at $1/share for 200k shares.
  - 6 employees and 2 consultants each get 100k shares at $0.10, 800k shares in total.
  - That makes 3m shares outstanding and a $3m valuation. The angel owns 6.7%, the 8 hires own 26.7% together, and each founder owns 1/3.
- **Why convertible debt can be better than an equity round:**
  - It postpones the valuation question to Series A investors, which helps when angels can't value companies.
  - It mathematically eliminates a down round, which matters where angels systematically overvalue hot companies such as Y Combinator ones.
  - It is cheaper and faster than equity rounds, which cost $30k to $40k in Silicon Valley.
  - Two structures: cap and discount (for example a $4m cap and a 20% discount), or no cap and no discount with warrants or options accumulating per round.
- **Series A process:** a term sheet, then about a month of final diligence on people, finances and technology, then closing and wire.
- **Option pool:** 5% is small and 15% is large. Investors want it created before the round so they avoid dilution, while founders want it created after, so it is negotiated. Too greedy and you keep more of something that may be worth zero. Too fearful and you give away too much.

chunks.heading: Investor protection, down rounds and the board
chunks.text:
- **Liquidation preference** keeps founders from taking the money and running. A 1x preference returns the investment first, and an Nx preference returns it N times. Multiples and participating preferred skew incentives in intermediate exits: investors may want to sell and double their money while founders make nothing. Peter says the best arrangement is **1x, non-participating**.
- **Anti-dilution** reprices earlier investment after a down round. The full ratchet, which reprices as if the investor had just invested in the down round, "sounds like a form of medieval torture" because it effectively is, and it is bad for everyone but investors. Broad-based weighted average is more common, and narrow-based is sometimes used.
- **Never have a down round.**
  - With tough anti-dilution terms they wipe out founders and employees and make the company less appealing to other investors.
  - They make everybody mad: owners blame controllers, who blame possessors. "Companies are essentially broken the day they have a down round."
  - If one is unavoidable, make it catastrophic, so the angry people are wiped out and don't cause more trouble. If every round is an up round you make at least some money, but with a single down round you probably won't.
- **Other terms:**
  - Pro rata rights give VCs a free option on the next round, but a prior investor not participating is a red flag to new investors.
  - Sale restrictions align founders and VCs on growth but limit early employees' ability to cash out. VCs are wealthy and can wait, while employees may want some security.
  - Co-sale, preferred dividends, no-shop, redemption and conversion terms are worth understanding but are less crucial.
- **The board:** it is in charge of governance, and every person on it matters and must be a really good person. A typical board is two VCs, one "independent" and two founders. Five is large and more than five is suboptimal, since "less is often more". The ideal board is three people: one VC and two founders.
- **Dilution is relentless.** At IPO the Google founders held 15.6%, Steve Jobs 13.5% of Apple, and Mark Pincus 16% of Zynga. Holding more than 10% after many rounds is generally a very good outcome.
- **The no-investor alternative** gets short shrift but works:
  - Craigslist would be worth about $5bn if run more like a company than a commune.
  - GoDaddy never took funding, and Trilogy had no outside investors in the late 1990s.
  - Microsoft took one small venture investment before its IPO, at which point Bill Gates still owned 49.2%.
- Choosing VCs is like choosing co-founders and employees: who are the best people, and who do you want or need on board?

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel explains that venture returns follow a power law: the best investment can equal the rest of a fund combined. That implies concentrated portfolios, treating up rounds differently from flat rounds, and judging a company's place on the curve over mere equity percentage. Guests Botha and Graham add views not attributed to Thiel.

chunks.heading: Why power law distribution is the key structural fact of venture capital
chunks.text:
- Peter calls "exponential power" "far and away the most important structural element of venture capital," yet "surprisingly poorly understood."
- Successful companies have an exponential arc: say 50% annual growth, compounding for years. Valuations rise exponentially during that period.
- A fund's J curve: early investments fail, management fees come due, then exponential winners lift the fund above water. Many funds never get there.
- The naive model has three buckets: failures go to zero, mediocre ones return about 1x, great ones return 3-10x. Peter says this misses that returns are "incredibly skewed."
- Bad VCs think all companies are created equal. The better a VC understands the skew, the better the VC.
- Example: in Founders Fund's 2005 fund, the best investment ended up worth about as much as all the rest combined. The second best was worth about as much as number three through the rest.
- Rule of thumb: "a VC portfolio will only make money if your best company investment ends up being worth more than your whole fund."
- Exponential thinking is hard because life is mostly linear. People vastly underestimate exponential things.

chunks.heading: How venture funds work: 2-and-20 and what it means for returns
chunks.text:
- VC began in the late 1940s. Before that, wealthy individuals and families invested in new ventures directly. The Sand Hill Road version arrived in the late 1960s with Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins and Mayfield.
- Mechanics: VCs pool money from limited partners (LPs), invest it in portfolio companies, and hope those companies grow so everyone makes money. VCs must both win over LPs and pick winners.
- The standard model is 2-and-20: an annual management fee of 2% of the fund, plus 20% of gains beyond the original investment (the carry). A $200m fund earns $4m a year in fees.
- The fee is theoretically just enough to keep the firm running; the real payout is the carry.
- Funds last several years because companies take years to grow. Many investments go to zero, and the winners must return all the money and then some.
- Management fees aside, VCs only get paid if they return all invested capital plus more. So the key question for every deal: "Is there a reasonable scenario where our stake in this company will be worth more than the whole fund?"
- PayPal sold to eBay for $1.5bn. Its early investors held enough that their stake was worth about their fund's size, so they roughly broke even on the fund. PayPal's series B investors did well on PayPal but still did not break even on their fund. Like many early-2000s funds, theirs lost money.

chunks.heading: Portfolio construction: concentrate instead of spreading
chunks.text:
- Given a power law, Peter wants a fairly concentrated portfolio. Investing in 100 companies "to cover your bases through volume" suggests sloppy thinking, because there are not that many businesses you can hold high conviction about.
- A better model: invest in maybe 7 or 8 promising companies from which you think you can get a 10x return. Founders Fund tries to invest in 7 to 10 companies per fund, aiming for a 10x return.
- In theory the math is the same with 100 companies each expected to return 100x, but in practice that looks less like investing and more like buying lottery tickets.
- The curve is "fractal-esque all the way up." It is about as hard to go from $10m to $100m as from $100m to $1bn or $1bn to $10bn. Going from $100bn to a trillion is harder "because the world isn't that big" (Apple's market cap was $500bn, Microsoft's $250bn).
- VC is not private equity, where you shoot for consistent 2x or 3x returns. VCs' eggs are in the founder's basket too: "They have a few more baskets than you do, but again, because of the power law, not many."
- Even later-stage investors targeting 3-5x with low mortality still face a power law; the curve is just less steep.
- Angels are saturated and tend to be less aware of power law dynamics, so they often overestimate a given company.

chunks.heading: Up rounds, flat rounds and the pro rata heuristic
chunks.text:
- Backtesting Founders Fund's portfolios, one heuristic worked "shockingly well": always exercise pro rata rights when a smart VC leads an up round, and never increase your investment in a flat or down round.
- Why the inefficiency may exist: people do not believe in power laws. A big valuation step-up feels too large, so most VCs underprice it. Insiders also discount the change because the office and daily life still look the same.
- Flat rounds should be avoided because they signal that something has gone badly wrong. Flat rounds are driven by people expecting maybe a 2x return.
- Peter says not to be mechanical about the rule, but it forces you to think about power laws.
- Even with dilution, a company does well if every round is an up round. A single down round tends to be disastrous, mainly because it destroys relationships among all the players.
- If you take money from a not-so-intelligent investor who offers a huge valuation, take it only if it is the last money you will take.
- Peter's PayPal example: the most successful up round was a 5x valuation increase, pitched with a forward-looking narrative rather than "take x and multiply by 5." His point: "The real value is always in the future." Without a specific future to point to, people anchor to the past and ask how it can be worth 5x what it was three months ago.

chunks.heading: What the power law means for founders, employees and careers
chunks.text:
- Equity percentage needs a modifier: where your company sits on the power law curve can matter as much as or more than your stake. Having 1% beats 0.5%, all else equal, but "the 100th employee at Google did much better than the average venture-backed CEO did in the last decade."
- This is not an argument against joining startups. It means thinking hard about where a given company will land on the curve.
- Peter rejects the view that the curve is random and you are just a lottery ticket. He says that is wrong and promises to explain why later.
- Key life decisions and starting businesses also produce such distributions, but people think about them too moderately. Reality is "probably more extreme."
- Some things really are flat: the Postal Service is his example, where what you see is what you get. People are trained to think that way, so they miscalculate in tech startups, where skew is "really vast."
- Co-founders through a power law lens: one co-founder means giving up half the company, two means giving up 2/3. If you pick the right people, the outcome is likely more than 2x or 3x better, so co-founders work well. A core team of two with equal shares tends to work very well, or sometimes one brilliant founder far above everyone else.
- A paradox: people who build the really great companies are usually hesitant to sell them, not for lack of offers. People heavily motivated by money are never the ones who make the most money in a power law world.
- He prefers hedgehogs to foxes in business, citing Isaiah Berlin: "foxes know many little things, but hedgehogs know one big thing." You should still try to know lots of little things too.

chunks.heading: Raising venture money, competition and a startup's own power law
chunks.text:
- Peter says a startup that insists it will make money in many ways is troubling. Revenue also follows a power law: "one source of revenue will dominate everything else." Making money with A is key; making money with A through E is "terrifying, from an investor's perspective."
- If a company has a winner-take-all dynamic or a power law at play, take venture funding. "Giving up 25% of your business is worth it if it enables you to take over your industry." If you do not need to move as quickly as possible, rethink taking VC.
- He says you never land just one investor: "Chances are you have at least two people who are interested or you have zero." The cynical explanation is that most VCs lack confidence in their decisions and wait to ape others.
- A slide at the end of a deck saying you want to sell for $20m in 18 months would raise a big red flag.
- A power law also operates within a VC's portfolio: there is a perverse misallocation where problem companies consume the most board time, and reputational costs to leaving boards. Peter says there is a gap between VCs' public branding (loving attention to all companies equally) and reality. "The unspoken truth is that the best way to make money might be to promise everyone help but then actually help the ones who are going to provide the best returns."
- On incubators: in a long-cycle incubator, people start in similar boats but end up in very different ships because of the power law, which creates jarring intercompany dynamics.
- He will not take a stand for or against Y Combinator, but says attending an incubator that is not Y Combinator is perceived as a negative credential, "like getting a degree at Berkeley" instead of Stanford.
- Failure is not free: "One still shouldn't take failure lightly, though. There is still a reasonably high cost of failure."
- Asked who the smart VCs are: "The usual suspects."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel argues distribution is the most underestimated part of a startup. The best product doesn't always win, sales is hidden and non-rational, CLV must exceed CPA, and most businesses fail by never getting a single channel to work. Pick one optimal channel and nail it, because that can produce a terminal monopoly even with an undifferentiated product.

chunks.heading: Distribution as an underrated determinant of success
chunks.text:
Peter argues that distribution is the single topic people understand least. Team, structure, and culture get plenty of attention, and even "avoiding competition is usually better than competing" gets discovered and implemented. Distribution gets overlooked.

- The engineering bias holds that great products sell themselves. Peter says "nothing is further from the truth."
- The best product does not always win. Tesla's alternating current was better than Edison's direct current, but Edison was the better businessman and went on to start GE. Tesla also developed radio transmission, but Marconi took it and won the Nobel Prize.
- Claims that "this product sells itself" are almost never true. People say it to convince others the product is good, because nobody wants to say "our product is so bad that it takes the best salespeople in the world to convince people to buy it." He says to ask whether it is an empirical fact or a sales pitch.
- Great distribution can give a company a terminal monopoly even with an undifferentiated product. Product differentiation alone gets nowhere.
- Poor distribution, not product, is the number one cause of failure.
- Every tech company has salespeople. "If you don't see any salespeople, you are the salesperson."

chunks.heading: The math of distribution: CLV versus CPA
chunks.text:
Peter frames distribution quantitatively.

- Metrics: customer lifetime value (CLV), average revenue per user per month (ARPU), monthly retention rate r, average customer lifetime = 1 / (1 - r), and cost per customer acquisition (CPA).
- CLV = ARPU x gross margin x average customer lifetime.
- In a frictionless world, a great business needs CLV > 0. With friction and uncertainty, it needs CLV > CPA.
- Worked example, a second-tier cell phone plan: $40/month, 24-month average lifetime, so $960 lifetime revenue. At a 40% gross margin, CLV is $384. The business is in good shape if acquiring a customer costs less than $384.
- Different customers have very different acquisition costs, so the distribution approach should match what is being sold:
  - Cheap products such as steak knives, sold to individuals at a couple of dollars each: advertising and viral marketing.
  - Roughly $10,000 packages for small businesses: marketing aimed at small businesses.
  - $1m-$50m sales to big businesses or governments: salespeople and business development people ("basically just fancy salespeople who do three martini lunches and work on complex deals"). As unit value rises, the process shifts toward people-intensive selling.

chunks.heading: Sales is hidden, strange, and not purely rational
chunks.text:
Peter argues that selling and advertising are not about rational information sharing.

- Scale: about 610,000 people work in U.S. advertising, a $95bn market. About 3.2 million work in sales, a $450bn industry.
- Advertising works, but everyone believes it only works on other people. The ad industry also had to convince the people who buy ads that advertising works, which is self-referential.
- Sales pays well for those who are good. At Oracle, an engineer with 4-6 years of experience gets a $105k salary and $8k bonus, while a sales manager with the same experience gets $112k and a $103k bonus. At Google, salespeople earn a $96k base, $86k in commissions, and a $40k bonus, more than engineering counterparts. He does not say everyone should go into sales.
- Engineers are truth-oriented, since in engineering something either works or it doesn't. So they see attempts to change surface appearance, meaning sales, as dishonest (a point he credits to Marc Andreessen).
- Sales works best when hidden. In the Tom Sawyer story, none of the kids recognized the sale.
- Bill Gross story: at a late-2001 lunch, the IdeaLab founder told Peter his apathetic 14-year-old son had written a beautiful email to friends on why to sign up for PayPal and use the referral structure. Peter calls it a "literary masterpiece" with many nested levels of conversation. Gross was also tacitly signalling to the other investors how smart he was to have invested.
- Distribution roles should carry job titles that don't say sales, marketing, or advertising: "account executives" for salespeople, "corporate development" for fundraisers. People don't want to admit they're being sold to.
- A 2x2 of product (sells itself or needs selling) against sales effort (none or strong):
  - Sells itself, no sales effort: does not exist.
  - Needs selling, no sales effort: no revenue.
  - Needs selling, strong sales: a sales-driven company.
  - Sells itself, strong sales: ideal.
- Engineering is transparent, so it is easy to judge who is good. Sales is opaque, with gradations from amateurs to mediocrities, experts, masters, and grandmasters. Great salespeople are "much better than you think," and the skill is deeply hidden. Peter compares this to experts versus politicians in big companies: people drift to being politicians because it looks easier. He says "probably every President of the United States was first and foremost a salesman in disguise."

chunks.heading: Distribution methods by deal size: complex sales and mid-sized sales
chunks.text:
Peter walks through companies that found unique, effective distribution.

- **SpaceX (complex sales).** Elon Musk won about $500m in government grants across SpaceX and Tesla. The U.S. space industry has close to 500,000 people spread roughly evenly over the 50 states, and congressional lobbying keeps almost the entire industry alive. Things are designed to be expensive, while SpaceX aims to cut launch costs by 90%. SpaceX has about 2,000 people and effectively took on the entire House and Senate. Peter calls Elon a sales grandmaster.
- **Palantir.** Sells to governments and large financial institutions, with deals from $1m to $100m. It has no "salespeople." It uses "forward deployed engineers" and a CEO who travels 25 or 26 days a month. The counterpoint to "not scalable" is that at that level people only want to talk to the CEO, and a large sales army "sounds bad."
- **Knewton (Founders Fund portfolio company, adaptive learning).** It chose a non-disruptive route and partnered with Pearson, the textbook company, rather than outselling incumbents school by school, which it would probably lose.
- **Yammer ($10k-$100k tickets).** David Sacks was vehemently anti-sales at PayPal ("Networking is not working!") but at Yammer built a scalable sales system and hired a top Salesforce person to run it.
- **ZocDoc.** Signs doctors' offices at $250/month, with market-by-market launches and an internal team of recruiters that only hires salespeople. At the lower end, things get more transactional and marginal.

chunks.heading: The missing middle and the Intuit example
chunks.text:
Peter identifies a structural gap in distribution channels.

- Large-ticket items support a person driving the sale (Palantir, SpaceX). The far end has mass marketing and advertising. In between, for most small businesses, there may be no good distribution channel at all.
- ZocDoc example: TV ads would overpay because no channel only doctors watch. A sales team can't knock on every doctor's door. Most doctors aren't technologically advanced, so internet marketing is imperfect.
- A great product with no channel doesn't get sold. If you do crack the channel, you may have a terminal monopoly.
- Intuit is the classic case. Small businesses needed accounting and tax software and Intuit got it to them. Because it nailed distribution, Peter says it is probably impossible to displace today. Microsoft tried to acquire Intuit and the DOJ struck down the deal.

chunks.heading: Marketing and advertising: differentiate, and measure
chunks.text:
Peter argues advertising is creative but competitive, so an edge has to be hard to replicate.

- In the 1950s and '60s advertising was iconic (Mad Men; Cary Grant in North by Northwest). As more people learned to do it in the '70s and '80s, entrants grew faster than the market and profits fell.
- The core problem is opacity. He quotes John Wanamaker: "Half the money I spend on advertising is wasted: the trouble is I don't know which half."
- Google was the first to let people figure out whether advertising works, through metrics like CPM, CTR, CPC, and RPC and straightforward ROI calculation. He says this is core to why Google is so valuable, since people pay a lot for advertising that demonstrably works.
- Priceline's marketing is powerfully differentiated and hard to copy. Its William Shatner is "in a league of his own." PayPal's James Doohan (Scotty) palm-pilot money-beaming event was a flop.
- Zynga combined viral growth with a lot of targeted advertising, monetized users more aggressively than expected, and used that revenue to buy more ads. Other gaming companies relied on viral growth alone.
- The internet bias that "advertising does not work" is a double standard, since many sites earn their living selling ads. Peter says there is a lot of room for creativity in distribution strategy.

chunks.heading: Viral marketing: it must be built into the product
chunks.text:
Peter says viral marketing is easy to underestimate and cannot be bolted on.

- Two points: shorter viral cycle time is better, and viral coefficient must exceed 1 to get viral growth.
- PayPal started with 24 users, all employees, and used cash incentives to refer others. It reached 7% daily growth, with the user base roughly doubling every 10 days. Held for 4-5 months, that gives hundreds of thousands of users.
- Win the key segment first. Hotmail put a sign-up message at the bottom of every email, and later copycats were "a whole segment behind." The first mover that achieves viral growth can be the last mover.
- PayPal's first high-growth segment was eBay power buyers and sellers. Money moved fast there, which linked to virality. By the time others understood, the segment was locked in. Other segments, like sending money to family overseas, had much lower velocity.
- Other examples he names: Dropbox (file sharing implies someone to share with), Spotify's social angle, and possibly Pinterest, though he says it is unclear whether it is good or a fad.
- "Marketing people can't do viral marketing." There is no viral add-on or "tell your friends" button. The product's core use case must be inherently viral. He calls advocating it as an after-the-fact choice "wrong and lazy."

chunks.heading: The power law of distribution: find the one channel that works
chunks.text:
Peter applies the power law to distribution channels.

- As with revenue streams (LinkedIn is the exception that proves the rule, per Roelof Botha), companies probably won't have several equally good channels. Engineers who don't understand distribution try a bit of sales, BD, advertising, and viral marketing, "everything but the kitchen sink," which he calls a really bad idea.
- One channel is very likely optimal. Most businesses get zero channels to work. One working channel makes a great business, and trying several without nailing one is fatal.
