- Think hard about who is most likely to buy. For an enterprise software company, that means narrowing to the likeliest buyers rather than sending the sales team to talk to everybody.
- Distribution also covers selling the company to employees and investors. "This company is so good, people will be clamoring to join" and "investors will bang down our door" are the same error. When they seem to happen, something else is usually going on behind the scenes.

chunks.heading: PR, uncertainty, and distribution for fundraising and hiring
chunks.text:
Peter extends distribution to media, investors, and talent.

- **PR.** Palantir had a strong anti-media bias for years. Media still mattered for investors and employees, since candidates Google the company and parents say things like "Palantir? Never heard of it. You should go work at Microsoft." PR is "the art of getting trusted, objective third parties to give you press," not plugging yourself on your own website.
- **Uncertainty.** People are very uncertain about what they want and insist otherwise. With poorly formed demand functions, people copy what they believe everyone else wants, as in fashion. In VC, a rational market would produce single-investor deals priced at the most bullish bidder. In practice you get zero investors or many.
- **Corporate development.** Once a company is worth roughly $30m or more, hire a full-time person who only travels and finds prospective investors. Example: a company worth about $300m, where valuation can swing about 2:1. Raising $50m at $300m gives away 16%, while raising it at $500m gives away 10%. A 6% delta is huge, so why not give the best person 1% of the company?
- **Hiring.** Traditional recruiters assume rational people who decide well once informed. Since the best people make the best companies, founders or one or two key senior people should spend 25% to 33% of their time identifying and attracting talent.
- **Authenticity myth.** People claim ads don't work on them and that their wants are authentic, yet fashionable people all wear the same clothes. The question to ask is how big the distribution problem is and whether the business can solve it. Distribution works best when hidden, and people only show the tip of the iceberg.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel argues the Internet has been a lightly regulated frontier, that being right about the future but wrong on timing is the classic failure, and that the best path is working with computers rather than competing with them or China. Q&A adds his views on paddling early for big waves, small boards, and betting on the single best company.

chunks.heading: Technology futures: software eating the world and the 2x2 of competition
chunks.text:
Peter frames the Internet as a "Wild West" frontier of the past 20 years: few rules, room to do almost anything. He notes the world of stuff has been heavily regulated for 40 years while the world of bits has not, so computers and finance were the best places to be. Finance got too innovative and regulators noticed, so there is probably less to do there now.

- He flags quieter threats than PIPA and SOPA, chiefly software patents.
- Absent regulation, no one can shut you down just because you are small. Patents do exactly that.
- Big companies with economies of scale can afford such regulation or skirt it; small companies cannot.

Peter Thiel's patent-fight view: in litigation there are four parties, the two sides and their two sets of lawyers, and lawyers are almost always scared of losing, so defense lawyers talk clients into settling.
- High litigation costs can be worth it if you only have to fight a few times.
- The danger is fighting and winning without setting a deterring precedent, so the suits keep coming and you are worse off.
- Patent problems are ones you want to have: no one would come after you without good technology.

chunks.heading: Software eating the world: which sectors are next
chunks.text:
Peter agrees with the thesis and lists sectors already eaten: telephone directories, journalism, accounting brokerages, and arguably music. Incumbents often miss it. The New York Times declared in 2002 that the Internet was over, and the record industry cheered when it took down Napster. "Those celebrations were premature."

Candidates he names for being eaten next:
- Healthcare: better EMR technology, analytics and transparency, but heavy regulation and bureaucracy.
- Education: many attempts to computerize and automate learning.
- Labor: Uber and Taskrabbit circumvent traditional regulated models.
- Law: computers may replace many legal services. Things stay inefficient because people "very oddly" trust lawyers more than computers.

He says not to bet against computers in these spheres, and it may not be wise to become the kind of doctor or lawyer that technology could make obsolete.

Further out: broadcast media, space and transportation, biology shifting from an experimental to an informational science, and the intelligence and government sectors.

chunks.heading: The 2x2: compete with or work with computers, compete with or work with China
chunks.text:
Peter builds a 2x2. One axis is compete with computers vs. work with computers (anti- vs. pro-technology). The other is compete against China vs. work with China (anti- vs. pro-globalization).

- Globalization axis: collaborating beats competing. "Competing is too hard. People never really make any money. They just beat each other to bloody pulp." Even if you can win against China, it is a Pyrrhic victory.
- Technology axis: do not compete with computers. Even if you can do square roots faster than a computer, they will catch up. Human vs. computer chess has gone badly for humans since 1997.
- Working with China is better than competing, but too many people are myopically focused on it, so it may be too competitive now. Most focus on globalization instead of technology.
- By indirect proof, that leaves working with computers.
- Caveat: indirect proof is tricky. Everything may point one way and still be wrong if your inputs or perspective change. It is still a useful tool: if nothing else works, look closer at what seems better.

chunks.heading: Timing: when the future arrives and why predictions miss
chunks.text:
Peter argues you must study how people in your shoes got the future wrong if you hope to get it right. Instead, "we tend to abdicate thinking about the future entirely."

- Wrong predictions are old: Lord Kelvin in 1895 said "heavier than air flying machines are impossible"; Patent Commissioner Charles Duell in 1899 said "everything that can be invented has been invented."
- Some predictions were too optimistic: in the 1960s people expected nuclear-powered everything and flying cities. Why that did not happen is worth thinking about.
- More interesting are cases where people were right on substance and wrong on timing.

Examples of right-but-early:
- Mobile: everyone who tried it in 1999 failed. No one thought the best mobile investment would be buying Apple stock.
- Apple's Newton launched in 1993; the iPhone took another 15 years to get the timing right.
- Rockets were developed in China in the 13th century, but that was not the time to go to the moon.
- Napster was too early and probably too disruptive; now there is Spotify.
- AI "just doesn't quite work yet."

His conclusion: "If we learn the right lessons, the future of the past can come back and become true."

chunks.heading: Surfing: paddle early, and err toward the future
chunks.text:
Peter on the pitfalls of thinking about the future: either it is too far away, so you are right on substance but wrong on timing, or it is already here and everyone else is doing it.

- The goal is to catch a big wave, so you paddle hard. Sometimes there is no wave, "and that sucks."
- You cannot wait to be sure there is a wave before paddling, or you miss it entirely. "You have to paddle early, and then let the wave catch you."
- At the margins, it is better to paddle where there is no wave than to paddle too late and miss a good one.
- Starting the next great social networking company is current-wave thinking. "Social networking is not the next wave." So the bias should be toward the future.
- "Then again, the bigger bias should be to not err at all."

chunks.heading: Distribution, complex sales and gatekeepers
chunks.text:
- Peter says never take it at face value when successful companies claim they do no sales or marketing; that claim is itself probably a sales pitch.
- He argues it may be time to rethink complex sales. The 1990s scarred people because complex-sales businesses failed, and business development deals were hard to get in the early 2000s, but such deals can be very advantageous.
- His example: Google's BD deal with Yahoo was phenomenal for Google. Google does not talk about it because it wants to talk about engineering; Yahoo does not because it is embarrassing.
- On mobile, the big worry is that any great distribution technique will be disallowed and then copied by Apple and Android. It is a big market, but it is far from clear you can wrest power from the gatekeepers.

chunks.heading: Boards, experience and power laws
chunks.text:
- Boards: for effectiveness, keep the board small. Three people is best, since coordination gets worse with each person added. To make a board do nothing, make it enormous. Non-profits sometimes have 50-person boards, which gives the quasi-dictatorial head effectively no checks.
- Experience: the founders of Google, Microsoft and Facebook had little prior experience. The questions are what translates, and how.
  - A failed 10-20 person startup might teach what not to do, but it may have failed for other reasons, or leave you scarred and averse to risk.
  - Big companies like Microsoft or Google are great, but everything works automatically, and "there are shockingly few companies started by those people." One theory is that they are too sheltered from startup processes.
- Better than asking where to go is asking what to do: what do you believe in, what makes sense, what will work.
- "If there is indeed a power law distribution in company outcomes, it's really important to get into the single company you think is the best." The company's stage matters less than the substance of what you are doing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel argues the biggest secret is that many important secrets remain, even though society has stopped believing in them. He explains why people disbelieve (incrementalism, risk aversion, complacency, egalitarianism), why that view is wrong, and how to find and use secrets, especially human ones.

chunks.heading: The core question: what important truth do very few people agree with you on?
chunks.text:
Peter treats the question "what important truth do very few people agree with you on?" as the starting point for a company. To a first approximation, the correct answer is a secret: an unpopular or unconventional truth. Restated for business, the question is "what great company is no one starting?"

- If there are many good answers, many great companies can still be created. If there are none, starting a company is probably a very bad idea.
- So the number of secrets left in the world is roughly equivalent to how many startups people should start.
- The question is easy to ask and hard to answer. When people try, they often conclude it is impossible, swinging from one extreme to the other. Peter says that is too big a move: answers not coming easily does not mean they do not exist. Finding secrets is "neither easy nor impossible, just hard."

chunks.heading: Easy, hard and impossible: the taxonomy of truths
chunks.text:
Peter sorts truths by how hard they are to obtain, and says the distinction decides whether you pursue lucrative ventures or guaranteed failure.

- **Easy truths** are accepted conventions that nearly everyone knows.
- **Mysteries** are impossible to figure out. His example is superstring theory: you cannot really design experiments to test it, so the question is whether it is just very hard or a fool's errand.
- **Secrets** sit in between: difficult but possible.
- Discovery means removing the cover from a secret. Pythagoras's triangle math was once the subject of mystery cults and later became convention.
- It also runs the other way. Conventions can be forgotten and become secrets again, as people stop believing what earlier generations believed.
- Only big secrets that are true matter. Silly secrets (gossip), esoteric ones (tarot, numerology) and small incremental ones are of little importance.
- "Those who believe something is hard might still try. If you think something is impossible, you won't even try."

chunks.heading: Past secrets, and the biggest one left
chunks.text:
Peter lists the secrets covered so far in the class as a template, and notes that each has a human side as well as a natural one.

- **Monopoly vs. competition:** "Capitalism and competition are antonyms." Monopolists pretend they are not monopolists ("Don't regulate us!"), and non-monopolists pretend they are ("We are so big and important!"), so firms only look similar on the surface.
- **The power law:** startup outcomes follow a power law. Investors find it psychologically hard to admit their best investment is worth more than the rest of the portfolio combined, so it stays hidden. People are uncomfortable talking about inequality and ignore or rationalize it.
- **Distribution:** it matters far more than people think, and people in distribution work to hide what they do. "Salespeople do best when people do not know they're dealing with salespeople."
- **The biggest secret:** that many important secrets are still left. Forty or fifty years ago this was convention and everyone believed much remained to be done. It has since become a secret again.

chunks.heading: Why people stopped believing in secrets
chunks.text:
Peter says the common view that no secrets are left is plausible, and he explains where it comes from.

- **Extreme version:** Ted Kaczynski (IQ 167, Harvard, math PhD, Berkeley professor) argued in his manifesto that human goals are either easy or impossible, so people are depressed and technology should be destroyed so that people can work on hard problems anew. Peter calls this the easy/hard/impossible trichotomy with the hard middle removed.
- **Milder forms:** the hipster who ironically rejects useful technology, and fundamentalists generally. Religious fundamentalism has easy truths and the mysteries of God, with heresy in between. Environmental fundamentalism says protect nature, then "Mother Nature knows best." Market fundamentalism says prices are easy truths that must be accepted, not questioned.
- **Geography:** the map has no white spaces left. In the 18th century you could become an explorer. About 72% of the planet is ocean and some 90% of the inhabited ocean is deep sea, with only about 200 hours of human exploration, but few people find it magical. The frontier of knowledge seems to have closed with the geographic one.
- **Four sociological drivers:**
  - **Incrementalism:** do what is asked a bit better than others and get the A. Academics are incented by volume, not importance.
  - **Risk aversion:** secrets are likely to be wrong, and dedicating your life to something no one believes in is unbearable if you are wrong.
  - **Complacency:** the Harvard and Yale law deans tell incoming students they are set. Peter suspects that is only true if you do not believe it.
  - **Egalitarianism:** the idea that some people have insight others lack has fallen out of fashion. In 1939 Einstein's letter to Roosevelt about atomic weapons was taken seriously; today it would get lost in the White House mailroom.
- Peter concedes these attitudes serve most people well. Distrusting prophets is a good heuristic, and it is probably impossible now to start the cults people joined 30 years ago.

chunks.heading: The case against the case against secrets
chunks.text:
Peter argues that the belief in a world without secrets has strange implications.

- **Injustice:** every injustice involves a secret that a small minority understands. Views in the 1950s and 60s that things were unjust became convention once the majority was won over. Saying no secrets remain means we are either fully just or should not try to be.
- **Markets:** disbelief in secrets implies efficient markets, but there have been decades of extraordinary inefficiency. You were not allowed to say in 2000 that people were acting irrationally about Internet companies, or in 2007 that there was a housing bubble. The Fed's model said the worst-case loss was no more than $25bn.
- **Political dissent:** extreme criticism of government rests on some secret truth. Disbelieving in secrets means no dissident can ever be right. Each party tries to discredit the other by tying it to conspiracy theorists (Tea Party, Occupy Wall Street).
- **Corporate governance (HP):** in 2004-2005 Tom Perkins, an engineer and Kleiner Perkins co-founder, wanted the HP board to discuss new technology and hard substantive problems. Patricia Dunn argued science was beyond the board's competence and it should focus on process. Leaks about the Compaq acquisition led to wiretaps, which were illegal, so a board obsessed with process broke process rules. Peter's lesson: "It's hard to work toward a radically better future if you don't believe in secrets."
- **Evidence for secrets:** hard problems do get solved. Andrew Wiles started on Fermat's last theorem in 1986 and proved it in 1995, and he would not have tried if he thought it impossible.
- **Web 2.0:** many small secrets add up. Twitter's 140-character messages are individually trivial but aggregate into something powerful. WikiLeaks showed how many secrets exist, and the order in which they are revealed can matter more than what they are.

chunks.heading: How to find secrets: ask what nature won't tell you and what people won't tell you
chunks.text:
Peter says there is no formula and no complete list, because no one person knows every secret and a widely distributed list would turn secrets into conventions. He offers a method instead.

- **Filter first:** discard anything small or false and keep the big, true secrets.
- **Two kinds:** secrets of nature (science, the world) and secrets about people (things people hide). Ask "What secrets is nature not telling you? What secrets are people not telling you?"
- **Start with people:** he thinks human secrets are underappreciated. What people will not say is a good signal of where to look, and the most interesting secrets sit at the intersection of the two kinds. His lab analogy: if someone sneaks in every night and messes with your results, you will not understand what is happening if you only think about nature.
- **Physics bias:** the view that natural secrets are foundational leads to treating physics as the fundamental science. He jokes that physics PhDs are hard to work with because "they know fundamental things, they think they know all things." A PayPal candidate interrupted his interviewer with "Stop! I already know what you're going to ask!", was wrong, and was not hired.
- **Questions to ask:** what are we allowed to talk about? Which areas can people not look into? What is forbidden, implicitly off-limits or taboo?
- **Tradeoff:** natural secrets are transparently hard but politically safe (no one cares about superstring theory), while human secrets are more dangerous because more is at stake.
- **Worked examples:** the monopoly secret comes fast from asking what people running companies cannot say. The power law secret comes from asking what VCs cannot say. Both can also be reached by Econ 1 reasoning or by plotting startup outcomes, but the people question is faster.

chunks.heading: Where Peter points the search: nutrition, biotech, cleantech, agriculture, government
chunks.text:
Peter shows the method by applying it to specific fields, framing each as a place where structure or taboo has kept people from looking.

- **Nutrition:** it is not a real major at Stanford or other real universities. Most big studies were done 30 or 40 years ago and there is little incentive to study it now. A company Founders Fund found interesting is a "Manhattan Project for Nutrition" with the six best people. He argues the food pyramid (low-fat, heavy on grains and carbohydrates) was probably more a product of Kellogg's lobbying than science, and obesity has exploded since.
- **Biotech:** stem cell and cancer research have surprisingly little overlap. The pro- and anti-stem-cell camps are both politicized, and neither wants to dwell on the fact that injected stem cells divide and multiply like cancer. Perhaps some cancer cells behave like stem cells, and research at that intersection looks promising.
- **Cleantech:** very few cleantech investments worked, because investors and entrepreneurs got involved to make an environmental statement and fashion was decoupled from business merit. "Saying you're doing something because it's cool is decidedly uncool." Rather than swear off the field, one can use the insight, and Elon Musk did with Tesla: high-end electric sports cars that build a brand first, with rich buyers underwriting R&D for cheaper mid-market cars. In 2005 Tesla seemed crazy and better solar panels seemed the way to go; seven years later Tesla has a fantastic brand and Solyndra does not. A monopoly is built by starting with a brand and building a tech company under it.
- **Agriculture (from the trade deficit):** the US trade deficit, around 4% of GDP, is probably unsustainable and awkward to discuss. If it must close, raising exports is more plausible than cutting imports, and the US's biggest comparative advantage is probably agriculture. Agritech looks counterintuitive for tech investors, which he takes as a good sign.
- **Government:** the debate is big versus small government, but nobody discusses "do more with less," which is the definition of technology. Pro-government people dislike criticizing government and anti-government people prefer abolishing it, so applying technology to government is ignored even though it could benefit everyone.
- **General rule:** find things that are hard but doable, and "don't simply accept others' definitions of the frontier."

chunks.heading: What to do with a secret: tell, hide, or time it
chunks.text:
Peter treats the decision of whom to tell as a core strategic question.

- **Two extremes:** tell no one and keep it safe, but no one works with you and it dies with you. Tell everyone and you may build a team, but more people may compete with you.
- **Type matters:** intellectual and natural secrets are cheap to share. Secrets about people can be costly. He quotes Faust: "Mankind has always crucified and burned" those who "reveal their feelings to the crowd below."
- **Timing:** the right time to bring people in is rarely all at once at the start, and rarely never. An intermediate answer is usually best.
- **Speed vs. secrecy:** if you think others are about to find the same secret, move as fast as possible and tell whomever you need to.
- **PayPal in summer 1999:** after failed models such as beaming money between Palm Pilots, the team realized linking money and email would be powerful. It looked like a big secret but not a hard one, so they scrambled and shared it liberally. The risk is that listeners compete instead of joining. In June 1999 a management candidate told Peter in his interview that he wanted Peter's job. Peter liked his job and did not hire him, and the candidate tried to launch a competitor a few weeks later.
- **Fraud at PayPal:** fraud was endemic in banking but nobody discussed it. Banks do not say "we have hundreds of millions stolen every year and no idea how to stop it"; they build loss budgets and reserves and stay quiet.
- **Small and vocal vs. big and quiet:**
  - In Silicon Valley most secrets are small and get copied quickly, so the play is hypergrowth: reveal fast and get your exponential curve going so no one can catch you.
  - For bigger secrets that you alone hold, there may be no need to reveal early. Keep a low profile, use trade secrets and unique expertise, and build over several years.
  - The incremental fast-growth companies are very visible. People working on bigger ideas on longer timelines are in stealth, so there may be far more people going after hard secrets than we think.

chunks.heading: Secrets and choosing a job: hidden companies
chunks.text:
Peter applies secrets to picking where to work, going beyond knowing the power law in theory.

- Companies are bimodal: a few great ones and many that do not work. Media and the tech community broadly agree on which are best, so the obvious plan is to shoot for startup A with B as a backup.
- That plan works in a world with a power law but no secrets. "In a world with many secrets, the best companies may be hidden." The power law still holds, but the perceived ranking may be wrong.
- Your task is to identify hidden companies with the potential to be the best, and to ask what potentially great company people are overlooking. Taking the perceived best-to-worst ordering as given is the fundamentalist view: the market, media and blogs know better than you.
- This does not mean joining obscure companies. Esoteric truths are not the aim; important truths that are hidden are.
- He closes with Tolkien: "Still round the corner there may wait / A new road or a secret gate." His message is to take the hidden paths.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel argues that conflict is mostly Shakespearean, not Marxist: rivals grow alike, obsess over each other and lose sight of the real question. Founders should avoid wars, merge or win fast if forced, and prevent internal fighting by giving each person distinct roles.

chunks.heading: Why war happens: theater, mimesis, and the Marx vs. Shakespeare frame
chunks.text:
- Peter says conflict often starts as theater: threats, missile-pointing, and nations copying each other. His examples are the space race, Fischer-Spassky (1972), and the Miracle on Ice (1980). He calls the whole Cold War "essentially theater".
- Rivalry is a strong motivator. People work harder when racing an enemy, but the end of the rivalry is awkward (the 1975 Apollo-Soyuz joint flight).
- The Charles Atlas example: a skinny kid bulks up and beats the bully, and in doing so becomes the bully. His working theory is "you must choose your enemies well, since you'll soon become just like them."
- This is the psychological counterpart to the economics of perfect competition, where profits are competed away. The economic snapshot shows the problem but not why people still compete.
- He quotes Kissinger: "the battles are so fierce because the stakes are so small."
- Escalation runs: conflict, then obsession with the opponent, then growing similarity, then sometimes total destruction. Losers lose everything and winners can lose a lot too.
- Two models of conflict:
  - **Marx:** people fight because they disagree, and the bigger the difference, the bigger the fight. This is the internal narrative, and good-vs-evil is useful propaganda.
  - **Shakespeare:** from the outside, combatants look alike ("Two households, both alike in dignity"). They grow more similar as they fight and forget why they started.
- On Hamlet, he notes that true greatness means fighting "even for an eggshell". Heroes fight for what doesn't matter, while Hamlet is too fixed on meaninglessness to fight at all.
- In tech, he says it is "straight Shakespeare" in the great majority of cases.

chunks.heading: Tech examples of imitative, destructive competition
chunks.text:
- **1970s computers:** IBM, NCR, Control Data and Honeywell all built minicomputers that were slightly different but conceptually similar. They missed the microcomputer, and IBM developed the microprocessor and eclipsed its rivals.
- **1990s pet stores:** Pets.com, PetStore.com, Petopia and about 100 others fought to dominate online pet supplies. They fought over Super Bowl ads and never asked whether the market was worth fighting for. The same went for Kozmo, Webvan and Urban Fetch.
- **Oracle vs. Siebel:**
  - Siebel was founded by a top Oracle salesman and copied Oracle almost exactly, down to the office design.
  - Oracle parked a huge ad truck in front of Siebel HQ to lure its employees away.
  - Oracle acquired Siebel in 2005.
- **Oracle vs. Informix:**
  - Informix put up billboards near Oracle HQ: "You just passed Redwood Shores. So did we."
  - Oracle answered with snail ads on TPC benchmark results.
  - The ads were aimed at each other and each other's employees, not customers.
  - Ellison's theory was that you always need an enemy, small enough that it can't beat you but big enough to motivate. Peter's takeaway is that fake enemies for motivation can turn into real enemies, and Informix self-destructed in 1997.
- **Square card readers:**
  - Square did software, hardware and the iconic white square device.
  - Copycats followed: PayPal's triangle, Intuit's cylinder, Kudos' semicircle.
  - He says copycat reader makers are in "a great deal of trouble" and that it is better to be the original or do something original elsewhere.
- **Microsoft vs. Google:**
  - Both were started by nerds obsessed with being the smartest, and he cites Gates' IQ-testing obsession.
  - They started in different businesses (Office, Explorer and Windows vs. search), then converged into direct rivalry (Bing vs. Google, Chrome vs. Internet Explorer, Google Docs vs. Office).
  - Meanwhile Apple overtook both: market cap $531B vs. $456B for Google and Microsoft combined, though three years earlier each was individually bigger than Apple.
  - His lesson: "fighting is costly. And those who avoid it can often swoop in and capitalize on the peace."

chunks.heading: The PayPal vs. X.com war and the merger
chunks.text:
- Confinity's PayPal launched in late 1999. X.com (Elon Musk) was four blocks away on University Avenue in Palo Alto.
- X.com launched a feature-for-feature matching product, down to the same cash bonus and referral structure.
- December 1999 and January 2000 were intense, with people working 90-100 hours a week. The focus was beating X.com, not usefulness.
- One engineer presented a schematic of an actual bomb in a daily war update. It was axed and blamed on sleep deprivation.
- In February 2000 the leadership met at a restaurant equidistant from the two offices. They agreed to a 50-50 merger in early March, then raised money before the crash and had years to build the business.
- In early March 2000 PayPal had $15M in the bank and was about six weeks from running out of money. CFO Roelof Botha raised the alarm, but engineers cared only about beating X.com.
- Peter says the hard part after the merger was de-escalating. Rivalries are remembered more fondly when things work out and exaggerated when they don't.

chunks.heading: Fight rarely, win fast, and prefer peace (and monopoly)
chunks.text:
- If you must fight, use overwhelming force and end it quickly, because a long war turns you into your enemy. He means real "shock and awe", not the fake kind that produces a 10-year war.
- Since a quick win usually can't be guaranteed, his main job is to find ways to avoid the war entirely.
- He returns to the class five 2x2 of athletes (zero-sum competitors) vs. nerds (non-zero-sum collaborators), against war/competition vs. peace/monopoly. A company should optimize for peace, with nerds to build the business and athletes to fight and win if competition is forced on it.
- The hybrid creates an internal problem: competitive people can fight each other. Most companies are killed by internal infighting, like an autoimmune disease. The proximate cause may be external, but the ultimate cause is internal.
- On the other side of the argument, Peter holds that the reasoning for expecting a long-run payoff from competition fails because the long run "never really arrives as planned". His example is Microsoft losing a billion dollars a year on Bing.
- He also argues people are bad at assessing probability. Pouring gold into taking the other guy's gold is irrational when success is unlikely, so he sees a crazy psychological component rather than pure calculation.

chunks.heading: Preventing fights inside the company
chunks.text:
- Marx would say colleagues fight over big disagreements about direction. Peter says the Shakespearean answer is almost invariably correct: people fight because they want the same thing, usually the same role. People who want different things just go and own them.
- At PayPal the conflicts centered on the product team. David Sacks wanted the product to be one seamless whole, which meant product overlapped with everyone else and couldn't act without stepping on someone's turf.
- The CEO's job is to stop this at the source by keeping prospective combatants apart through clear definitions and precise roles.
- Startups are more dangerous than big companies because roles change constantly and you can't simply silo people.
- PayPal's approach:
  - Redraw the org chart every three months, repositioning people to head off conflicts before they started.
  - Evaluate each person on a single criterion, one thing only, different from everyone else's.
  - It was unpopular at first because people wanted three or four things, but it focused them on getting things done rather than on each other.
- "Focusing on your enemy is almost always the wrong thing to do."
- Title inflation at PayPal (lots of VPs, then lots of Senior VPs) was a status fight, since prestige is not a scarce resource. He admits it probably wasn't stable, but PayPal was acquired before it blew up.
- External war can forge internal peace, but at a cost: PayPal's engineers didn't care if the company went broke as long as it beat X.com.

chunks.heading: Having a plan, and being 10x better
chunks.text:
- Peter's view is that a bad plan beats no plan, which he links to a chess lesson. Most people default to no plan.
- On law students: most had no idea what to do with their lives, and few expected to make partner. Many planned to work at a firm for a few years and "figure it out".
- His rule is that you should either like what you're doing, see it as a direct plan to something else, or see it as an indirect plan to something else. Adding a resume line every two years to "buy options" is bad.
- Hill-climbing metaphor: step back and look at the hill from time to time, or you may get old and find it was "a really low hill".
- People avoid planning because it is unfashionable to believe you have an edge and can make things happen.
- A marginal improvement doesn't win. His anti-spam example: the startup claimed to be better than about 100 competitors, but took half an hour to explain why. His line is "A half hour pitch on anti-spam is just more spam."
- The benchmark is a pitch as concise as "we are 10x better/cheaper/faster/more effective." (Reid Hoffman made the "plan to be 10x better" point; Peter endorsed it with the anti-spam example.)
- A secret plan from last class's theme is still the goal. He says probably not enough companies even have a plan, let alone a secret one.

chunks.heading: Network, secrecy, and Silicon Valley vs. New York
chunks.text:
- On the tradeoff between secrecy and networks, Peter says you can't tell everyone your secret plan and must guard information. But you also need to talk and be somewhat open to get the benefits of the network, so it is "a very fine line".
- On how to tell whether your product is really different from a competitor's, when everyone has an internal story about being different, Peter put the question to Reid. He did not give his own answer.
- On New York vs. Silicon Valley, he says New York is "a pretty distant second", with some cool companies. His critique:
  - Media plays a much bigger role there, which induces competition. People focus on each other rather than on creating things.
  - People live on top of each other and are trained to fight and enjoy it. It may be motivating, but it points people at the wrong battles.
  - Original, great companies will keep coming out of Silicon Valley.
- He also noted that PayPal got to a million users in 4 to 5 months, versus about 460 days for LinkedIn. His point is that if you target a non-competitive space, slower growth is fine, and you want to grow fast but also be able to grow more slowly.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel argues the luck-vs-skill question can't be settled, but society has swung too far toward luck and indeterminacy (statistics, diversification, process over substance). Founders do better with definite plans and conviction about the future, as Apple's design-led, secret-plan approach shows.

chunks.heading: The Core Question: Luck vs. Skill in Startups
chunks.text:
- Peter says the biggest philosophical question under startups is how much luck is involved in success. It is nearly impossible to answer rigorously, because statistics are meaningless with a sample size of one. His thought experiment: start Facebook 1,000 times under identical conditions; 1,000 successes would mean skill, 1 would mean luck. Such experiments are impossible.
- He argues the starting view is mostly a bias. The internal narrative says talented people worked hard and made it work; the external narrative says right place, right time.
- He believes people are "extremely biased towards the luck side of things" and that skill plays a much greater role than people think.
- His weak argument against luck is repeatability: Steve Jobs (Next, Pixar, Apple), Jack Dorsey (Twitter, Square), Elon Musk (PayPal, Tesla, SpaceX, SolarCity). He finds it very odd to argue they just got lucky.
- A successful entrepreneur who credited skill alone would be seen as "ridiculous, arrogant, and wrong," whatever the proof. Nobody is allowed to show how he controlled everything.
- A startup class only makes sense if luck can be "channeled and mastered." A guide to slot machines would be odd. He notes this is class 13, and says: "Luck isn't something to circumvent or be afraid of. So we have class 13. We'll dominate luck."

chunks.heading: From Jefferson to Gladwell: How Views of Luck Shifted
chunks.text:
- Peter cites Jefferson: "I'm a great believer in luck, and I find the harder I work the more I have of it." From the 18th century through the 1950s or '60s, luck was something to be mastered, dominated and controlled.
- Today's default is closer to Malcolm Gladwell: success stems "as much from context as from personal attributes." You can't control your destiny.
- The startup community shares this ethos. Paul Graham attributes much startup success to luck, and Robert Cringely wrote *Accidental Empires*. Peter says he isn't picking on them; they show the dominant view.
- He splits luck into past luck (birth country, genes, inheritance) and future luck. He thinks the past debate is less fruitful. The real question is whether the future is determinate or indeterminate.

chunks.heading: The 2x2: Optimism/Pessimism and Determinate/Indeterminate
chunks.text:
- Peter frames the future on two axes: optimistic vs. pessimistic, and determinate (knowable, controllable) vs. indeterminate (too many chance events).
- If the future is indeterminate, you diversify and chase optionality. People spend 10 years building a diverse resume (junior high, high school, many clubs) for an unknowable future.
- If it is determinate, you hold firm convictions and do the one best thing.
- The four quadrants:
  - **Determinate optimism** (US until the 1950s-'60s): e.g. go west and get 640 acres; specific projects to improve society. Fits engineering and art.
  - **Indeterminate optimism** (US roughly 1982 to at least 2007): the future will be better, but not in ways you can know. Wait for progress, do incremental things. Fits law and finance.
  - **Determinate pessimism** (China): there is a calculus, but it gives no cause for celebration. "China will get old before it gets rich." He ties the one-child policy, pollution and coal-mine deaths to this view. Fits wartime rationing.
  - **Indeterminate pessimism** (Japan since the 1990s, Europe today): the future isn't great and you don't know what to do. Fits insurance. He calls it the worst of all worlds.
- He notes a widespread view that the US is drifting toward China's quadrant. The pessimistic quadrants are stable and self-reinforcing.

chunks.heading: Savings, Investment and the Missing Future
chunks.text:
- Optimism means a low savings rate; pessimism means a high one.
- US savings is about 4%, or about -6% including government deficits (-10% of GDP). China's is close to 40%. Peter says it is hard to consume your capital when you believe you'll get old before you get rich.
- Determinate worlds have many things to invest in; indeterminate ones have low investment. US corporations generate about $1 trillion a year in free cash flow and hoard it, because "almost by definition, you wouldn't have free cash flows if you knew where or how to invest."
- The puzzle: low savings plus low investment. People are optimistic about a future nobody is working toward. He asks whether indeterminate optimism can be stable at all.
- Money circles through the system with nobody knowing what to do with it: founder to bank, bank to institutional investors, to a diversified stock portfolio, to companies chasing free cash flow, back to investors. Money matters more in an indefinite world because "having is always better than specific things."
- Government bonds: 1.8% yield against 2.1% expected inflation gives a -0.3% expected real return over the decade. "You get negative returns when people run out of ideas."
- Investors now focus on managing risk. Hedge funds rarely ask what will happen; the VC question has become access to good deals. Peter says VC should in theory have little in common with a statistical approach.

chunks.heading: Calculus vs. Statistics, Substance vs. Process
chunks.text:
- Determinate worlds run on calculus: a rocket to the moon must be calculated precisely, not iterated. He jokes that many '90s companies "had launch parties but no landing parties."
- Indeterminate worlds run on probability: bell curves, random walks, distributions. There is a push to replace high-school calculus with statistics. Peter says "today, all prophets are false prophets," and cites Larry Summers on the economy.
- Indeterminacy makes people think procedurally rather than substantively. He ties this to the HP board debate: Perkins' substance (talk tech and engineering) vs. Dunn's process.
- Politics: pollsters become more important than politicians. He says McCain chose Palin from polling data, since she had an 89% approval rating in Alaska. Government now mostly shifts money around instead of backing specific projects like the space program.
- Other cultural markers he cites:
  - Sci-fi: Clarke's *2001* (1968) imagines specific, auto-updating news; Gibson's *Neuromancer* (1984) has "the color of television, tuned to a dead channel."
  - Philosophy: Marx and Hegel (optimistic, determinate); Rawls and Nozick (optimistic, indeterminate); Plato and Aristotle (pessimistic, determinate); Epicurus and Lucretius (pessimistic, indeterminate).
  - Physics: belief in many-worlds among theoretical physicists rose from about 10-15% to 55-60% over 50 years, with no experiment proving it. Physicists call it "aesthetically better."

chunks.heading: The End of Big Projects
chunks.text:
- The US once believed in grand definite plans. Examples: the transcontinental railroad; Robert Moses, who held twelve high-level posts and rebuilt New York state over 30-40 years, at one point more powerful than the mayor or governor.
- People then asked who would do big projects well, not whether anyone should. Moses' Greenwich Village highway was blocked in 1965, and no new state highways were built after.
- The Reber plan: in the 1940s John Reber, a San Francisco teacher and amateur theater producer, proposed two dams across the Bay, about 20,000 acres of fill, a 32-lane highway and high-rises. It drew Congressional hearings. Today it would be dismissed as lunacy, and "the John Rebers of the world have long since learned to keep their plans to themselves."
- Definite optimism yields underwater cities and cities in space; indefinite optimism yields finance.

chunks.heading: Life Extension, Cities and Indeterminacy in Practice
chunks.text:
- Peter says people treat actuarial tables as binding (about 1 in 1,000 odds of death for a college student per year, 50% for a 100-year-old, 1 in 10,000 reaching 100, 1 in 10 million reaching 110), so life extension gets a bad rap.
- From 1600-1850 people searched for the fountain of youth. Once belief in a literal fountain died, the belief that things could change died too.
- His key line: "Belief in secrets is an effective truth. Belief in luck is an *ineffective* truth; it will stop you from actually doing things."
- Evolution is the model for indeterminate optimism: never-ending, monotonic progress without a plan. He doubts it extends to economies:
  - Los Angeles could have been a magnificent planned city but became incremental sprawl.
  - São Paulo: the airport is 5 miles from downtown, a 10-minute helicopter ride that can take 3 hours by car at rush hour; about 20 million people; high-rise slums.
  - Mumbai and Lagos are similar cases of decline.
- On the environment, markets solving problems iteratively is indeterminate optimism and "we're all screwed" is indeterminate pessimism. Definite ideas like iron filings in the ocean (to feed CO2-absorbing phytoplankton) are not in the public debate.

chunks.heading: Implications for Startups: Design, Plans and Secrets
chunks.text:
- Peter lists the startup symptoms of indeterminacy: Darwinian A/B testing, iterative processes, machine learning, no thinking about the future, short time horizons. He says they aren't self-evidently wrong, but not self-evidently right. Darwinism takes billions of years, startups don't have that, and it is carnage for participants. Iteration and machine learning often excuse the last two.
- The 2007 finance bubble peak was the peak of indeterminate thinking. Apple is "the absolute antithesis of finance," with deliberate design at every level, definite multi-year plans and methodical rollouts.
- Apple stock: Jobs took over at $3 per share, and it traded at only $6 in 2003. Institutions underweighted it because they can't value a secret plan. He gives no investment advice.
- The return of design: Airbnb, Pinterest, Dropbox and Path have an "anti-statistical feel," a "telepathic link" with what people want that works faster than A/B testing a huge search space.
- Companies with real plans tend not to sell. PayPal sold in 2002 only because it had run out of ideas. A definite plan anchors people against selling; "there is no reason to stop when you can do so much more."
- In an indefinite world, investors value secret plans at zero, so a company with a good one is undervalued. The ability to execute a long-term secret plan is "incredibly powerful."

chunks.heading: Career Advice: Have a Plan, Not a Resume Line
chunks.text:
- Peter says young people iterate one resume line at a time, which gives luck too much dominion and is a crowded strategy.
- You can form a definite plan even in law or finance. The usual path of hopping to another firm for more money is "a recipe for disaster." Better: stay at one bank or firm for 10-15 years until you're the only one who knows what's going on. "You should plan on being partner or managing director from day one."
- "Your plans can change, but if you don't have them, you're just floating with the current."
- His closing hope: computer science is as deterministic as it gets, so it is odd to view tech startups through an indeterminate lens. An alternative title for the lecture was "Control Alt Delete": "The best edit is often a complete re-write."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel uses the cleantech bust to review his startup checklist: markets, competition, secrets, incrementalism, durability, teams, distribution, timing, financing and luck. He argues energy follows a power law, so a definite, optimistic bet (he sketches thorium) beats the indeterminate portfolio thinking that sank Solyndra-style ventures.

chunks.heading: Applying the 2x2 of determinacy and optimism to energy
chunks.text:
- Peter reuses his matrix of determinate/indeterminate and optimistic/pessimistic futures as the framework for energy.
- Determinate optimism: one specific energy type is best and should be developed. Peter thinks this quadrant "arguably makes the most sense," yet it is the least talked about today.
- Determinate pessimism: nothing is considerably better, so ration and conserve.
- Indeterminate optimism: better, cheaper sources exist but nobody knows which, so build a portfolio.
- Indeterminate pessimism: the sources will probably be worse and costlier, so take a portfolio approach anyway.
- Planned indeterminacy doesn't work. "I intend to get rich and famous" is an aspiration, not a plan. A portfolio only works with granularity, e.g. "if I do x, it leads to 5 specific options at a certain time, then I choose the best."
- In practice statistical thinking breeds radical indeterminacy, and aspirations replace plans.
- He rejects the conventional wisdom that detailed plans are worthless because everything changes. Winning without a plan is hitting the jackpot, and most people don't. To maximize mastery over outcomes, plan.
- He splits energy into two markets: power generation (wood, coal, gas, nuclear, biomass, hydro, solar, feeding the grid) and transportation (oil, plus electricity for buses and trains, where you carry the power with you). The first question is always which market you are actually in.

chunks.heading: Where each country and era sits on the matrix
chunks.text:
- 1950s-60s: nuclear was the one thing nearly everyone expected to be better. Eisenhower's 1953 Atoms for Peace speech said it would be "too cheap to meter." Transportation was also determinately optimistic (space jets, ever-faster supersonic planes).
- Today determinate optimism in energy is dead. Agreement on a single better, cheaper source is gone.
- The U.S. sits in indeterminate optimism. Republicans want to remove regulation to get a range of better things; Democrats want to subsidize cleantech to get them.
- China is determinately pessimistic: the future is coal and oil. It buys oil fields in Africa and mines domestic coal, with roughly 3,000-5,000 coal mining deaths a year, "essentially fighting a small war each year."
- Japan and Europe show indeterminate pessimism: bikes, tiny cars, long train commutes.
- High-speed rail is determinate pessimism. It requires rearranging where everyone lives, and "gone are the days where Robert Moses could unilaterally re-architect the state of New York."

chunks.heading: Energy sources follow a power law
chunks.text:
- Historically one source dominates at a time: wood until the mid-19th century, coal from mid-19th to early 20th, petroleum from the 1930s-40s. Natural gas has now overtaken coal as number two, and nuclear is a distant third.
- Britain ran out of trees, which is one reason America's living standard was higher.
- Peter's ex ante logic: solar, wind and nuclear are very different, so it would be "extremely odd" if their price and effectiveness were nearly identical. Expect one dramatically better source, with the second and third filling niches.
- People still think about energy through a statistical/portfolio lens ("you can't predict the future"), ignoring the power law just as they do elsewhere.

chunks.heading: Demand and resource constraints
chunks.text:
- China's GDP growth and energy consumption moved 1:1, both about 8% a year over the last decade. In energy terms that means no real efficiency improvement: "You get more only if you expend more."
- World oil use is 85 million barrels a day; the U.S. uses about 18 million (just under 25%) and China 9 million. China has 4x the people. At U.S. per capita use China would need 72 million barrels a day, roughly all world production; even smart-car downsizing gets to about 45 million.
- Oil price inelasticity is on the order of 10:1: a 10% demand rise means a 100% price rise.
- Only 1 billion of 7 billion people live in the developed world, so lifting the other 6 billion needs enormous energy increases. When everybody in Uttar Pradesh gets a fridge, it cancels out Western conservation.
- Resource constraints look more real than population constraints. Ehrlich's 1968 Population Bomb said 3.5 billion was beyond carrying capacity; there are now twice as many people.
- Peak oil: in 1956 Shell geologist M. King Hubbert saw new discoveries falling, with a 20-30 year lag to production, and predicted U.S. output would peak in the mid-1970s. He was right. The Texas Railroad Commission, which set world prices, gave way to OPEC by 1973. OPEC quadrupled prices from $3 to $12 a barrel, and again in 1989 to $40.
- By the Hubbert projection the world is now where the U.S. was in 1970.
- Peter floats a provocative reading: the 2007 "financial" crisis may partly be an energy crisis. Oil hit $140, the economy was contracted to contain it, oil fell to $32, and it is back to $100. "Crises about money and central banks may not just be about money and central banks."
- He offers the working thesis that most major conflicts in the last 2000 years involved energy: the Pacific theater of WWII (oil embargoes), Churchill nationalizing Anglo-Persian oil fields before WWI, and West Virginia's secession giving the North about 20x the Union coal of the South.
- Oil's cheap Indian summer overlaps the U.S.'s indefinite optimism from 1982 to 2007.

chunks.heading: Why cleantech failed: the 10 questions
chunks.text:
- Cleantech drew more investment than the Internet did in the last decade, partly from environmental and social motives (Al Gore's Nobel, John Doerr's 2007 TED talk).
- Good intentions did not make it profitable. Peter lists ten things a startup must get right, or at least have a plan for: markets, mimesis and competition, secrets, incrementalism, durability, teams, distribution, timing, financing, luck.
- "8 out of 10 is sort of a B-, and 5 of 10 earns you an F." Cleantech companies were often starting at 0 or 1 out of 10.
- The sector was ambiguous about what was scarce: resources or the environment. They imply different remedies. Believing in an environmental problem but no resource problem favors subsidizing cleantech; believing in resource scarcity but no environmental problem favors rationing conventional supply. Stiglitz noted peak oil theory may have been pushed by environmentalists, since carbon emissions are solved once oil runs out.

chunks.heading: Market framing, mimesis, secrets, incrementalism and durability
chunks.text:
- Energy is a commodity and the market is huge, and in huge markets you can't protect yourself from the monsters.
- Market-size games, using a hypothetical Solyndra-like company: 100 MW against U.S. solar of 950 MW is 10.5% of the market; against global solar of 18 GW it is under 1%; against global cleantech of 420 GW it is smaller; against 15,000 GW of global power generation it is "just a dot in the ocean."
- Some firms shrank their market rhetorically to look dominant. Others pitched trillion-dollar markets, which is "even more dangerous" because it looks like perfect competition. Peter says you would be better off opening a pizza restaurant in Palo Alto.
- In perfect competition "the battles are so fierce because the stakes so small." People still fight for scraps because it feels cool.
- Social entrepreneurship ("doing well while doing good") usually ends up doing neither. Companies should have a specific mission and solve a discrete, important problem. Peter asks whether something is actually good for society or merely approved of by society. If good just means what the masses approve, everyone does the same thing: everyone has a solar startup with a slightly different story.
- A secret can escape mimesis, but with 10-15 year time horizons a small secret doesn't build a decisive lead. Most wind, solar and battery progress was incremental, with no step function.
- Durability: solar has thin-film, multi-junction concentrator, crystalline Si and emerging photovoltaics, each with many executions, and you must also beat wind and hydro. The goal is to dominate your market for 20-30 years. With steady incremental progress, a marginal addition rarely gets last-mover advantage. Like 1980s manufacturing, things improved but no great, lasting companies emerged.

chunks.heading: Team, distribution, timing, financing and the three requirements
chunks.text:
- Culture: cleantech teams were shockingly non-technical and zero-sum. Peter's tell: "when cleantech people started wearing suits and ties." Tech people wear t-shirts and jeans; cleantech people looked like salesmen, and were. If a product is incremental and of doubtful durability, you must be a great salesman to convince people it's dramatically better. Salespeople and athletes are important but shouldn't run things, because they think only about defeating people like themselves.
- Distribution: companies couldn't deliver the power. A huge solar farm in Southern California still needs lines to L.A., and grid connection was treated as uninteresting but often proved decisive. Peter Orszag said little of the Stimulus went to infrastructure because zoning permits for power lines would take too long, so the administration avoided building unconnectable wind farms.
- Timing: "start paddling before the wave" is right in principle, but if the wave is years away it's unclear when to start, especially when cost curves shift fast.
- Financing: because of the power law, VCs need 10x returns. Solyndra took $1.65 billion in late-stage venture-type financing, so it had to become phenomenally large. His rule of thumb: never invest in companies seeking under $1 million or over $1 billion. Under $1 million, things may be too easy and it's just a timing game; over $1 billion, the story gets implausible, especially with many near-identical competitors.
- Three requirements of innovation:
  - Incremental technology: cleantech did fairly well, with falling costs, but there were no secrets and "the questions almost answered themselves."
  - Complex coordination: left to luck. The attitude was "I'm a scientist; delivering it to L.A. is not my job." When everyone thinks that, it doesn't get done. The Internet allows the "Asperger's approach" of succeeding without talking to anyone; cleantech requires getting many people to act.
  - Breakthrough technology: for the most part nobody tried, and nobody asked the biggest questions.

chunks.heading: Solyndra and what the aftermath revealed
chunks.text:
- Peter says what was striking about Solyndra was how people talked about it afterward. Nobody asked whether the technology worked, which is the substantive engineering question of a determinate world.
- In an indeterminate world people ask legal and financial process questions. Republicans said officials were too entangled with the company; Democrats said the process was legitimate and transparent.
- From a definite optimist's view, if the technology worked, minor wrongdoing over funds is a footnote. A better defense would have been for the President to say "here are 2 or 3 technologies that we think are going to work" and get serious about them.
- He calls the episode a government version of the HP board fiasco.

chunks.heading: Thorium as a determinate, optimistic bet
chunks.text:
- Peter proposes thorium as an example of determinately optimistic energy thinking, "a big secret." He says this is an illustration of how to think, not a pitch to start a thorium company.
- Background: in the 1940s the government found nuclear power in plutonium, uranium and thorium. Thorium has no fissile isotopes, so it can't be weaponized, and the government wanted bombs, not power. Atoms for Peace began as a warning about thermonuclear obliteration and was retooled to promote non-weaponized nuclear energy. With no need for more weapons today, he says thorium is worth revisiting.
- Claimed advantages:
  - Far more abundant than uranium: enough to power the world for a million years at current consumption.
  - Cleaner: uranium reactors use about 0.7% of the fuel with lots of enrichment waste; thorium is a self-contained cycle.
  - Reactors don't need hundreds of atmospheres of pressure.
  - No runaway reaction, for the same reasons it can't be weaponized.
  - About 1/10 the cost of other nuclear: roughly $250 million per plant versus $1.1 billion for uranium.
  - Together, roughly an order of magnitude better than what is currently possible.
- Scoring against the ten questions, thorium gets about 6 of 10 immediately, versus 0 for most cleantech:
  - Mimesis: solar is hot, thorium isn't.
  - Secret: thorium was underexplored for political reasons.
  - Not incremental.
  - Durability: an order of magnitude cheaper means you could own the energy market.
  - Timing seems right.
  - Financing: about $250 million raised over several years against milestones seems reasonable.
- Still unsolved: market, team, distribution and luck, plus regulation and coordination. Open questions include which countries to target and whether any nuclear engineers are left to hire. Solve these before moving forward to maximize mastery over luck.
- His other IT ideas: use software to shift daytime power consumption (smart appliances and thermostats, since prices swing during the day) and transport tech like self-driving cars and defeating traffic. He calls the Internet cleantech's "closest cousin": eBay is a recycling company, Amazon cuts suburban sprawl, Airbnb cuts hotel construction.

chunks.heading: Government: sell, take, or replace
chunks.text:
- Technology's relationship with government takes three forms: selling to it, being subsidized by it, or replacing it. All are hard. VCs dislike government-dependent companies because selling to government is difficult, large subsidies are harder still, and the government objects to being replaced, so keep such a plan secret.
- The U.S. budget deficit runs about 10% of GDP. Optimistic projections reach about 2%; less optimistic ones reach 6-7% and rise again after 2020. Peter calls this a secret hidden in plain sight that nobody knows what to do about, so we're not allowed to discuss it.
- The implication is to avoid relying on subsidies, since there probably won't be money when you need it.
- Contrast SpaceX with Solyndra. SpaceX sells technology to government and may replace parts of it now that the government has decommissioned its own rocket programs. Its risk is government running out of money, but that is minimal next to the risk of relying on heavy subsidization.
- His anchor for the future of energy: the optimistic determinate quadrant. Ask the same questions as for Internet businesses: "What can be done that's better and cheaper? Can you do more for less?" That is "the classic definition of technology." First find the big breakthrough, then improve it incrementally. "The first step, as usual, is to think big and think boldly about the future."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel argues the failed futures of the 1950s-60s (energy storage, weather, robotics, space) are fertile ground for startups: find where the past went wrong, learn the right lessons, and attack the problem from a radically different angle. He also covers why unique ideas are hard to fund, why enterprise sales must start small with good references, and how to disguise a sale.

chunks.heading: The retrofuture thesis: go back to the future, but don't copy it
chunks.text:
- Peter argues the best way to think about the future is to think about how the future used to be. Mid-20th-century visions included precisely predicted or controlled weather, flying cars, civilian submarines and widely useful robots.
- Most of those futures "didn't work": weather still "just happens to us," people still sit in traffic, and robotics produced the Roomba instead of the Lost in Space robot.
- Computer science is the exception. Moore's Law held, power consumption fell and connectivity grew. The Dick Tracy 2-Way Wrist Radio/TV is essentially an iPod nano, and Arthur C. Clarke roughly predicted the Internet in 1956's *The City and the Stars*. In CS there is little left of the old future to retrieve.
- Elsewhere, he suggests revisiting lines of research that were underexplored at some point in the past. Example: thorium power, which may have been neglected because the military favored plutonium/uranium R&D. It is "at least worth taking a look at."
- The catch: nostalgia is useless, and the old future failed. The goal is to tap the past, learn from it, and apply that knowledge in some new, important way. In his words: think about where the past failed, learn the right lessons, make it work this time, and approach old problems from a very different perspective.

chunks.heading: Energy storage: a physics approach instead of chemistry
chunks.text:
- Peter frames the core problem: energy production costs vary a lot, and power is far more expensive at peak times. Because off-peak power is hard to store, there is a large arbitrage between peak and off-peak cost.
- Batteries are about 200 years old, and he sees the trajectory as asymptotic: limits on packing density, corrosion, and possibly chemistry itself. A better battery may be like "finding a new element on the periodic table."
- The chemical paradigm "has done wonders, but maybe it's done doing them." The open question is whether non-chemical approaches are worth pursuing.
- He highlights LightSail Energy, which treats storage as a physics problem. It uses Boyle's law: power compresses air into steel tanks, and decompressing it later releases the energy. Compression heats the air and lets power dissipate, so water is sprayed into the air to cool it.
- LightSail claims a trillion-dollar market. Peter says they should be pushed on whether that is a huge opportunity or "a rather huge competitive ocean where you can't actually defend yourself." He still calls physical rather than chemical storage a very orthogonal and promising approach.
- Historical note from the guest discussion: compressed air storage with water spray was tried in the 1870s and abandoned for unknown reasons. This is the retrofuture pattern in practice.

chunks.heading: Weather: statistics in an area where people gave up
chunks.text:
- Peter says it is "sort of amazing" that we are still really bad at predicting weather, especially short-term. Chaos and complexity are the excuses, but he sees a sense in which people "just stopped trying." Forecasting looks like fortunetelling and could be made more accurate, which would be valuable.
- Weather control is largely abandoned territory because it is seen as dangerous. Cloud seeding strikes some as crazier than terraforming Mars. He describes a backlash against even thinking about it, with a "pick your preferred mix of impossible/undesirable/unnecessary."
- He points to The Climate Corporation (formerly Weatherbill) as fighting this consensus. It improves crop loss insurance by predicting the weather at a particular parcel of land and adjusting quickly with advanced computer modeling.
- He grants that a statistical approach deserves initial skepticism, but argues it is a statistical approach in an area where people grew wary of statistics because earlier attempts failed. That makes interesting statistical approaches possibly underexplored.
- Secret hidden in plain sight: hardly anyone looks at agritech, since by definition it happens outside Silicon Valley, so it tends to be overlooked and undervalued.

chunks.heading: Robotics: reconceive the robot instead of building the butler
chunks.text:
- Peter notes 1950s-60s visions of a household butler/maid/cook/driver robot that would raise living standards by doing chores for free. That has not happened. Humanoid bots are expensive and limited; the state of the art is a laundry-folding robot that takes 45 minutes per piece.
- Experts say a Lost in Space-style robot is 25 to 50 years away. Peter reads that as being just beyond the horizon where people are accountable: "It will happen, but I don't have to do anything. Someone else will do it."
- His example of re-imagining robots is RoboteX, which treats the robot as an intermediary rather than a humanoid duplicate of human tasks. Robots go into dangerous situations first, for SWAT teams, hazmat experts and bomb squads.
- Detail: RoboteX robots have been effective at hostage situations. Amped-up bad guys psychologically break when a little robot enters and surrender on the spot. Organizations pay considerably to keep people out of harm's way.
- Lesson: pick a use case where the robot's limits don't matter and the value is high, rather than chasing the sci-fi form.

chunks.heading: Space: fix the cost structure, not just the rocket
chunks.text:
- Peter notes the moon landing era lasted 3.5 years: Apollo 11 in July 1969 to Apollo 17 in December 1972. It has been about 40 years since anyone was on the moon, so Mars seems very ambitious.
- He says the Space Shuttle was "oddly Pareto inferior": it cost more, did less and was more dangerous than a Saturn V rocket.
- Launch cost per kg to orbit had barely changed in 40 years. The key insight is that traditional space work was accounted for on a cost-plus basis. Contractors built cushy margins into rockets, everyone had incentives to inflate costs, and things got more expensive and arguably more dangerous.
- SpaceX re-approached the problem by getting the cost structure right, driving launch costs down, and revisiting basic designs with new technology and materials. By most accounts the improvements were quite successful, and he says SpaceX is arguably ushering in a new era of space flight.
- He says the open questions are whether better telemetry software and radically new rockets can bring a new era of space technology.

chunks.heading: Selling to big customers: start small, get references, grow iteratively
chunks.text:
- Rule of thumb from Peter: the larger the cost of a product, the slower the sales process.
- The classic mistake is the fantasy of a single $100 million contract that makes everything golden. In practice that "almost never works out that way."
- Even with a technology an order of magnitude better, you can't make the golden sale. People don't know what they want, buying is never completely objective, and the person writing the check will ask who else has bought. If the answer is no one, they may stop, since something is probably wrong.
- Example: a nuclear plant should in theory deploy RoboteX robots (they would have been useful at Fukushima), but you can't simply sell to the theoretically ideal customer.
- Successful enterprise startups use iterative sales models, with 50-100% growth per year for several years. Example: $5M in year one, doubling every year for a decade. Revenue doesn't 10x in year four, because no customer will do a deal 10x your largest to date; 2x your biggest deal is a more realistic hope.
- Strategy: get the smallest customer that is also a good reference customer, move quickly and collect references. A police department that buys a robot that stops a hostage-taker becomes proof the robot may be good for other things.
- Agreeing with a guest: start with people who are desperate for what you provide.
- VC analogy: VCs fantasize about one rich LP who removes the need to talk to anyone else, but LPs cluster like everyone else. "Everybody likes to act like they know what they're doing. But in reality no one has a clue."

chunks.heading: Selling the company, and why unique ideas are hard to fund
chunks.text:
- Peter says "sales works best when it's disguised." If you want to sell, act like you don't, and declaring you'll never sell is a good first step. Parallels: if you want advice, ask for money; if you want money, ask for advice; politicians solemnly say they have no interest in running for President.
- M&A has two typical drivers. One is grinding out inefficiencies, like banks buying smaller banks and firing half the people. The other, in tech, is product synergy, such as PayPal and eBay. He calls that the exception: synergy rarely exists, and genuine complementarity between truly novel technology and what incumbents do is very unlikely.
- On fundraising, he says it is very hard for investors to invest in things that are unique, and the psychological struggle is hard to overstate. People gravitate to the modern portfolio approach and say their portfolio will hold different things, which he finds odd.
- Truly different things are hard to evaluate. Asking a would-be rocket founder about rocket experience gets "zero" (Elon had none before SpaceX), and a VC investing in rockets knows "nothing" since no one has invested in rockets in over 40 years. iPhone games are familiar to everyone.
- SpaceX example: NASA more or less required SpaceX to take outside funding in 2008. Founders Fund invested then. Various Silicon Valley VC firms warned that it was risky and maybe crazy, even though the company had already built rockets and attempted launches.
- The upside of the unfamiliar: if you are unfamiliar with rockets, so is everyone else. The competitive bar is lower, and you can focus on learning and substance over process, which is perhaps better than competing against experts.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In Class 16 of CS183, Thiel frames longevity as the fight against bad luck and argues that drug discovery is too stochastic and increasingly costly. He suggests computation could make biology more determinate. Guest founders' views are excluded; only Thiel's own remarks and questions are used.

chunks.heading: Life expectancy trends and why Peter treats longevity as a bet against bad luck
chunks.text:
- Peter notes that even without a biotech revolution, life expectancy has risen steadily, by roughly 2.3 to 2.5 years per decade since the mid-19th century.
- Plotting the longest-lived demographic in each country gives a very straight line, "analogous" to Moore's law. In 1840 life expectancy was about 45-46 years; before that it was flat for thousands of years.
- Every day you survive adds about 5 or 6 hours to your life. He asks whether the line will continue, slow, or accelerate: a short burst that stagnates, or the start of a fierce acceleration.
- The U.S. lags the global maximum by several years (bad food, inactivity), but the upward trend is relentless.
- Keeping people alive longer has been an exponentially harder problem for a century and a half.
- He frames longevity as "the opposite of bad luck": death comes from accidents, so the real question is whether and how far luck can be overcome.

chunks.heading: Death as accident: micro, macro and cosmic, and the case against pure probabilistic thinking
chunks.text:
- Accidents sit on a spectrum: microscopic (a DNA mutation starting a cancer), macroscopic (a car crash), cosmic (an asteroid strike).
- Solving longevity completely means removing all of them, but macro and cosmic accidents are likely to stay probabilistic. He would take those on later.
- If the microscopic accidents are solved, the best estimates put lifespans at between 600 and 1,000 years.
- From the 17th to the mid-19th centuries the prevailing view was that accidents could be overcome. Bacon's *New Atlantis* was the classic accident-free utopia, "new" because its people had complete mastery over nature, unlike the old Atlantis the gods destroyed.
- That view has receded since about 1850. He attributes this partly to actuarial science and life insurance, which reduced life and death to probability functions (a 30-year-old has a 1 in 1,000 chance of dying in a year; at 100 the chance is 50%).
- He warns that "unchecked probabilistic thinking can be dangerous" because it defeats one's ability to shape the future. His example is *No Country for Old Men*: if everything is a probability distribution, eventually your luck runs out and you resign yourself to it.
- The alternative is to think and avoid playing games that depend too heavily on luck.
- Historical footnote: around 1700, claims of living forever seemed stronger because salesmen claimed to be 150 years old, and poor record-keeping let them get away with it. A 70-year-old in London was seen as wretched, while a 150-year-old might get a pension from the King.

chunks.heading: Why drug discovery and biotech investing are too luck-driven
chunks.text:
- Peter argues that modern drug discovery is "too much a matter of luck." Scientists start with about 10,000 compounds, screening cuts them to maybe 5 that reach Phase 3, and maybe 1 is approved by the FDA.
- Starting a biotech company is usually brutal: most last 10 to 15 years, with little control along the way. What looks promising may not work, there is no iteration or sense of progress, and the outcome is binary at the end of a largely stochastic process. You can work 10 years and not know if you wasted your time.
- In Internet businesses, the basic rule is that the company succeeds if every financing round is an up round. In biotech that is very hard; investors get tired, and some candidly say they don't care about valuations because everything gets wiped out in their favor in the inevitable down round. "Why negotiate valuation if luck dominates everything?"
- Luck-driven, stats-driven processes worked well for a few decades, but the costs may be rising because the easy discoveries have been found. Developing a new drug cost $100 million in 1975 and $1.3 billion at the time of the lecture.
- He says probably all life sciences investment funds have lost money, and that biotech investing has been roughly as bad as cleantech.

chunks.heading: Can computing make biology determinate? The search-problem view of biotech
chunks.text:
- Peter calls drug discovery "fundamentally a search problem" with an extremely large search space of possible compounds. The key question is whether computing can reduce the role of luck.
- Biological processes involve some luck against irreversible degradation, and traditional therapeutics largely mirrors them. Computational processes are reversible: "you can dive in and re-program things."
- The open question is how far biological problems can be reduced to computer problems.
- Sequencing costs are collapsing: about $500 million per genome in 2000, about $5,000 at the time, and probably $1,000 within a year or two.
- The Human Genome Project was seen as revolutionary in the late 1990s but hasn't lived up to the hype. Peter suggests it may have been too early or too costly, but the deeper reason may be that the main problem is not sequencing at all: "we just don't know what to do with the data."
- He says exactly how much of biology is computational is still an open question.

chunks.heading: Three computational-biotech companies Peter highlights
chunks.text:
- **Stem CentRx** is the closest to traditional biotech, with a heavy computational piece. It aims to cure all cancer by targeting the cancer stem cells that drive tumor growth. Chemo is hard to dose: too low is ineffective, too high kills the patient. Targeting the driving subset precisely would be less destructive and more effective. Mouse studies were very promising, with human results expected over the next year or two.
- **Counsyl** is a bioinformatics company aiming to be the default for pregnancy genetic screening.
