It built a single simple test covering about 100 genes for inherited traits and focuses only on Mendelian diseases, since more complicated genetic combinations are poorly understood. It had identified a "tractable and well-defined subset of the problem." It screened about 2% of U.S. births and expected that to rise dramatically.
- **Emerald Therapeutics** is the most computational and was in stealth. Its goal is to cure all viral infections by reprogramming cells, building a molecular machine that tags virus-containing cells and releases a sequence making them self-destruct.
- He says the high paranoia around programmable anti-viral companies is understandable: these are "big secrets that play out over long time horizons, not web apps that have a 6-week window to take over the world."

chunks.heading: Timing, secrecy, and competition in biotech
chunks.text:
- Peter asks whether the field is early or right on time, echoing Marc Andreessen's point that many late-'90s Internet ideas were right but too early: "how do you know you're not paddling too early?"
- He asks how a company can be confident no one else is secretly running the same strategy, and whether its own secrecy is actually working.
- If competitors like a hypothetical "Ruby Therapeutics" were out there, he asks whether it would make more sense to be open and collaborate, and how you recruit if you are secretive.
- On recruiting, he says referral-based hiring has worked well at every company he has been involved with, but you must keep a clear head. Ask MBAs for referrals and you get far too many; ask engineers and you may get shocking silence because they are shy. You have to make them comfortable referring people.
- He asks why Silicon Valley entrepreneurs default to web or mobile apps instead of computational biotech.
- On advertising, he jokes that it usually works best hidden but sometimes works when completely transparent. He finds opaque games tiring, such as the VC adage "If you want money, ask for advice. If you want advice, ask for money," and finds it refreshing when someone says "I really just want money."

chunks.heading: FDA bottleneck as a future opportunity, and Internet vs. biotech startup friction
chunks.text:
- Peter calls it "very odd" that the FDA is a bottleneck on global drug development. There has to be a tipping point beyond which the U.S. no longer dictates what drugs are developed worldwide, and the U.S. may then have to compete with China on how quickly drugs get developed, a potentially huge paradigm shift.
- He argues things look bad now but the future may be promising. SpaceX was heavily regulated at first but persevered, and aerospace regulations have eased in the last decade. "The sheer unfriendliness of the baseline could be a great opportunity."
- On startup friction, he contrasts Internet businesses, where you can be up and running while doing hardly anything, with biotech's physical setup costs.
- His PayPal example: the biggest interface with reality was that, on Max's orders, people had to assemble their own desks. Luke Nosek found even that too much and hired a service called Delegate Everything, which sent an elderly woman handyperson to assemble his desk so he could do more work on the computer.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel's CS183 Class 17 lecture on artificial intelligence. He frames AI as an enormous and strange space, debates Luddite versus Ricardo views of technology, and argues AI beats consensus biotech on engineering freedom, regulation and contrarian positioning. He also backs human-computer augmentation as a practical path.

chunks.heading: Why AI is a huge, strange space, and why the timing and opportunity favor it
chunks.text:
- Peter argues the range of possible AI is far larger than the range of human or even alien intelligence. Evolution can't produce "supersonic birds with titanium wings," but AI is built, not evolved, so it isn't limited by gradual natural selection.
- Peter's spectrum example: a mouse, a moron, and Einstein. People assume AI lands just past Einstein, but he sees no a priori reason the scale can't go much higher. It "might be easier for a mouse to understand the relativity than it is for us to actually understand how an AI supercomputer thinks."
- A future with AI would be unlike any other future. Biotech yields humans who function better but are still recognizably human. A retrofuture resurrects old ideas. AI could be radically different and strange.
- He draws a theological parallel: God may have been to the Middle Ages what AI will become to us. Will it be all-powerful, will it love us? Incomprehensible questions, but still worth asking.

chunks.heading: Luddite vs. Ricardo: does AI replace or complement people?
chunks.text:
- The history of technology is largely a history of technology displacing people (plow, printing press, cotton gin). Peter sees two paradigms.
- The Luddite paradigm: machines are bad, destroy them before they destroy you.
- The Ricardo paradigm: technology is fundamentally good. Per Ricardo's gains from trade, displaced people are freed up to do more. If China makes cheaper cars, buying them is good for the US; Detroit workers lose jobs but can be retrained, and total value rises.
- Applied to AI: if humans and computers are good at very different things, they trade and AI is a complement, not a substitute.
- Caveat: this depends on the relative magnitude of advantage. If AI is dramatically better ("3000x what humans can do across everything"), it may make no sense for it to trade with us. "Humans, after all, don't trade with monkeys or mice." In extreme cases there is something to the Luddite view.
- Peter reframes this as control. Most technology gives people more control over the world with no cliff. AI may hit an inflection point where it goes superhuman and humans lose control altogether. He jokes of a cloud supercomputer that "calls itself Zeus and throws down lightning bolts at people."
- Peter also notes the popular concern has shifted from intelligent computers to empathetic ones: a computer that doesn't find human eye movement emotionally provocative is seen as inferior, "like Vulcans."

chunks.heading: Is it too early for AI? Timing risk and the consensus trap
chunks.text:
- Peter says timing matters a lot here, and it may still be too early. Futures fail often: 1970s supersonic airplanes (too noisy), 1990s handheld iPad-like devices, 1999 smartphones. Siri is "probably still a bit too early today." Whether the timing is right is hard to know ex ante.
- The conventional view is to pick biotech 2.0 over AI, since bioinformatics is being applied to humans sooner while AI applications are further out. Peter notes "the conventional view isn't always right."
- At a "5 Top VCs, 10 Tech Trends" event in Santa Clara, his prediction that biology would become an information science got 100% agreement from the audience, with no dissenter. His reaction: "Perhaps that should make us nervous. Unanimity in crowds can be very disconcerting."
- The prediction that all cars would go electric drew 92% disagreement. Peter's quip: there are many reasons to be bearish on electric cars, "but now there is one less."
- On whether Moore's law would continue to accelerate, the audience split 50-50. Peter's point: if computing can more than double every 18 months, something like AI would seem to arrive within a few years, yet most people thought AI was much further off than biotech.

chunks.heading: Hidden limits: exponential hope vs. asymptotic reality
chunks.text:
- Peter's test for comparing fields is whether there are serious, possibly hidden, limits in each.
- Biotech example: telomerase lets cells split without bound, which stops aging, but unbounded splitting looks like cancer. Aging and cancer may cancel each other out: fix one problem and you create another. It's unclear whether such barriers exist or can be overcome.
- AI's leading candidate for an invisible barrier is code complexity. Past a point there may be so much code that no one knows what's going on and debugging becomes impossible. He suggests something like this happened to Microsoft Windows over decades: "It used to be elegant."
- The fundamental tension he names: "exponential hope versus asymptotic reality." The question is whether and when the asymptote sets in.
- He also raises the track-record worry: after a long history of small advances (e.g. the War on Cancer, 40 years in), things may just be harder than people think. People in the 1980s thought AI was around the corner. He asks how we know AI isn't the same, and likens it to waiting for luggage at the airport, where the probability of arrival rises each minute until it eventually drops.

chunks.heading: Three reasons AI beats biotech 2.0
chunks.text:
Peter gives three distinct advantages to focusing on AI:

1. **Engineering freedom.** Biology is a recipe, not a blueprint: "add food and water and bake for 9 months." If the cake gets messed up, the cookbook rarely tells you how to fix it. AI is much more of a true blueprint, less dependent on a precise sequence of steps, so you can build from scratch in different ways.
2. **Regulatory freedom.** Biotech is heavily regulated: about 10 years and $1.3 billion to develop a new drug, with 4,000 people at the FDA and many precautionary principles. AI is an unregulated frontier. You can launch as fast as you can build software, it may cost $1 million or a few million rather than $1 billion, and you can work from your basement. Synthesizing Ebola or smallpox there would get you in trouble; hacking on AI would not. Maybe the legislature "simply has no mind for AI-kind of things."
3. **Underexplored and contrarian.** On a 2x2 of underexplored vs. heavily explored and consensus vs. contrarian, biotech 2.0 sits in the heavily explored, consensus quadrant, "which, of course, is the worst quadrant." AI is underexplored and contrarian. After decades of talk without delivery, many people have turned pessimistic and moved on, which could be very good for those who do focus on it.

- Peter adds a joke that PayPal, at Luke Nosek's urging, offered cryogenics in its employee benefits ($50k neuro, $120k full body), but the sales rep couldn't get a dot matrix printer to print the policies. Maybe the way to make biotech work is to push harder on AI.

chunks.heading: Intelligence augmentation: Palantir and the PayPal fraud model
chunks.text:
- Peter frames Palantir's approach as intelligence augmentation, not strong AI, falling squarely within the Ricardo gains-from-trade paradigm. The key is the right balance between human and computer.
- His view on counter-terrorism: the best way to stop terrorists isn't regression analysis on past behavior to predict the next move. A more game-theoretic approach is better.
- His PayPal parallel on fraud: humans couldn't solve it because there were millions of transactions; computers couldn't solve it because the fraud patterns kept changing. Having the computer do the heavy computation and humans do the final analysis, "while a weaker form of AI, turns out to be optimal in these cases."
- He describes the three companies in the room as taking different routes: Vicarious (brain-inspired principles, starting with a vision system, then general intelligence), Prior Knowledge (Bayesian methods for patterns and causation in large datasets, deliberately unlike human reasoning), and Palantir (augmentation).

chunks.heading: Peter's pressure-test questions for AI founders
chunks.text:
In the guest conversation, only these lines are Peter's. The questions he asks show what he looks for in an AI startup:

- **Timing:** "Why is *now* the time to be doing strong AI as opposed to 10-15 years from now?"
- **Approach:** why is brain emulation (or, for Bob, augmentation instead of strong AI) the right approach?
- **Time horizon:** being 5-7 years from the goal is one thing; 15-20 years or beyond is quite another.
- **Recruiting:** AI differs from the web and mobile apps most engineers gravitate toward, so how do you hire?
- **Secrecy and competition:** "Are there other people who are working on this too? If so, how many, and if not, how do you know?" He adds that it's a bad idea to open a pizza restaurant in Palo Alto even if you're first, because others will come, so what is the strategy for avoiding competition?
- **Danger:** how dangerous is the technology?
- **Science project risk:** is the team developing technology looking for a problem, with no applications yet?
- **Track record:** how do you know AI isn't another long history of undelivered expectations?
- On convincing people to accept human-computer collaboration over 100% human or 100% computer, which people usually frame as antagonistic, he asks Bob how to persuade academics and Google-type researchers that Palantir's paradigm is better.

chunks.heading: Long-failed ventures and the pivot to the New World
chunks.text:
- Peter's example of a long-lived failure: Xanadu, which tried from 1963 to 1992 to connect all the world's computers. It ran out of money and died, and Netscape arrived the very next year and ushered in the Internet.
- He tells the "probably apocryphal" Columbus story: everyone thought the world was much smaller than it was and they were heading to China. When the crew wanted to turn back, Columbus convinced them to postpone mutiny for three more days, and they landed on a new continent.
- The lesson he draws is about persistence and timing under uncertainty: sometimes the breakthrough lands just after a long stretch of seeming failure, but, as with futures that arrived too early, it's hard to know in advance which case you're in.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Thiel draws on PayPal's eccentric founders, mythology and René Girard's scapegoat theory to argue founders are extreme insiders and outsiders at once, worshipped before they are sacrificed. He shows how to survive: keep the founding moment alive through continued innovation, structure power carefully, and use co-founders to avoid a single scapegoat.

chunks.heading: Founders as extreme insiders and outsiders
chunks.text:
- Peter argues founders are not average. He asks whether the founder distribution is a fat-tailed one, then pushes further: perhaps it is an inverted normal distribution, with both tails extremely fat.
- Founders may be complex combinations of extreme insider and extreme outsider at once. He says ideological narratives isolate and reinforce just one side, but "the truth about founders comes from both sides."
- PayPal's six-person founding team as evidence: four were born outside the United States, five were 23 or younger, and four built bombs in high school (Max in the Soviet Union, Yu Pan in China).
- Other PayPal oddities: Russ escaped a trailer park for the one math and science magnet school in Illinois. Max came to the U.S. weeks after the Soviet Union collapsed, "a citizen of no country," so the team decided he couldn't leave the country. Ken took a 66% pay cut to join PayPal instead of going into investment banking.
- Applied examples: Jack Dorsey went from nose ring and unkempt hair (outsider) to Prada suits (insider). Sean Parker had no college, underground hacking, Napster, a Forbes 400 cover, and extreme swings between insider and outsider.

chunks.heading: Four explanations for the founder distribution
chunks.text:
Peter lists four explanations for why founders look so extreme:
1. Natural: founders really are different (Max Levchin really has 3 kidneys).
2. Nurtured: cultural feedback makes them different.
3. Self-created: founders exaggerate their own traits.
4. Other-created: everyone else exaggerates them.

- The first two assume the distribution is real. The last two treat it as possibly fictional.
- He says generally all four apply to some extent and are hard to disaggregate. They feed each other: people start different, get nurtured, learn to exaggerate, others exaggerate in turn, and the cycle repeats.
- Examples of cultivated or mythologized personas: Richard Branson's lion-like hair, Lady Gaga's "Born This Way," and Howard Hughes, who pretended to be crazy on the theory that no one would take the time to stop or compete with a crazy person. Hughes also claimed a December 25th, 1905 birthday.

chunks.heading: Mythology and the archaic sacrificial cycle
chunks.text:
- Classical myth overlaps with the inverted bell curve: "There are monsters and there are gods. And very often they are one and the same."
- Founding myths follow the pattern. Oedipus was both king and abandoned foreigner. Achilles was perfect except where flawed. Romulus and Remus were orphans raised by wolves who became founders and lawmakers, and Romulus killed his brother over a boundary line.
- In archaic cultures there were no rules and a war of all against all. Peter says the social contract story never happened. The common resolution was to polarize all hostility onto one person (a scapegoat), then sacrifice him, restoring peace. The cycle repeated.
- The scapegoat is omnimalevolent (peace followed his death, so he must have been bad) or omnibenevolent (he died so others could live), probably both. Cultures that ritualized the process lasted longer.
- Finding the victim: Gaelic Scots baked a cake with one piece blackened with charcoal. The Gauls ran a footrace to the battlefield and sacrificed the slowest.
- The perfect scapegoat is both an extreme outsider (so the crowd doesn't see itself in him) and an extreme insider (so he can plausibly be blamed for the community's strife).

chunks.heading: Monarchy, tragedy and revolution
chunks.text:
- Peter's working theory is that monarchy originated from scapegoats worshipped before being killed. "Every king was a living god. Every god was a murdered king." The scapegoat simply figured out how to delay his execution.
- Examples: the Aztecs crowned a quasi-god king for a period, then sacrificed him. Pharaohs may have started as stoned scapegoats, with pyramids as the piles of stones. A Zulu king was deposed and killed once white hair and wrinkles showed, which is why Zulu kings wanted hair coloring lotion on first contact with the British.
- Aristotle's view as he presents it: tragedy reduced ordinary people's anger toward successful people by showing that even the greatest have tragic flaws, transforming envy and anger into pity.
- Julius Caesar was a classic insider/outsider, and later Roman emperors had to be a Caesar. Marie Antoinette was an insider turned foreigner. He says all great revolutions are a rapid shift from insider to outsider.
- Robespierre argued the king should not get a trial: a trial meant the king might be innocent, which meant the people might be guilty, which was unthinkable.

chunks.heading: The sacrificial dynamic in modern culture and politics
chunks.text:
- The 12-person jury has the same structure: the unlucky 13th is the scapegoat. Peter notes it is never a jury of your peers, since murderers are not judged by 12 murderers.
- Celebrities are anointed kings (King of Rock, King of Pop, Princess of Pop), then torn down. Britney Spears drove $100 million of a $400 million/year paparazzi industry, with 1,000 to 2,000 people chasing her. After death, stars are resurrected as god-kings, e.g. the Forever 27 club.
- Alexander the Great died at 32 after drinking marathons, yet lives on as a conqueror.
- Politics: each side obsesses over the other's scapegoat, when the truth is "some strange combination of both." Lincoln was an extreme outsider turned insider, assassinated with "Sic semper tyrannis." Kennedy was one of the richest presidents (about $1 billion in today's money) with a bootlegger father.
- Lincoln's 1837 Lyceum Address warned that "Towering genius disdains a beaten path" and that ambitious people won't be satisfied maintaining an edifice built by others. Peter's takeaway: "we have to be really careful because such people might exist."

chunks.heading: Tech founders as scapegoats, and the odds
chunks.text:
- Bill Gates was treated like a god in the '90s, then ganged up on after Larry Ellison, Scott McNealy and other CEOs started a "We Hate Gates" club and stirred up the DOJ. From Gates's view he was on a winning arc and the haters were envious. Peter says when it turns, it turns fast, and falls are so big it's hard to recover.
- Howard Hughes became the wealthiest person in the U.S. by 45 across movies and aviation, then after the 1946 crash became addicted to painkillers and holed up for 30 years. Steve Jobs (dropout, LSD, phreaking, eccentric diets) was kicked out of Apple and replaced by John Sculley.
- Marc Andreessen sat on a throne-like chair on Time's February 1996 cover, was vilified after Netscape, then recovered. Mary Meeker, the "Queen of the Net," fell after the bubble and returned as a venture capitalist.
- Peter's numbers: 44 American presidents, four (9%) assassinated in office, four more nearly killed. If you want the crown, risk comes with it, and mistakes are hard to spot at the time.

chunks.heading: How founders can avoid becoming the victim
chunks.text:
- Startups are structured as monarchy, "more tyrant than mob because it should be." Voting on new things yields lowest-common-denominator results. But pure dictatorship fails because you can't attract people. The best arrangement is a king-like founder who can do more than a democratic ruler but is far from all-powerful.
- 0 to 1 is monarchy; 1 to n is democracy. He frames "the 99% vs. the 1%" as the modern scapegoating mechanism, since the victim must be a single whole person.
- Extend the founding moment. Founding lasts as long as technological innovation continues, so delay the shift to ossified, process-based normality. Peter says this needs "a healthy amount of paranoia": treat every board meeting as a trial, where the board is at best a jury and at worst a mob. Most fatal wounds come from internal, not external, conflict.
- Minimize the title risk. Augustus never called himself king, only "first among equals."
- PayPal, October 2000: burn rate $10 million/month, about 4.5 months of runway. Peter returned as interim CEO after a 6-7 month search. When the board wanted a COO before the IPO (code for the #1 replacement candidate), he got David Sacks in, "perceived to be crazier than I was." He calls this a powerful insurance policy against being deposed.
- Co-founders (Hewlett and Packard, Moore and Noyce, Page and Brin) get in less trouble because a mob board cannot easily isolate a single scapegoat.
- The return of the founder: Apple went through 12 years (1985 to 1997) of conventional CEOs who couldn't build anything new, then changed course under Jobs from 1997 to 2011. Jobs survived the options backdating scandal partly because he was terminally ill, and there is less power in scapegoating someone whose life is waning. "Resurrections are possible. But you can only be resurrected after you die."
- Peter closes by suggesting society should focus more on people who don't play by the rules, since they may be the most important.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Final CS183 class with futurist guests debating who builds the future and whether progress is inevitable. Thiel's own contributions: timing matters, and his closing call to treat your life as a singular event, find the many remaining secrets, and refuse the conventional path.

chunks.heading: Technology stagnation, definite optimism, and why the future must be built
chunks.text:
- Peter frames the final class around "going from 0 to 1": creating new technology, and radically better technology building toward a singularity.
- He applies the same framework to individual lives: "There is a mini singularity whenever you start a company or make a key life decision. In a very real sense, the life of every person is a singularity."
- The default advice runs the other way. People are told to play it safe and be conventional, and "the future, we are told, is just probabilities and statistics. *You* are a statistic."
- Peter calls that "selling yourself short." Statistical processes, the law of large numbers and globalization are "timeless, probabilistic, and maybe random," but technology and a life are "a story of one-time events."

chunks.heading: The case against waiting for the singularity
chunks.text:
- Peter poses the Kurzweil-style objection to the class: if progress follows an exponential curve that is "a law of nature," the singularity happens regardless of what individuals do, so one could "sit back, grab some popcorn, and enjoy the show."
- He puts the question to the panel as a real challenge ("Is there anything wrong with that argument?") rather than endorsing the passive view.
- His closing remarks give his own answer: "If we don't take charge and usher in the future, if you don't take charge of your life, there is the sense that no one else will."
- He tells students: "Don't be deterred by notions of luck, impossibility, or futility. Use your power to shape your own life and go and do new things."

chunks.heading: Secrets: white spaces on the map of knowledge
chunks.text:
- Peter's closing claim: singular events are hard to teach or generalize about, but "the big secret is that there are many secrets left to uncover."
- He describes "many large white spaces on the map of human knowledge" that anyone can go discover.
- His instruction: "Get out there and fill in the blank spaces. Every single moment is a possibility to go to these new places and explore them."
- The advice is to "go find a frontier and go for it" and to choose to do something important and different, not follow the well-trodden path.

chunks.heading: Timing: not paddling too far ahead of the wave
chunks.text:
- Peter treats timing as decisive for technology that is still speculative. If something is only barely plausible science fiction, it may not make sense to work on it yet.
- His example: a Chinese man who tried to launch a rocket into space in the 11th century. "No one was or should have been working on supersonic flight in the Middle Ages. That would be paddling way too far in advance of the wave."
- He proposes a middle path: a roughly 20-year goal with milestones along the way.
- He flags the tradeoff himself: too many milestones make the achievability of the end goal speculative.
- Even with an uncertain date for radical technology, he says the timing "does make a great deal of difference."

chunks.heading: Who builds the future: Peter's framing of the options
chunks.text:
- Peter summarizes the panel's three answers to who forges the technological future: a top-down/bottom-up combination, social opinion molders, and small tribes.
- He chooses to "run with some version of" the tribe theory (a small cabal of tech people driving change) and steers the discussion from there.
- He asks whether people who think about radical technology get dismissed as crazy, and presses the panel on why, which sets up the discussion of cultural resistance to long-term technological thinking.

chunks.heading: Why now is the moment to start
chunks.text:
- Peter says there is "perhaps no specific time that is necessarily right to start your company or start your life," but "some times and some moments seem more auspicious than others. Now is such a moment."
- The close ties the course together: new technology, new companies and individual life choices are all singular, one-time acts, and the obvious conventional answer for what to do with your own singularity is the wrong one.
